filterSecondaryServiceNames() is extracted as a pure function so the
primary/secondary decision itself is unit-tested, since the reflection-
heavy adapter construction around it isn't (no androidTest directory
in this project).

Retry the Native AA wake poke continuously and try HFP before HSP

Cross-referencing two independent open-source wireless Android Auto
implementations (nisargjhaveri/WirelessAndroidAutoDongle,
mossyhub/openautolink) for how they handle the same "wake the phone
up" problem surfaced two gaps versus HUR's own poke logic:

- Both reference implementations retry the wake connection
  continuously (15-20s intervals) for as long as the session is up.
  triggerPoke() made one pass through the device list and stopped.
  Every log collected on issue #706 shows the poke succeeding at the
  socket level but Android Auto never reacting - a continuous retry
  directly increases the odds of landing in whatever timing window
  makes the phone actually respond, instead of gambling on one shot.
  manualPoke() stays one-shot since it's an explicit user action.

- openautolink's _connect_device() tries HFP-AG (0000111f-...) first,
  falling back to HSP-AG (00001112-...). HUR's poke only tried the
  latter, stored in a constant misleadingly named A2DP_SOURCE_UUID -
  its actual value is HSP-AG, not A2DP Source (real assigned number
  0000110a-...), confirmed against both reference projects' own
  constants. Renamed for clarity and added the HFP fallback pair via
  a shared pokeDevice() helper used by both triggerPoke() and
  manualPoke().

triggerPoke()'s retry loop needs no separate give-up cap: stop()
already cancels pokeJob, and the loop's own
`while (isRunning && isActive && !handshakeInFlight)` ends it the
moment a real handshake starts or another session takes over.

Log the local Bluetooth radio's name instead of its always-masked address

The "primary radio [...]" / "local radio [...]" log lines introduced
for dual-radio head units used adapter.address, which is always the
fixed placeholder "02:00:00:00:00:00" for a non-privileged app (the
same masking that broke the secondary-radio detection itself). That
made the log lines useless for telling radios apart.

adapter.name isn't masked - BluetoothHelper.getAdapterDescription()
already relies on it successfully for the Settings picker. Confirmed
on-device: logs now show the real name (e.g. "Navegadortz2") instead
of the masked address, for both the primary listener and secondary
ones.

Add manual service-name override for dual-radio Bluetooth detection

listBluetoothServices() enumerates secondary radios via
ServiceManager.listServices(), filtered to names containing
"bluetooth" - but some ROMs may block that reflection call entirely,
or name the service something that doesn't match. On a device like
that, the automatic secondary-radio detection would never find a real
second radio no matter how correct the matching logic is.

The local radio's real MAC can't help here even if a user reads it
off Android's own Settings app: BluetoothAdapter.getAddress() and
Settings.Secure.bluetooth_address are both gated behind the same
system-only LOCAL_MAC_ADDRESS permission, and there's no API that
goes from a MAC string to a specific local BluetoothAdapter instance
regardless. Service name is the only identity HUR can actually act on
(the existing "Bluetooth Adapter" picker already selects primary this
way), so the fallback follows that: a manual text field where the
user supplies the exact system service name for a radio they've
found some other way (adb shell service list, an OEM engineering
menu), unioned into the discovered set before the existing
primary/secondary split runs.

Verified on-device: a bogus service name and the one real non-adapter
"bluetooth"-named service on our control hardware
(IBluetoothAudioProviderFactory, an audio HAL) both fail to resolve
and are logged and ignored cleanly, matching how the automatic path
already handles them. Entering the current primary's own service name
is correctly deduped with no resolution attempt. Blank (default) is a
strict no-op; a full connection still completes normally throughout.

Condense the HSP/HFP UUID comments into one block

The two separate multi-line comments obstructed the view between the
declarations. Merged into a single explanation above both, with a
short inline note per constant.

Accept the AIDL interface descriptor in the manual secondary-radio field

A user testing the dual-radio fix on issue #706 pasted the bracketed
interface descriptor from `adb shell service list` (e.g.
com.qf.btsdk.IBTBinderPool) into the manual override field instead of the
actual service name before the colon (btBinderPool) - the two look similar
in that output and the descriptor is the more distinctive-looking of the
pair. Resolve either form: try the input as a literal service name first,
then fall back to a reverse lookup by interface descriptor across all
registered services (safe: IBinder.getInterfaceDescriptor() is a read-only
query, unlike actually invoking methods on a mismatched proxy).

Cancel the in-flight wake poke as soon as a real handshake starts

pokeDevice() holds an HFP/HSP profile connection open for up to 20s to
wake the phone, but once a real AA_UUID connection lands, that poke has
already done its job - continuing to hold it open means two RFCOMM
channels compete for the same physical radio right as the WifiStartRequest
needs to land cleanly. triggerPoke()'s loop already stops starting *new*
pokes once a handshake is in flight, but nothing cancelled an
already-running one. Part of narrowing down andreknieriem/open-headunit#706's
"WifiStartRequest sent, no response ever" symptom on a specific
dual-radio unit, per the phone-side Gearhead log finally confirming the
phone's own RFCOMM read never receives a single byte before its own
12s timeout - reducing radio contention during that window is one of two
targeted, low-risk mitigations for it.

Add a short delay before sending WifiStartRequest over Bluetooth

Some Bluetooth stacks report the RFCOMM socket "connected" slightly
before the underlying channel is actually ready to carry data - a real,
previously-documented class of issue (the Linux kernel's own "Move
pending packets from RFCOMM socket to TTY" fix addressed the same
symptom on the HFP profile: data written immediately after accept can be
silently dropped). Confirmed via a phone-side Gearhead log on #706: HUR
sends WifiStartRequest ~6ms after accept(), but the phone's own RFCOMM
read never sees a single byte before its ~12s first-message timeout
fires, every time. A 300ms delay costs nothing against either side's
timeout budget (phone ~12s, HUR's own watchdog 15s) but gives a flaky
chip a moment to settle before the message that matters most.

Soften the manual secondary-radio override's help text

Set clearer expectations rather than removing the feature: the reflection
trick this depends on requires BluetoothAdapter to have a constructor
taking a lone IBluetoothManager, which some head units' customized
Bluetooth stacks don't provide - no service name typed in here can fix
that. Confirmed on one real device (#706): the same NoSuchMethodException
fires regardless of which service is targeted. Still worth keeping for
hardware where the only problem is a second radio's service name not
being auto-discovered - that's a genuinely different, unrelated failure
mode this can still help with.

Fix H.264 stream misdetected as HEVC on decoder restart (issue #749)

detectCodecType()'s NAL-type heuristic can misclassify an ordinary H.264
slice byte as an HEVC VPS/SPS/PPS NAL (nal_unit_type=1/nal_ref_idc=2 ->
byte 0x41 -> 0x41 >> 1 == 32). Since decode() re-ran this heuristic on
every decoder restart (not just the initial session setup) while stale
SPS/PPS were still cached, a single restart could permanently hijack an
otherwise-working H.264 session into repeatedly reconfiguring a broken
HEVC decoder with garbage codec-config data, producing audio with no
video until the app was closed.

Pin the codec type once a decoder has been started successfully so
restarts reuse it instead of re-detecting. Add a bounded restart
counter with a one-time codec fallback and a permanent-failure cutoff
so a genuinely broken hardware decoder can no longer loop forever.

Back up and restore all settings, not just some

The settings backup silently skipped several settings, so a restore came back
incomplete. Add the ones that were missing: the custom loading screen display
options, the wireless hotspot SSID and password, the static BSSID, the measured
touch surface fix, and toast visibility. The loading screen media itself is not
backed up because it lives in the app private folder and its path cannot be
restored on another install.

Keep the original Play Store package id, still display as Open Headunit

Revert only the applicationId to com.andrerinas.headunitrevived so the app stays
the same Play Store listing and existing users get a normal update. The display
name stays Open Headunit and the whole code package stays openheadunit, so the
applicationId now differs from the namespace, which is a supported setup (the
same idea as Hangouts still being com.google.talk). Also point the app shortcuts
at the restored applicationId so they keep resolving.

Fix AapVideo comparing settings.videoCodec against the wrong constant

settings.videoCodec only ever holds "Auto", "H.264", or "H.265" (see
the picker in SettingsFragment.kt), matching every other comparison
against it in the codebase (ServiceDiscoveryResponse.kt, AapControl.kt,
HeadUnitScreenConfig.kt). AapVideo instead compared it against
VideoDecoder.CodecType.H265.mimeType ("video/hevc"), which can never
match, so the HEVC branch was permanently dead code at all three call
sites:

- messageBuffer was always sized for H.264 (~2MB) even during a real
  HEVC session, risking reassembly overflow on large HEVC I-frames.
- checkKeyframe() always applied the H.264 NAL bitmask to real HEVC
  bytes, so a genuine HEVC IDR/VPS/SPS/PPS could never be recognized
  as a keyframe. Once waitingForKeyframe was set on an actual HEVC
  session, it could never clear, permanently freezing video until the
  connection was torn down and recreated.

Found while auditing VideoDecoder.kt/AapVideo.kt for other issues
related to the codec-misdetection bug fixed for issue #749.

Centralize H.265 settings-string comparisons on VideoDecoder.CodecType

settings.videoCodec comparisons against the literal "H.265" were
duplicated across AapVideo.kt, AapControl.kt, ServiceDiscoveryResponse.kt,
and HeadUnitScreenConfig.kt. Added CodecType.settingsValue as the single
source of truth for the settings-string form ("H.264"/"H.265"), distinct
from the existing mimeType ("video/avc"/"video/hevc") and displayName
("H.264/AVC"/"H.265/HEVC") fields, and switched all four call sites to
reference it instead of a bare string literal.

The Auto/H.265 `when` branch in ServiceDiscoveryResponse.kt and the
SettingsFragment.kt codec picker array are left as-is, since "Auto" has
no CodecType counterpart to centralize against.

Stop tearing down the decoder on transient input buffer overflow

Decoders with a small, fixed input buffer count (e.g. MediaTek's
OMX.MTK.VIDEO.DECODER.AVC, which also rejects raising
nBufferCountActual) periodically fall behind and fail
dequeueInputBuffer. Restarting the whole MediaCodec instance for
that was causing periodic blinking once the HEVC misdetect loop from
issue #749 was fixed and H.264 decoding actually ran long enough to
hit it. Drop the frame and request a keyframe instead; a genuinely
stuck decoder is still caught by the output thread's sync_stall
watchdog.

Also set KEY_FRAME_RATE alongside KEY_OPERATING_RATE when configuring
the decoder, since some vendor decoders reject the latter outright
and KEY_FRAME_RATE is the documented fallback for realtime priority.

Fix infinite HEVC-unavailable restart loop after codec fallback (issue #757)

The bounded codec-fallback safety net added for issue #749 could flip to a
codec type the device has zero decoders for (hw or sw), and start()'s
failure path never fed that back into the restart bookkeeping, so it kept
retrying the doomed codec on every incoming packet forever instead of
giving up. Check fallback-codec availability before flipping, and wire
start()/startBundledHevc() failures into scheduleRestart() so any decoder
start failure is bounded by the existing restart-then-give-up logic.

Throttle video recovery keyframe requests and add sync_stall backoff

Route VideoDecoder's input-buffer-overflow drops through AapVideo's
already-throttled markCorruptAndRequestRecovery() instead of firing an
independent, unthrottled focus-cycle recovery per drop. On decoders
with a small, fixed input-buffer count (MediaTek), that path could
recur every few seconds during normal playback and each one was a
separate visible blink (issue #755 follow-up).

Also add a cooldown/cap to the sync_stall watchdog in
outputThreadLoop(), mirroring the pattern already used by
AapProjectionActivity.maybeRecoverFromDisplayStall() for issue #650.
A decoder that renders intermittently but stalls under load isn't
caught by the existing "never rendered a frame" restart cap, so this
watchdog could otherwise tear the MediaCodec down indefinitely on
marginal hardware (issue #742).

Stop pokeDevice() from swallowing cancellation and firing a second connect

pokeDevice()'s catch (e: Exception) caught CancellationException too, so
cancelling pokeJob once a real handshake starts (handleHandshake) didn't
actually stop the poke - it just fell through to try the next UUID in the
HFP/HSP fallback list, firing another real blocking socket.connect() right
in the critical window before WifiStartRequest is sent. Rethrow
CancellationException instead so a cancelled poke stops immediately.

Bugfixes for 3.2.0

Stop the native join watchdog from tearing down live sessions

Two related fixes, confirmed live on-device:

1. WifiDirectManager's native join watchdog only checked isClientConnected
   (WifiP2pGroup.clientList) before recreating the group. Native/quiet-host
   joins happen out-of-band over Bluetooth rather than through P2P peer
   invitation, so clientList can stay empty for the entire lifetime of a
   fully working session - the watchdog was forcibly recreating live,
   working connections roughly every 60 seconds. Added a session-connected
   provider (wired from AapService's commManager.isConnected) that the
   watchdog, recoverNativeGroup(), and armNativeJoinWatchdog() all check
   before tearing anything down.

2. NativeAaHandshakeManager.triggerPoke() unconditionally cancelled and
   restarted its poke job on every call. WifiDirectManager can redeliver
   identical credentials repeatedly (e.g. WIFI_P2P_CONNECTION_CHANGED_ACTION
   re-firing with no real state change), which was cancelling the poke
   before it ever finished. Now skips the restart when the credentials are
   unchanged and a poke is already running.

Stop the app's own HFP poke from self-triggering a BT auto-start re-arm

NativeAaHandshakeManager's wake-up poke opens an RFCOMM socket to the
phone's HFP/HSP service record, which itself generates an OS-level
ACTION_ACL_CONNECTED broadcast. AutoStartReceiver listens for that same
broadcast, and AapService's ACTION_BT_AUTO_START handler only checked
isActive() before force-reinitializing WiFi mode - which can read false
for a brief window right as a new poke starts (stale state from the
previous handshake cycle's closeAaListeners(), or the gap before
start() reruns), well before a real handshake exchange. That let the
receiver's own re-arm tear down and recreate the P2P group in the
middle of an attempt already in flight.

Confirmed via zd3sf's retest logs on #760 (connects ~1/5 times, slow)
and reproduced live: the guard now also checks a new
isAttemptInFlight() (poke-in-flight OR handshake-in-flight), closing
the gap. Verified on-device across repeated BT reconnect cycles - the
re-arm now only fires when the manager is genuinely idle, never while
a poke/handshake is running.

Sync auto-start-on-boot/USB to device-protected storage when disabled

AutoStartFragment.onResume() force-disables auto-start-on-boot and
auto-start-on-usb when the overlay permission isn't granted, but was
missing the matching syncXToDeviceStorage() calls that
auto-start-on-screen-on already had right next to them. That left the
device-protected copy BootCompleteReceiver actually reads at boot
stale at true, so the app kept auto-starting on boot even though the
UI toggle correctly showed disabled.

Verified on-device: after enabling auto-start-on-boot, revoking the
overlay permission, and reopening the Auto-Start screen, both the
regular and device-protected prefs now read false (previously only the
regular copy did). Confirmed with a real reboot too - no auto-start
with the setting off, and auto-start still works normally after
re-granting the permission and re-enabling it.

Wait for the WiFi session before releasing Bluetooth after handoff

handleHandshake() released the Bluetooth link on a flat delay(3000) after
delivering the WifiInfoResponse (Type 3). That is a race, not a grace
period: the phone still has to associate, run WPS and get a DHCP lease,
and it takes however long it takes.

zd3sf's logs on #760 show the whole progression on one phone/head unit:

  3.1.1   never closed Bluetooth ("Maintaining Bluetooth session...").
          The phone took 21s to associate and connected fine.
  beta4   closed at T+3.0s. The TCP session landed at T+2.89s - it won
          the race by 110ms.
  3.2.0   closed at T+3.0s and lost. From the failing log:

            19:32:12.098  delivered Protobuf TYPE 3
            19:32:12.828  WifiDirectManager: Connected. Requesting info...
            19:32:15.098  Handshake session ending, releasing Bluetooth
            19:32:15.098  AA Server socket closed after successful handoff
            19:32:15.268  Client disconnected from P2P group

          The phone joined 0.73s after Type 3 and left 0.17s after we
          dropped Bluetooth, never having got an IP. On the phone that
          is "stuck on Obtaining IP address", which is exactly what was
          reported.

3.2.0 loses the race where beta4 won it because it puts far more traffic
on the same radio: the wake poke now holds an HFP/HSP RFCOMM socket for
15s, retries on a loop, and runs an HFP responder alongside.

Replace the timer with awaitWifiHandoff(), which polls CommManager until
the session is Connecting/Connected or 45s elapse. On success, close as
before - the reconnect-storm guard closeAaListeners() exists for is still
wanted. On timeout there is no session for a reconnect to collide with,
so keep the AA listener open (start() early-returns while isRunning, so
closing here would strand the manager until AapService restarted it) and
restart the wake poke, which handleHandshake() had cancelled.

Also stop the poke from firing into that window. AapService re-invokes
triggerPoke() on every credential re-delivery, and the phone joining the
group is itself a P2P connection change, hence a re-delivery - which is
why the failing log has a real socket.connect() at 19:32:14.868, 0.4s
before the phone gave up. isHandoffSettling() now gates triggerPoke(),
the retry loop and isAttemptInFlight().

The timing rules go in a pure NativeHandoffPolicy with unit tests, per
the repo's convention for anything decidable without Android.

Not compiled or unit-tested: this checkout has no JDK or Android SDK.

Keep the native quiet host quiet while the phone is joining

Three ways the group could be disturbed between handing the phone its
credentials and the phone finishing its DHCP exchange (#760).

Discovery. When a client left the group we restarted a 10s discoverPeers()
loop. On the Native AA path that is wrong twice over: we run a quiet host
there and the phone finds us by SSID from the credentials we sent it over
Bluetooth, never by discovery - and discoverPeers() takes the group owner
off-channel. In the failing log the loop starts the instant the phone
drops mid-DHCP, and from then on every retry is stuck at "Obtaining IP
address" with no way to complete. Gate it on the mode.

Join watchdog. Its deferral hung off isHandshakeInFlight(), which goes
false the moment Type 3 is written - so it could fire while the phone was
still associating and hand it a freshly recreated SSID it could no longer
join. Report settling as in-flight too.

BT auto-start re-arm. A successful handoff closes the AA listeners, so
isActive() reads false for the entire life of a working session. Any
later ACL_CONNECTED - the phone's own profiles reconnecting, or one of
our pokes - would then force initWifiMode(force = true) and tear down a
session that was projecting fine. Check the connection state too.

Stop the setup wizard from breaking the display, and make DPI and resolution consistent

Some head units ended up stuck on a black Android Auto screen (audio still
working) after running the new setup wizard. The wizard was overwriting a
display config that already worked, and it forced SurfaceView on devices where
SurfaceView cannot be observed for stalls, so there was no way to recover.

Wizard:
- Do not overwrite view mode, codec, resolution or orientation for users who
  already ran the app (upgraders keep their working config). Fresh installs
  still get the recommendation.
- Fresh installs start on TextureView instead of SurfaceView on 5.0-8.1 with
  HEVC. TextureView failures are observable, so the existing stall watchdog can
  escalate to SurfaceView on its own if needed.
- After the wizard changes the renderer, the first projection shows a small
  'Do you see the screen?' bar with a Switch renderer action that rotates the
  backend live. It is also offered when the phone streams video but nothing is
  drawn, and when the stall watchdog escalates to SurfaceView, so a blank
  renderer that cannot be detected in software is no longer a dead end.

DPI:
- The recommended DPI is now derived from the resolution Android Auto actually
  draws (the panel-capped resolution), not the raw panel pixels, so downscaled
  panels are no longer over-reported.
- The magic 1.2 multiplier is now a named, documented legibility factor set to
  1.1.

Resolution:
- Unify the three different 'what fits the panel' rules (the too-high warning,
  the runtime cap and the recommendation) into a single panelCeiling source of
  truth, so the warning, the cap and the DPI always agree.
- When a chosen resolution is above the panel the image is limited to what the
  panel supports (hard cap, unchanged), and the dialog now says so honestly
  instead of implying it will be used.
- The DPI screen and the wizard DPI step now warn, in red, when the chosen
  resolution is above the panel and the DPI is computed for the capped one.

Cache the hardware HEVC check since it scans the whole codec list and is now
used on UI paths. Translations updated for all locales.

fix: move mic timestamp inside encrypted payload (byte 4)

The mic audio timestamp was placed at byte 2 in the packet, which falls
within the plaintext header area (HEADER_SIZE=4). On Android 11+, the
receiver expects the timestamp to be inside the encrypted payload at
byte 4, after the 4-byte header. With the timestamp in the wrong
position, the phone cannot parse the mic audio data and mic input
fails silently.

Fix by placing the timestamp at byte 4 (inside the encrypted payload)
and adjusting the buffer size (+12 = 4 header + 8 timestamp + PCM) and
PCM data offset accordingly.

Tested on two Android devices (Android 11 and 12) — mic works with
only this protocol fix applied.

Bound the native handshake window so it cannot latch true

isSettling() is already a bounded, timestamped window precisely so a missed
reset can't leave the state stuck. The handshake state had no such bound: it
was a plain boolean that handleHandshake() cleared in its finally.

#706's logs show why that is not enough. On the reporter's ROCO K706 the
socket close that is supposed to unblock the wait for the phone's Type 2 does
not unblock it, so the coroutine never reaches its finally at all — three
"Handshake failed - No response from phone" lines and not one "BT Handshake
socket closed." Downstream, everything gated on that flag stopped:

  - no "Attempting active poke" lines for the rest of the capture
  - "Native AA join watchdog fired but a Bluetooth handshake is in flight —
    deferring recovery" at 13:10:27, 13:11:27, 13:12:27, and again at 13:26:27
    in a later export taken with Bluetooth disabled on the head unit

Add isHandshaking(startedAtMs, nowMs), sharing isSettling()'s window logic, so
the state expires on its own. 90 s covers the longest legitimate exchange (up
to 60 s waiting on P2P credentials plus the 15 s Type 2 wait) with slack.

Unwind the native handshake on timeout, and hold the poke link across it

Two fixes to handleHandshake() from the first time #706 has produced a clean,
time-aligned pair of head-unit and phone-side Gearhead logs.

Stop depending on socket.close() to unblock the read. The response wait was
bounded by a watchdog that closed the socket to interrupt readFully(), which
only works on stacks where close() actually does interrupt a pending read. The
reporter's does not, so the function never unwound: the handshake state stayed
set for the life of the process, the wake poke stopped retrying and the P2P
join watchdog deferred recovery forever. Run the blocking read in its own
coroutine and await it under withTimeoutOrNull instead, so this resumes on
schedule whether or not the read ever returns. The close is still attempted.
Paired with the timestamped window in the previous commit, the state now
expires even if a read thread is stuck for good.

Keep the wake poke's HFP/HSP link up during the exchange. It was cancelled on
entry, on the reasoning that a real AA_UUID connection means the poke has done
its job and is just competing for radio time. The phone disagrees — within
milliseconds of that close it logs:

  GH.BtConnectionTracker: profile connection removed
  GH.CurrentCarTracker:   current car bluetooth connection is lost / is gone
  ...WIRELESS_SETUP_CAR_BLUETOOTH_DISAPPEAR

and when its own 12 s first-message timer expires it refuses to retry:

  GH.WIRELESS.SETUP: WiFi Projection Protocol cannot start as HU is not present

Release it on the Type 3 path instead, where the phone already has what it
needs and where holding an RFCOMM channel on the radio it is about to
associate over is what #760 was about.

Neither change is claimed to fix #706's core symptom — the phone still never
acts on our first message, and our framing and message ids match a working
reference dongle. They stop the unit latching after the first failure, and
stop us telling the phone the car went away mid-exchange.

Say so when the phone answers the poke but never calls back

On the #706 reporter's ROCO K706 the head unit log looked healthy for weeks:
successful pokes every 15 s and nothing else. The phone-side Gearhead log from
2026-08-04 21:01 shows why nothing was happening:

  14 x  Creating rfcomm socket for device: 00:02:5B:D3:50:BC
        and uuid: 4de17a00-52cb-11e6-bdf4-0800200c9a66
  14 x  WPP_CONNECTION_FIRST_MESSAGE_TIMEOUT     (attempt counter 45 -> 58)
  13 x  WIRELESS_SETUP_SHARED_SERVICE_IGNORE_DIFFERENT_BLUETOOTH_DEVICE
   0 x  any rfcomm socket to 78:85:C8:E2:44:B5   (us)

00:02:5B:D3:50:BC is the head unit's own OEM Bluetooth module ("CAR8032"), a
separate chip the head unit's Android cannot see, identified from the reporter's
ZLink log (bttype:extra). It still advertises the Android Auto service record
after its OEM app stopped answering on it, so Gearhead binds its wireless setup
session to it and reconnects every 12 s forever, discarding each of our pokes
~40 ms after it lands:

  HU    20:59:09.782  Successfully poked HONOR Magic8 Lite via 0000111f...
  phone 20:59:09.019  WIRELESS_SETUP_SHARED_HFP_CONNECTING
  phone 20:59:09.062  WIRELESS_SETUP_SHARED_SERVICE_IGNORE_DIFFERENT_BLUETOOTH_DEVICE

Nothing in this app can fix that - the fix is one unpair on the phone - but the
silence cost this issue most of its ~70 comments. So count the pokes the phone
answers without ever opening the AA channel, and warn with the actual cause and
the actual remedy once it has ignored three of them.

The bound lives in NativeHandoffPolicy beside isSettling/isHandshaking, per the
repo's pure-policy-object convention, with unit tests. everAcceptedAaConnection
deliberately survives stop(), so a unit that has connected before is never
warned.

Stop serving handshakes once the phone has gone silent five times

Bounds a leak the previous commit made visible by fixing the wedge above it.

The wait for the phone's Type 2 is a blocking read on a background coroutine.
On a head unit where close() does not interrupt a pending read - #706's does
not - that coroutine never returns and its Dispatchers.IO thread is stranded
for the life of the process. reader.cancel() cannot help: a blocking JNI read
has no suspension point to cancel at.

That leak is not new. What changed is the rate. Before d47b351f the manager
wedged after about three failures and stopped trying, so it was self-limiting.
Now that handshakes unwind correctly the phone keeps reconnecting - measured at
12.889 s and 12.805 s apart on the reporter's unit - which is roughly 4.6
stranded threads a minute. Dispatchers.IO caps at 64, so a quarter of an hour
of retrying would exhaust it and other IO coroutines would queue behind dead
threads.

Since the threads cannot be reclaimed, the only lever is to stop creating them.
After five consecutive timed-out handshakes, incoming AA connections are
accepted and closed instead of served.

A hard stop rather than a growing delay, because this failure is not transient.
The reporter's HCI trace shows 15 complete sessions and not one data frame: if
the stack drops our write, the 200th attempt fails exactly like the first, and
each one costs a thread and radio time for nothing.

Only the timeout path counts, because it is the only one that strands anything.
A reader that returns clears the counter whatever type it carried, and so do
stop() and a manual poke - the last of those matters because it is the only
"try again" the UI offers, so a transient failure is never a dead end.

Log decode and display throughput so low-fps reports are readable

Issues #755 and #757 both came back as "it works but it is slow" after the
input-buffer-overflow rework in #766, and neither reporter's log can tell us
where the frames go.

In #757's log (HUR_Log_20260804_124008_147.txt) the phone delivers ~50
complete video frames per second for 31 seconds straight, with exactly one
"Input buffer feed failed (full)" and one sync_stall in the whole session. If
the codec were emitting 3fps while being fed 50, its input queue would
saturate within ~100ms and the overflow message would repeat constantly. It
does not, so everything upstream of releaseOutputBuffer kept up - yet the
reporter sees 3fps. #755's log is cleaner still: one overflow in 54 seconds,
no restarts, no stalls, and a user reporting 15-20fps.

Nothing output-side has ever been written to the log. VideoDecoder does count
rendered frames, but onFpsChanged feeds only the on-screen overlay, which is
gated on settings.showFpsCounter. So "the decoder is slow" and "the decoder
keeps up and the display consumer drops frames" are indistinguishable from a
HUR_Log_*.txt, and every hypothesis for either issue sits on that fork.

- VideoDecoder: count frames fed, dropped and rendered, and emit a summary
  every 5s from the output thread. That loop turns over at least every 10ms
  (dequeueOutputBuffer's timeout), so the tick still fires while nothing is
  rendering - the case worth reporting. The bundled FFmpeg path has no output
  thread, so it drives the tick from onSoftwareFramesRendered().
- VideoDecoder: reset frameCount/lastFpsLogTime in stop() alongside
  syntheticPtsUs. They straddled restarts, so the first FPS sample after every
  restart was averaged across the teardown and read near zero.
- VideoDecoder: log when the sync_stall watchdog fires but is suppressed by
  its cooldown or its 4-restart cap. Past the cap that branch took no action
  and printed nothing, so a permanently degraded decoder produced a clean log
   - which is exactly what both of these look like.
- TextureProjectionView: log displayed frames per interval from
  onSurfaceTextureUpdated(). Comparing that against the decoder's rendered
  count settles #757 directly, since the decoder reports what it hands to the
  surface and this reports what the compositor put on screen.
- TextureProjectionView: AppLog has no (tag, message) overload, so
  setVideoSize's second argument was consumed as a format parameter and the
  line only ever printed "TextureProjectionView".

No behaviour change.

Do not strand a P-frame lockout behind the keyframe request throttle

markCorruptAndRequestRecovery() does two things: it sets waitingForKeyframe,
which makes checkKeyframe() drop every frame until an I-frame arrives, and it
asks the phone for that I-frame. Only the second is throttled, to one request
per second, because AapTransport implements it as a video-focus loss/regain
cycle that is expensive and briefly visible.

So a corruption inside the throttle window arms the lockout with nothing
behind it to end it. Nothing else in the app requests a keyframe, so the
stream stays locked out until the phone happens to emit one on its own
cadence, and everything in between is discarded.

Measured in the two low-fps reports: 1.58s of video dropped from a single
transient input-buffer overflow in #757 (corruption 12:40:47.632, "Keyframe
received, resuming stream" 12:40:49.212) and 0.62s in #755. Before the
overflow rework in #766 an overflow restarted the decoder and never armed
this lockout at all, so this is new exposure rather than a pre-existing path.

Record the suppressed request instead of dropping it, and send it from
process() as soon as the throttle expires. Video packets arrive at roughly
the frame rate, so the deferred request lands within a frame or two of the
window closing without adding a scheduler to the transport thread. The
lockout itself is unchanged, so the anti-smearing property it was added for
still holds.

The pacing rules are extracted into VideoRecoveryPolicy, per the convention
of keeping Android-independent decisions in a pure object with unit tests.
The tests pin the throttle boundary and, most importantly, that a deferred
request can never overtake the throttle that deferred it - two requests
inside one window would reintroduce the visible focus cycling this throttle
exists to prevent.

Take the decoder's visible size from the crop rect, not the padded buffer

handleOutputFormatChange() read KEY_WIDTH/KEY_HEIGHT, which describe the
output buffer, not the picture. Vendors may pad that to their macroblock
alignment, and Intel's AVC component does:

  Output Format Changed: {height=736, ..., crop-bottom=719, ..., width=1280}
  Video dimensions changed via format: 1280x736
  Configuring decoder: OMX.Intel.VideoDecoder.AVC for 1280x736

A 720-line stream, reported as 736. Two things follow from taking it
verbatim. mWidth/mHeight feed onVideoDimensionsChanged(), so the projection
view scales the picture to an aspect ratio that is off by the 16 lines of
padding; and because start() reuses mWidth/mHeight, the next restart hands
MediaCodec the padded height as the configured input size.

The crop rectangle is the authoritative visible region, so prefer it. Its
bounds are inclusive, hence right - left + 1. Fall back to the buffer
geometry where a decoder omits the crop keys, and also where the crop it
reports is larger than the buffer, which would be self-inconsistent.

Seen on the Intel component; MediaTek's AVC reports height=720 with
slice-height=736 and is already correct either way, so this narrows the
divergence between the two rather than changing behaviour on decoders that
were reporting honestly.

Reject implausible crop rectangles instead of trusting any in-range one

The previous check only rejected a crop larger than the buffer, which lets a
decoder that fills the crop keys with placeholders through. All-zero keys are
the dangerous shape: crop-left=0/crop-right=0 is a legal 1-pixel extent, so it
passed, and 1x1 would then have been published as the video size and handed to
MediaCodec as the configured input size on the next restart. That turns a
cosmetic aspect-ratio bug into no picture at all, on hardware nobody here can
test.

Padding only ever rounds a dimension up to an alignment boundary, and nothing
aligns more coarsely than 64, so a crop that describes this stream sits just
below the buffer size. Accept it only in that band and fall back to the buffer
geometry otherwise, which is what the code did before this series.

Checked against both formats in hand - the Intel component's padded 736 for a
720-line stream, and MediaTek's already-honest 720 - plus absent keys, all-zero
keys, an oversized crop, a stale small crop, and 1080p padded to 1088.

NativeAA: fence handshake state behind socket ownership, honest TX logs

Four related lifecycle defects in NativeAaHandshakeManager, all rooted in
the same thing: a superseded handshake is not stopped by losing
ownership. Closing its socket only ends it on stacks where close()
interrupts a pending read, and #706's does not — its handshake coroutine
ran on to its own timeout long after a newer one had taken over, and
everything it wrote landed on the live session.

1. Retain the handshake's Job alongside its socket, and on supersede
   cancel it as well as closing the socket. Cancellation ends every part
   of the handshake that is a real suspension point (the 1 s pre-Type-3
   delay, the settle wait, the 60 s credential poll) even where the
   blocking read cannot be interrupted. stop() cancels it too. Ownership
   is claimed before the previous session is torn down, so the old
   coroutine's finally unwinds against a fence that is already closed.

2. Route every write a handshake makes to shared manager state through
   ifOwner(socket): the settling stamp, the poke cancel,
   closeAaListeners(), triggerPoke(), and resetHandshakeBackoff(). The
   last one mattered most — any byte arriving on a dead session cleared
   the backoff the live session had legitimately accrued.

3. sendProtobuf no longer claims "Successfully delivered ... over
   Bluetooth!". All that is known at that point is that write() and
   flush() returned. On #706's unit that was true of every send while
   the stack put nothing on the air, so the head unit log read as a
   clean handshake for weeks and hid the fault. It now reads
   "[TX] Wrote TYPE n (size m) to Bluetooth (write() returned; delivery
   unconfirmed)". The proof of delivery is the phone's reply, never our
   own send.

4. consecutiveHandshakeFailures is incremented in the fenced finally
   instead of inline at the 15 s timeout, so a socket error, a swallowed
   write or a cancellation count like the timeout does — from the
   outside they are the same failure, and counting only one of them let
   the rest retry unbounded while each attempt stranded another
   Dispatchers.IO thread. Gated on having actually sent the
   WifiStartRequest, so the manager's own pre-exchange aborts (no
   credentials after 60 s, masked BSSID, USB session already up) are not
   blamed on the phone: those repeat for as long as the user leaves
   location services off, and backing off on them would replace the log
   line that says what to fix with one that says the opposite.

proto: model the rest of the Android Auto wireless handshake

Regenerated with protoc 25.1, which matches the checked-in protobuf-java
3.25.1 runtime:

    protoc --proto_path=app/src/main/proto \
           --java_out=app/src/main/java \
           app/src/main/proto/wireless.proto

Verified before changing anything that this generator reproduces the
committed Wireless.java exactly, apart from the descriptor string being
emitted with C escapes (\n, \t, \r) where the old file used the
equivalent octal ones (\012, \011, \015) — same bytes, different source
formatting. That accounts for most of the apparent churn in the diff.

New messages, all fields optional so an absent or unexpected field can
never fail a parse: WifiInfoRequest (type 2), WifiVersionRequest (4),
WifiVersionResponse (5), WifiConnectStatus (6), WifiStartResponse (7),
WifiPingRequest/Response (8/9) and WifiSetupInfo (11). Shapes are
cross-checked against aa-proxy-rs's src/bluetooth.rs and the OEM ZLink
app's own exchange; fields that are never received are deliberately left
undefined rather than guessed at, since a wrong field number silently
mis-parses where a missing one costs nothing.

Status fields are int32, pinned from a capture rather than guessed. An
on-device run against a POCO X3 NFC logged WifiVersionResponse
status=2147483644, and that value is uniquely explained by a wire int32
of -8 read back as sint32: protobuf-java's readSInt32 is
decodeZigZag32(rawVarint32), and decodeZigZag32(-8) = (-8 ushr 1) xor 0
= 2147483644. No other int32 maps there. The phone said -8.

Only WifiVersionResponse.status is directly evidenced; WifiConnectStatus
and WifiStartResponse were only ever observed as 0, which decodes
identically under both declarations. They are changed together for
consistency.

Note this is a logging-truth fix, not a behaviour one. Zigzag is a
bijection, so zero maps to zero and non-zero to non-zero: the only thing
anything branches on ("did it succeed") was correct before and stays
correct. What changes is that the number in the log is now the number
the phone sent.

WifiInfoResponse.bssid, .security_mode and .access_point_type change
from required to optional. Wire-compatible for a field that is always
set — proto2 encodes both identically — and it removes a build()-time
assertion that would otherwise block omitting the BSSID, which
aa-proxy-rs does outright when it has none and ZLink ships without.

NativeAA: drive the handshake from a state machine, add the version exchange

The exchange this replaces sent WifiStartRequest, read exactly one
message, sent the credentials and then stopped listening. Types 6 and 7
arrive *after* the credentials go out, so the head unit never saw them:
it had no way to tell "the phone is still associating" from "the phone
gave up", which is the blind spot noted against isHandshakeInFlight().
It also never opened with a version exchange, which real head units and
the OEM ZLink app do, and which is the documented difference between the
abbreviated flow and the one Android Auto 17.4 wants.

aap/WppHandshakeSession is the exchange as a pure state machine —
AWAIT_VERSION -> AWAIT_CREDENTIALS -> AWAIT_INFO_REQUEST -> SETTLING —
with the ordering rules that are worth testing and impossible to test on
a real Bluetooth socket. aap/WppFraming is the four-byte header, split
out because it is the one part that can be wrong in a way no log shows:
a header we build by hand and the phone silently discards. Payloads
above 255 bytes exercise its high byte and had never been tested.

NativeAaHandshakeManager keeps the I/O and nothing else: a reader
coroutine feeds an unbounded channel, and a 250 ms tick loop feeds
events into the session and runs the actions that come back. Notable
consequences:

- The version request goes out *before* the wait for credentials, not
  after. The phone starts its own ~12 s first-message timer when it
  opens the channel and a cold P2P group can outlast that on its own; a
  head unit that has said nothing by then is one that "is not present"
  as far as Gearhead is concerned.
- WifiConnectStatus (type 6) is now read. A success report extends the
  settling window (capped at NativeHandoffPolicy.MAX_SETTLE_MS); a
  failure report ends the handoff immediately instead of waiting out the
  full 45 s, since the phone has stopped trying.
- Pings are answered by echoing the request's own payload back, so that
  path cannot fail on a schema guess.
- A repeated type 2 re-sends the credentials, as aa-proxy-rs does.
- awaitWifiHandoff() is absorbed into the SETTLING stage and deleted.
- Channel reads use tryReceive() polling rather than a timeout around
  receive(): cancelling a suspended receive can consume the element it
  was about to hand over, and losing the phone's type 2 that way would
  stall the handshake to its deadline for no visible reason.

sequence around type 3 are unchanged; ResumePoke is emitted only where
the old code already called triggerPoke() (settle timeout) plus the new
type-6-failure case, where the phone has given up and there is nothing
left to disturb; ExtendSettle re-stamps handoffSettlingSince rather than
only extending our own deadline, so isHandoffSettling() keeps the poke
off the radio for the whole join. The early type 4 opens no new
Bluetooth connection — it rides the socket the phone already opened.

Settings.nativeWifiVersionExchange (default on, "Modern handshake" in
the Android Auto mode block) turns the version exchange off, so a unit
that regresses on it can be recovered by toggle without a reinstall. Be
precise about what that reverts: with it off, the messages we *send* and
their order are exactly what shipped in 3.2.1 — types 1 then 3, nothing
before them. It does not revert the rest of this commit. We still keep
reading after type 3, so a type-6 failure report still ends the handoff
early and pings are still answered, on both settings. Anything suspected
of being a post-credentials regression has to be bisected against the
commit, not the toggle.

Version 1.1 is a guess and flagged as one in the code; it wants pinning
from a ZLink btsnoop. Nothing branches on the phone's reply, so a wrong
guess costs a wrong log line.

Tests: WppHandshakeSessionTest covers the transition table (both flows,
the 3 s version fallback, the impatient type 2, ping echo in every
stage, type 6/7 success and failure, the extension cap, the silent-phone
flag and terminal idempotence); WppFramingTest pins the header bytes and
the sizes either side of the byte boundary.

NativeAA: pure policies for the hotspot transport

Groundwork for running Native AA over this head unit's own access point
instead of a WiFi Direct group. Three decisions that are decidable
without Android, extracted and tested per the repo convention:

- SoftApNetworkPolicy: which network interface is our access point.
  There is no public API that answers this — WifiManager will not tell an
  ordinary app the address of its own soft AP — so it has to be
  recognised from outside: up, non-loopback, holding a site-local IPv4,
  not a p2p-* group, preferring ap*/swlan*/softap*/wlan* in that order
  but accepting an unfamiliar name over nothing. Plain wlan0 is
  deliberately eligible: that is what the OEM ZLink head unit serves
  Android Auto off.

- SoftApBssidPolicy: which of the available MAC sources to advertise —
  the user's staticBSSID, then sysfs/ip link, then
  NetworkInterface.getHardwareAddress() — uppercased, skipping any rung
  that yields a placeholder.

  Note what is *not* rejected: addresses merely beginning with 02:. That
  bit marks a locally-administered MAC and Android's own soft AP
  routinely uses a randomised one, so rejecting the range would discard
  the very BSSID this chain exists to find. Only the two exact masking
  placeholders and the all-zero address are refused.

- NativeCredentialsPolicy: what to do when no BSSID resolves, which
  differs by transport. WiFi Direct keeps its hard abort — that encodes
  real on-device evidence, a masked BSSID there means the phone rejects
  the credentials and the log should say so rather than showing a
  handshake that looks fine. The hotspot route omits the field and sends
  anyway: aa-proxy-rs omits it outright when it has none
  (`if include_bssid && !bssid.is_empty()`) and a teardown of ZLink shows
  it shipping credentials without one, so an ordinary AP is identified by
  SSID alone. Aborting there would make the route unusable on every
  device whose AP MAC is masked, which is most of them.

SoftApNetworkPolicy separates the access point from the station interface
by the station's own address, not by the shape of either. Measured on a
head unit that runs its soft AP as wlan2 while wlan0 is the station: the
two are indistinguishable by name, and the AP there holds
192.168.246.32, so the "an AP is the .1 of its subnet" rule that looked
obvious is simply false. The station address is knowable from
ConnectivityManager, so exclude it and let the name preference decide
among what is left; ap0 still wins where it exists.

Also excludes tun*/dummy*: the github flavour ships a dummy VPN service
that parks a site-local 10.x address on the device for as long as it
runs.

isApHost() applies the same rules to a single interface, for callers
asking "is an access point running at all" rather than "which of these
is it".

SoftApBssidPolicy validates the shape of an address instead of listing
known non-addresses. Settings.staticBSSID stores the string "0" when it
is unset — a convention WifiDirectManager already knows — and "0" is not
MAC-shaped, so it passed the placeholder check, beat the real interface
MAC to the front of the chain, and went out as BSSID=0. The phone
rejected those credentials on every retry (WifiConnectStatus status=-3,
in a ~7 s loop) until it was caught on device. A free-text field can
produce any number of such values, so the fix checks for six hex pairs
rather than adding one more sentinel to a list; dashes are accepted and
normalised so a hand-typed address still works.

Two station interfaces are excluded by name, both of which would
otherwise be chosen as the access point. On MediaTek and Ralink drivers
apcli0 is the AP *client* — the interface that joins someone else's
network, configured mode: sta — while ra0 is the access point; apcli0
starts with "ap", so it ranked best of everything. sta* is the same trap
spelled plainly, and is what aa-proxy-rs names its own managed station.

ra0/rai0 are deliberately not added to the preferred list. Two letters is
too loose a prefix to match on, and an unrecognised name is already
eligible, so excluding apcli* is enough to make a MediaTek unit pick ra0
by being what is left.

eligible() exposes what the choice was made from, so a caller can say
when more than one interface survived and the name broke the tie. That
tie is a guess, picking wrong hands the phone an unreachable address, and
nothing reported it before.

shouldPublishCredentials decides whether to advertise a network the
framework may not be running. The stored hotspot configuration exists
whether or not an access point is on air, so a device with some other
site-local interface up — ethernet, say — can produce a plausible name
and address for a network that is switched off, and the phone is told to
join something that is not there while the log says SUCCESS.

Narrow on purpose, because a wrong refusal is a route that stops working.
UNKNOWN never refuses: getWifiApState is not public API and is blocked
outright on some devices, and a question we could not ask is not a
question answered no. A name the user typed never refuses either — they
are asserting the network exists, and on a vendor that starts hostapd
outside the framework they are right while the framework is not. Only
"the framework is sure there is no access point" together with "we took
the name from stored configuration" is refused.

On-device round 4 found a third interface that is never an access point
and was being advertised as one: with the real AP down, the Unisoc
cellular bridge seth_lte0 was the only candidate up with a private
address, so the correct network name went out paired with an address no
phone could reach — logged as SUCCESS, twice. seth_lte joins the
exclusions, with a test built from the live shape.

That is the third extension of this list (tun/dummy, apcli/sta, now
seth_lte), which is the point: a blocklist is a guess about which unknown
names are not access points, and it will keep needing extension.
shouldPublishCredentials is the defence that does not depend on knowing
every name in advance, so its exemptions are narrowed to match.

It previously exempted a hand-typed SSID, which is what let seth_lte0
through: the state read said no access point was running and the gate
looked the other way, because a manual SSID is *required* on any device
that refuses the config-read API — exempting it disabled the check on
exactly the hardware that needed it. The exemption is now a named
interface instead. That names the network rather than a label for it, and
it remains the escape hatch for a vendor that starts hostapd outside the
framework. UNKNOWN still never refuses.

utils: lift the hotspot config reader out of the QR dialog, add a MAC reader

HotspotConfigReader is ShareHotspotQrDialog.getSystemHotspotConfig()
moved verbatim; the dialog now delegates to it. The Native AA hotspot
transport needs to read the same SSID and passphrase the QR dialog shows
the user, and neither getSoftApConfiguration() (API 30+) nor the older
getWifiApConfiguration() is public API, so there is exactly one piece of
reflection worth having and it should not exist twice.

InterfaceMacReader reads a network interface's MAC from sysfs, falling
back to `ip link`, for the usual reason: getHardwareAddress() returns
null or a placeholder for ordinary apps on most devices since Android
6.0.

It is a separate, minimal implementation rather than a refactor of
WifiDirectManager.getMacFromShell(). That method carries [BUG_FIX]
annotations and a six-deep fallback chain tuned against specific
reporters' hardware, and reworking it to be shared would put the WiFi
Direct path at risk to serve the hotspot one. About thirty lines are
duplicated on purpose. What is not duplicated is its leak: it runs `ip
link` through Runtime.exec() and never destroys the process or closes
its streams, and this new one runs on a polling loop where that would
accumulate.

NetworkAddresses answers "what is this device's address on the WiFi
network it has joined", which is what tells a hosted access point apart
from a station interface when both are up and both are called wlanN. It
asks ConnectivityManager for the WiFi transport specifically rather than
the active network, since the active one may be this app's own VPN or
the access point itself, and falls back to WifiManager on older devices.

SoftApStateReader asks the framework whether an access point is running.
getWifiApState() is the soft-AP counterpart to the public getWifiState()
but is not public API, so it is reflection with the constants written
out. A blocked call reports UNKNOWN rather than "no access point":
callers treat those two very differently, and collapsing them would make
every device with non-SDK restrictions look like it has no hotspot.

NativeAA: hotspot credentials provider, and make the handshake route-aware

SoftApCredentialsProvider is the hotspot counterpart to
WifiDirectManager's credential source, with the same contract
(setCredentialsListener / setInvalidatedListener / start / refresh /
stop) so a launcher can treat the two transports alike. It polls for an
interface that looks like our access point, resolves SSID and passphrase
(manual override first, then the system's own hotspot configuration),
takes the IP from the interface rather than assuming 192.168.43.1,
resolves a BSSID through SoftApBssidPolicy, and watches
WIFI_AP_STATE_CHANGED so the credentials are invalidated if the hotspot
drops.

Auto-enabling the hotspot is best effort only, after 5 s with nothing
found and only if the user opted in. ZLink can do better because it
holds TETHER_PRIVILEGED and runs root daemons; we cannot copy that, so
reading a hotspot the user configured is the load-bearing path and the
give-up message says exactly that (including that 5 GHz matters — AA
video over 2.4 GHz is poor).

In NativeAaHandshakeManager the transport is captured once per handshake
and drives two things: the BSSID abort now asks NativeCredentialsPolicy
instead of hardcoding "abort", and sendWifiSecurityResponse omits the
BSSID field when there is none (possible now the proto has it optional)
and sends AccessPointType DYNAMIC on a hotspot, which is what aa-proxy-rs
sends as an AP host, against STATIC on WiFi Direct as before.

Settings.nativeApTransport (key "native-ap-transport", default 0 = WiFi
Direct) selects the route. Deliberately not folded into
helperConnectionStrategy: that belongs to mode 2 and means something
different in each of its five values, and a wireless mode reusing
another mode's selector is how the two call sites of usesWifiDirect()
drifted apart in the first place.

Nothing here selects the route yet — the transport predicate, the mode-3
arm and the settings entry that make it reachable land later in this
branch, once the pieces they wire together exist. On the default
transport this commit changes no behaviour.

Settings.hotspotInterface names the interface outright and is consulted
before the heuristic. Every other implementation of this protocol does
the same or better: aa-proxy-rs has an `iface` setting defaulting to
wlan0, the Raspberry Pi dongles pin interface=wlan0 in hostapd.conf, and
ZLink carries ap_NIC_name as a field in its own protobuf. None of them
infer anything, because each of them creates the access point and so
knows its name. We are the only one reading an AP we did not create, on
hardware we do not control, which is the whole reason a heuristic exists
here at all — so it belongs behind an override, not in front of one.

A named interface that is missing or down falls back to the heuristic and
says so rather than failing outright, since the name is likelier to be
stale than the interface list.

publish() now asks whether the access point is actually running before
handing its details to the phone, and refuses only the one combination
that is definitely wrong (see NativeCredentialsPolicy). Refusing returns
to the poll loop rather than giving up, since the user may switch the
hotspot on while we wait — and auto-enable now triggers on any
unpublished pass, not only when no interface was found at all, because a
refused publish means "there is no hotspot yet" just as much as an empty
interface list does.

Fixes a compile error: pickApInterface() had an expression body and a
return inside it, which Kotlin disallows, so this branch did not build at
all. It is a block body now, and returns which interface was chosen
together with whether the user named it — the publish gate needs that to
tell an assertion apart from a guess.

[BUG_FIX] HotspotManager: four ways it lied about starting a hotspot

An on-device run (API 34, non-privileged install) went through every path
in here and produced no access point at all, while reporting success and
logging nothing about it. Three separate defects, all now covered by the
logcat evidence in that run:

1. setHotspotEnabled() returned as soon as SoftApConfigCompat.enableHotspot()
   reported success. That method only calls setSoftApConfiguration() — it
   writes the SSID and passphrase, it does not bring an access point up —
   so on API 30+ where the configuration applied we reported success and
   ran no start path at all.

2. tryTetheringManager picked the startTethering overload by argument
   count. API 34 carries two 3-arg overloads, (TetheringRequest, Executor,
   StartTetheringCallback) and (int, Executor, StartTetheringCallback),
   and reflection returned whichever came first, so passing the tethering
   type as an Integer threw "argument 1 has type TetheringRequest, got
   java.lang.Integer". Now selected by parameter type, with a reflective
   TetheringRequest built for platforms that only offer that overload.

3. The remaining paths reported success because invoke() returned. It
   does not mean the hotspot started: the framework answers
   asynchronously through a StartTetheringCallback, and the DexMaker shim
   that would build one uses com.android.dx, which predates API 28's ART
   changes. In the captured run the ConnectivityManager path did reach
   the framework and was refused a millisecond later — "Tethering is
   already active or in recovering" — and this method returned true
   anyway, silently. Success is now decided by looking for the access
   point (getWifiApState, falling back to the interface via
   SoftApNetworkPolicy.isApHost) rather than by the call returning.

The permission ceiling is unchanged and still expected: setSoftApConfiguration
throws SecurityException on a non-privileged install. What changes is that
the failure now says so instead of passing for success — the same
correction made earlier in this stack to the Bluetooth send logging, and
for the same reason.

Behaviour change worth watching: wireless mode 2 strategy 4 is the other
caller and will now report failure where it used to report success. That
is the truth, but it is a visible change and wants an on-device look.

The interface fallback used when getWifiApState is unavailable now takes
the station address into account, so a head unit sitting on a WiFi
network is not read as hosting one.

The AP-state check moves to SoftApStateReader, shared with the hotspot
transport so the two cannot disagree about whether one is running. A
blocked getWifiApState still falls back to the interface list here; only
a framework answer of "not enabled" is taken as a no.

Round 4 found a fourth, worse than the other three: a null
StartTetheringCallback. The framework dispatches onTetheringStarted() and
onTetheringFailed() onto that object through the executor with no null
check, so the app died with a FATAL EXCEPTION the moment tethering
finished starting — twice, once per auto-restart. It hid behind Round 1's
immediate "Tethering is already active" refusal, which never dispatches
anything. Both overloads now get a no-op built by java.lang.reflect.Proxy
(the callback is an interface of default no-ops, so DexMaker is not
needed), and the request is skipped rather than sent with null if one
cannot be made. The ConnectivityManager path gets the same guard: its
DexMaker shim returns null whenever it fails, which is the identical
hazard a layer down.

Also stops misreporting the radio. setWifiEnabled() is a no-op for apps
targeting API 29+ and this one targets far past it, so "Disabling WiFi
before enabling hotspot..." announced something the platform ignored —
which is how a radio state the framework caused got read as ours. It now
re-reads and says which actually happened, and when a failed start leaves
neither a station nor an access point up, says that too: nothing here can
switch WiFi back on at this target SDK, and the symptom downstream is a
WiFi Direct group that never forms for no visible reason.

NativeAA: make the head unit hotspot selectable as a transport

The hotspot pieces in this branch had no way to run: nothing constructed
SoftApCredentialsProvider, nothing read nativeApTransport except the
handshake's BSSID policy, and no UI wrote it. Worse, mode 3 was hardcoded
to use WiFi Direct, and that answer makes initWifiMode force-disable the
hotspot before starting P2P — so even setting the pref by hand would have
torn down the access point the route was about to advertise. The first
on-device pass could only smoke-test HotspotManager through wireless mode
2 strategy 4 for that reason.

- WifiModePolicy.usesWifiDirect takes the transport, defaulting to the
  answer it gave before. Mode 3 on the hotspot route now returns false,
  which is what keeps the force-disable off the access point.
- AapService constructs the provider beside WifiDirectManager and wires
  both credential sources through one onNativeCredentials(), so the poke
  rules that #760 tuned live in exactly one place regardless of transport.
  The mode-3 arm starts one or the other; triggerWifiDirectRefresh routes
  to provider.refresh(); stop paths cover it.
- "Network transport" (WiFi Direct / Hotspot) in the Android Auto mode
  block, with a banner saying to switch the hotspot on yourself and set it
  to 5 GHz.
- Manual hotspot name and password entries, shown on the hotspot route.
  Not polish: HotspotConfigReader reads the configuration through
  getSoftApConfiguration, the same non-public API that the tested head
  unit refused outright with "App not allowed to read or update stored
  WiFi Ap config". On such a device this override is the only way the
  route can learn the network name, and until now it had no UI at all.
- native-ap-transport joins the settings backup allowlist. It was
  deliberately withheld while the route was unreachable; that reason is
  gone.

This is the fallback wiring the design anticipated for the case where the
upstream wifi-code refactor has not merged. It has not, and the route was
otherwise untestable. When it does land, this wiring moves into
WifiLauncherNativeAA; everything else in this branch is unaffected by it.

Placement, from using it: the transport choice sits at the top of the
Native block, ahead of the two Bluetooth adapter entries, which are
dual-radio fallbacks most users never open — the structural choice
should not be below them. It is also in the Basic tab, along with the
banner and the manual name/password that only appear once Hotspot is
picked. Those come along deliberately: on a device that refuses the
hotspot config-read API the manual name is the only way to finish, so a
Basic user able to select the route but not to configure it would have
no visible way out.

The Hotspot group also carries a "Hotspot network interface" entry, blank
for automatic. Its message says where to find the name — the log line
after "Providing credentials from", or `ip -brief addr` from a shell —
and lists the names units actually use.

NativeAA: say when no interface looks like an access point

The automatic path rejected every candidate and logged nothing at all, so a
run with no hotspot up produced thirty seconds of silence from the provider
while the phone cycled handshake attempts against it. On-device testing read
that silence as a hang and went looking for a dropped code path; the refusal
line it expected lives in publish(), which is never reached when no candidate
survives name exclusion one layer earlier.

Report it once per resolve pass, listing the interfaces that were up, so the
reader can name one for the override if the access point turned out to be on
an interface the heuristic does not recognise.

NativeAA: say that a missing BSSID is why the phone refused

Phone-to-phone testing (OHU on a POCO X3 as the head unit, Gearhead on a
Motorola Edge 30 Neo) found both Native AA transports failing on a head
unit that cannot read its own MAC, and the logs did not say what to do.

Gearhead joins with a WifiNetworkSpecifier, which matches SSID *and*
BSSID under a full ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff mask. Credentials sent without a
BSSID came back as WIFI_INVALID_BSSID and a type 6 status=-3 on every
retry, with no fallback to matching on the name; a well-formed but wrong
address instead timed out as status=-11. So the address has to be real,
and NativeCredentialsPolicy's justification for omitting it -- that an
ordinary AP is identified by SSID -- is too strong. The behaviour is
kept: the field is optional in the protocol, other clients accept it
missing, and a rejection is at least a message we can explain. The
comment now records what was measured.

- Hotspot: a join failure after we omitted the BSSID now names the
  omission as the first suspect, rather than leaving the reader to
  connect it to the warning several seconds earlier.
- WiFi Direct: the abort blamed location services unconditionally. That
  is the usual cause but not the only one -- where the head unit is an
  ordinary phone, every source in the chain is permission-blocked and no
  setting will unblock it. Both causes are named, with the static BSSID
  override as the remedy.

Setting the real address by hand (read from the system's own dump)
connected both transports first try, so the override is the fix; this
only makes the log point at it.

NativeAA: the BSSID is required, and every implementation sends one

Checked the two reference implementations rather than trusting the
comment that said otherwise. Both declare a byte-identical proto2 schema

    required string bssid = 3;
    required SecurityMode security_mode = 4;
    required AccessPointType access_point_type = 5;

and both read the address from the access point's own interface:
aa-proxy-rs takes mac_address_by_name(iface) and refuses to start with
"No MAC address found" if it cannot, WirelessAndroidAutoDongle defaults
it to getMacAddress("wlan0"). Neither has a no-BSSID mode. The one
aa-proxy-rs path with no address to hand sets an empty string, because
required forbids dropping the field, and its comment anticipates that
phones may need a real one.

So the claim this code carried -- that those projects ship without a
BSSID, so an ordinary AP is identified by SSID -- was false, and it is
what made "omit it" look reasonable. Our wireless.proto had also relaxed
those three fields to optional, which is what made omitting expressible
at all.

Sending an absent required field risks a strict parser rejecting the
whole message, which would look like silence rather than like the
specific refusal Gearhead gives for an empty one. So all five fields now
go out every time, with an empty BSSID where there is no real address --
what aa-proxy-rs does in the same situation. UnusableBssidAction's
hotspot case is renamed to say that: SEND_WITH_EMPTY_BSSID, not
OMIT_AND_CONTINUE.

Behaviour is otherwise unchanged. Sending stays worth a try because a
refusal is a message we can explain where an abort leaves nothing to
read, but it is no longer described as the thing that normally works:
the static BSSID setting is the fix.

Also confirmed on the way past: DYNAMIC is the right access point type
for the hotspot route -- both references use it for a hostapd AP.

Video: name the failure when a session carries no video at all

Deliberate 2.4GHz testing on the head unit hotspot found a failure with
no explanation anywhere in our log. Over a 2472MHz access point at
1080p/60 the phone completed the Bluetooth handshake, joined the network,
opened the AAP session and the video channel, then closed the socket
0.04-4.2s later having sent not one video frame. Thirty-two cycles in
under five minutes, each looking like a fresh healthy connection until
the moment it ended, and 36 clean EOFs in the capture with zero decoder
output lines.

It is a throughput ceiling, not a broken route, and the controlled pass
proves it: same access point, same band, same everything, an 800x480/30
stream held for 308s with the decoder producing continuously, while
1080p/60 on 5GHz held too. The phone's own reason never reaches us --
Gearhead logs GAL_SOCKET_CONNECTION_FAILED on its side, 37 times in the
failing pass and zero in both passes that held.

We cannot read the band to warn about it directly: SoftApInfo's frequency
needs NETWORK_SETTINGS. But the shape is diagnostic on its own -- a
session that reached SSL and then died having rendered nothing, over and
over -- so CommManager now counts those and says what it means once a run
of three makes it more than coincidence. Rules in a pure
VideoStarvationPolicy with tests; CommManager only reads the decoder's
frame stamp before stopping it.

Advice given once per run, not per reconnect: at the measured cadence
that would have been thirty-two identical lines in five minutes.

Also, from the same captures: the poke failure line logged "to null" for
any unbonded device, since getName() is null there. It now carries the
address too, which is what identifies the phone in a bug report.

Settings: say what 2.4GHz actually does on the hotspot route

The hint said video is "poor" over 2.4GHz. It is not poor, it is absent:
the phone connects, opens the video channel, sends nothing and drops the
session, repeating for as long as it is left to. Measured at 1080p/60 on
a 2472MHz access point -- 32 cycles in five minutes, no frame ever
rendered -- while 800x480/30 held on the same access point indefinitely.

So the hint now describes the symptom a user would actually see, and
gives them the second way out rather than only the band.

Video: count starved sessions by frames, not by a stamp stop() clears

The starvation counter read videoDecoder.lastFrameRenderedMs at disconnect,
which VideoDecoder.stop() and setSurface() both zero. Leaving projection
destroys the surface, AapProjectionActivity answers that with
stop("surfaceDestroyed"), and the stamp is gone before doDisconnect reads it —
so a session that showed video for an hour and was ended by the user counted as
one that showed none. Three ordinary exits in a row and a working head unit is
told to move its access point to 5 GHz.

Count frames over the session instead, in a field stop() does not touch and
CommManager zeroes when the handshake completes. The true-positive case is
unaffected: a phone that gives up on the video stream drops the socket with the
surface still up.

Found by inspection while checking this branch for regressions against units
that already work; not seen in a capture, because every test session so far was
ended by the phone rather than by the user.

NativeAA: don't send a guessed protocol version by default

The version exchange shipped on by default, which made it the one change on
this branch that alters what a unit with a working setup puts on the wire
without anyone opting into anything. The version it announces is a guess: no
capture of a real head unit's Type 4 has been decoded, and 1.1 was chosen
because it was plausible.

The evidence for keeping it on is thinner than the evidence against. A phone
under test answered the guessed version with status=-8 and completed the
handshake regardless, so the exchange is survivable — on one Gearhead, on one
device pair. The reason to send it at all is a hypothesis that Android Auto
17.4 broke the abbreviated exchange, and no reporter has confirmed the exchange
fixes it. Defaulting to off costs that hypothesis nothing: the toggle is still
in the mode-3 block and still in the settings backup, so a reporter can be
asked to turn it on and say whether it helped, which is how the question gets
answered rather than assumed.

Off is also the pre-existing wire behaviour, so mode 3 now sends byte-identical
bytes to 3.2.1 unless the user asks otherwise.

Boot: stop a system-level crash from becoming an endless restart loop

Auto-start on boot turns one crash into a cycle with nothing to break it: the
system dies, the head unit soft-reboots, LOCKED_BOOT_COMPLETED arrives, we start,
we bring wireless up, and it dies again. Measured on a reporter's MT8163 unit at
a 20-26 s period across seven consecutive processes in two separate logs.

Nothing in the app counted failures of any kind, so count the one thing it can
observe: boot-started runs that did not last. Three in a row under 30 s and
wireless bring-up is skipped, with a notification saying so. USB and the rest of
the app are untouched, and the pause is sticky until someone opens the app, so
the cycle ends outright rather than resuming every fourth boot.

Two things this had to get right:

The healthy signal is uptime, not a successful connection. One cycle in the logs
reached a complete projection session with audio playing and the system died
anyway, so clearing the count on a connection would reset it on every pass and
the guard would never trip. 30 s separates the loop (8, 9, 10, 15 s) from the
runs that were doing real work (48 s, 173 s).

MainActivity releases the guard only when a person opened the app. The service
launches MainActivity itself on every boot auto-start, so clearing on any launch
would reset the count on exactly the runs being counted. initWifiMode() is gated
too, not just the onCreate path: the phone arriving over Bluetooth re-triggers
wireless init, which would walk straight back into the crash.

Rules in a pure BootLoopPolicy with tests that replay both logs' lifetimes.

Boot: correct the crash-loop figures the guard's tests replay

The 3.2.1 assertion claimed three failing cycles and asserted a trip, but that
log holds 48.1 s, 9.8 s and 15.2 s: the 48 s run clears, so the export ends two
strikes in, one short of pausing. The reporter stopped recording there. The test
failed for the right reason and the number it wanted does not exist.

Assert what was measured instead: the log ends at two strikes, does not pause,
and one more short run would. Same correction to the original log's fourth
process, which lasted 11.5 s rather than the 15 s written down, and its trip is
now modelled where it actually happens, at the start of the fourth boot rather
than after it.

Both exports end mid-cycle, so the last lifetime in each is a floor rather than
a confirmed death. Noted in the analysis alongside the corrected figures.

Video: distinguish the session frame counter from the throughput one

Rebasing onto main put framesRenderedThisSession next to framesRendered, which
arrived with the throughput telemetry. They look duplicative and are not, in the
one way that matters: stop() resets framesRendered on purpose, because a
throughput sample must not straddle a restart, and must never reset
framesRenderedThisSession, because a session survives restarts and that is the
whole point of it. Say so where the field is declared, so the next person to see
two rendered-frame counters does not tidy one into the other's reset block.

Also count frames rather than callbacks in the software path, matching the line
nine rows below it. Only ever compared against zero, so no behaviour changes.

Recover a dropped video frame without releasing video focus

On some head units the video collapses to a few fps and freezes shortly after
connecting (issue #755). From the logs, a transient decoder input-buffer-full
drops one frame, the stream is marked corrupt, and the recovery cycles video
focus (release then re-gain) to force a keyframe. Releasing focus makes the
phone stop sending video, and on these units it never comes back to full rate.

Request the recovery keyframe with an unsolicited focus gain only, without
releasing focus first, the same nudge the startup keyframe watchdog uses. This
leaves the genuine-corruption paths and the sync_stall watchdog untouched.
