Video: stop treating a busy decoder as a corrupt stream

Reporters on #755, #757, #744, #767, #787 and #788 all name 3.2.0-beta2
or beta3 as the last version whose picture was usable. Between beta3 and
beta4 exactly one commit changes decode behaviour: 18706589, the video
half of #738. Everything below reverts a piece of it.

  feedInputBuffer waited 3 x 10ms for a free input buffer instead of the
  30 it waited before. On every reporter unit the first "Input buffer
  full" then lands within a second of "Codec initialized" - 70ms after it
  on the Intel Atom in #757 - because the component has not drained its
  first buffers yet, not because the hardware is too slow. Back to 30.

  That drop was wired into recovery. decode() returned false, AapVideo
  called markCorruptAndRequestRecovery(), and the phone got a video-focus
  release/regain cycle for one lost frame. Before #738 the same event was
  a bare return. It is again: decode() returns Unit and the frame is
  counted in framesDropped and forgotten.

  markCorruptAndRequestRecovery() also armed waitingForKeyframe, which
  dropped every packet until checkKeyframe() positively identified a
  keyframe. It had no timeout and no re-request, and it read NAL headers
  using settings.videoCodec - a user preference defaulting to "Auto" -
  rather than the codec the decoder pinned. ServiceDiscoveryResponse
  negotiates H.265 at 1440p and 4K while that string still says "Auto",
  and H.264 when the user asked for H.265 on a unit without an HEVC
  decoder, so in three reachable configurations every keyframe was
  misread and the latch could never clear. Measured cost in the #755 log
  HUR_Log_20260806_214208_084.txt: fed=0, rendered=0 for 16.5 seconds
  with the phone still connected and sending. Removed.

  KEY_PRIORITY, KEY_OPERATING_RATE and KEY_MAX_B_FRAMES were added as
  latency hints. The MediaTek unit in #755 answers both of the first two
  with "codec does not support config (err -1010)", and the third is an
  encoder key. KEY_FRAME_RATE, added later as a fallback, declares the
  user's fps cap rather than the negotiated rate. All four removed.

  The synthetic PTS advanced by 1e6/settings.fpsLimit per frame to stop
  network jitter causing catch-up fast-forwards. releaseOutputBuffer is
  called with render=true, which ignores the timestamp, so it prevented
  nothing; it also divided by a settings value with no zero guard. Back
  to the wall clock.

checkFragmentState() stays. Orphaned-fragment detection is the one part
of #738 that addressed a real defect, and with the lockout gone its
markCorruptAndRequestRecovery() call is scoped to the current frame the
way it was before: flags 8 and 10 skip the rest of it and the next flag
9 or 11 clears the mark.

The sync_stall watchdog and its input-idle gate, cooldown and cap are
untouched, as are the crop-rect handling, the throughput telemetry and
the codec pinning from #754.

Video: grow the reassembly buffer instead of guessing its size

AapVideo sized its fragment reassembly buffer from settings.videoCodec:
8MB when that string said "H.265", 2MB otherwise. That string is the
user's preference, not the codec the session runs. ServiceDiscoveryResponse
enforces H.265 at 1440p and picks it at 4K whatever the setting says, and
falls back to H.264 when the user chose H.265 on a device with no HEVC
decoder - so both mismatches are reachable, and the first one gives an
H.265 stream the small buffer and turns its large frames into a fragment
overflow on every keyframe.

Reading the negotiated codec here is not an option either: AapVideo is
constructed with AapTransport in CommManager, and ServiceDiscoveryResponse
is not built until AapControl handles discovery, so at construction time
there is nothing to read.

Start at the H.264 size and grow when a fragment does not fit, up to the
same 8MB ceiling the H.265 branch used to allocate outright. Frames past
that are still invalidated. Nothing is allocated up front that the stream
does not turn out to need, and the size no longer depends on a setting
that can disagree with the stream.
changed BT Helper for finding better mac address, changed wifi handling

Video: keep the pinned codec type across a surface teardown

detectCodecType() accepts H.264 only on NAL types 7/8 (SPS/PPS) but accepts
H.265 on 32-34, and the ordinary H.264 P-slice header byte 0x41
(nal_ref_idc=2, nal_unit_type=1) reads as (0x41 and 0x7E) shr 1 == 32, an HEVC
VPS. #754 added codecTypePinned so the heuristic runs once per session instead
of on every restart, which is the only moment it is reliable: the first packet
of a session carries SPS/PPS, a mid-stream one carries a P-slice.

The pin was cleared by every stop() whose reason did not start with "restart",
and "surfaceDestroyed" is such a reason. Backgrounding the projection activity
with the phone still connected and still streaming therefore threw the pin away
and re-ran the detection on whatever packet arrived during the teardown.

Measured in HUR_Log_20260807_185250_428.txt (#755, MTK unit, 720p, H.264
throughout: negotiated 1280x720, no 1440p H.265 enforcement, every real frame
logs "H.264 SPS parsed"). Twice in 31 minutes, at 18:59:24 and 19:23:48, an
AapProjectionActivity.onPause is followed within 6 ms by

  Decoder stopped: surfaceDestroyed
  findBestCodec: hw=OMX.MTK.VIDEO.DECODER.HEVC ... selected=...HEVC
  Codec initialized: OMX.MTK.VIDEO.DECODER.HEVC

an HEVC decoder for an H.264 stream. Both times the surface was destroyed again
50 ms later and the session healed, which is luck: start() sets
codecTypePinned = true on any successful start, including a wrong one, so on a
unit where the surface survives, the session pins H265 against an H.264 stream
and the picture is gone until a non-restart stop() clears it. That is the "no
picture, audio still works" report in #749.

Split the two resets stop() used to do together. VPS/SPS/PPS, the dimensions and
the watchdog counters still clear on anything that is not a decoder restart, so
decoderPermanentlyFailed keeps its only escape hatch. The pin alone now survives
the surface lifecycle, because it describes the stream rather than the decoder
instance and only a disconnect can change what the phone is sending.

DecoderStopPolicy holds the classification and the four reason strings so the
call sites stop passing loose literals, matching WifiModePolicy and
VideoRecoveryPolicy. CommManager and AapService keep their descriptive strings
and end the session, as does any reason the policy does not recognise.

Video: report how long the decoder waited for an input buffer

AapVideo.process() runs on AapTransport's Poll thread, which also carries
audio and control and dispatches video first, so time spent in
feedInputBuffer's dequeue loop is time audio cannot be delivered. That wait is
currently invisible: a frame that spends some of its 30 attempts logs nothing,
and "Input buffer full" only fires when every attempt is exhausted. A log can
therefore read zero for that line while still having blocked for hundreds of
milliseconds per second.

That gap had to be closed by hand to answer a reporter on #755 who described
"sound and image latency" alongside the freezing. What settled it in
HUR_Log_20260807_185250_428.txt was comparing the arrival regularity of
AapMediaPlayback status packets, which ride the same thread behind video,
across windows:

  59-60 fps windows   median 1.00s, max 1.04s, no gap over 2s
  11-15 fps window    median 0.82s, min 0.31s, max 3.02s, two gaps over 2s

Blocking predicts the opposite. The 60 fps windows ask for an input buffer most
often and are the metronomic ones; the jitter sits where there is least video to
block on, in a bunch-then-stall shape, with no catch-up spike in fed afterwards.
So the delay was in the pipe, not on our thread. Worth noting because
fed == rendered on its own does not show this - a stalled feeder drops nothing,
it just feeds slowly, so it produces the same shape as a phone sending less.

Accumulate the wait and add it to the line that already reports the frame
counts:

  Throughput over 5000ms: rendered=300 (59fps), fed=300 (59fps), dropped=0,
  inputWait=0ms, codec=c2.unisoc.avc.decoder

Near zero while the frame rate is low means the frames were never sent and the
answer is upstream. Hundreds of milliseconds means the decoder is the bottleneck
and the 30-attempt budget is being paid for in audio latency, which is the
signal to tune the budget down rather than couple a busy decoder back to the
corruption path.

The whole dequeue is timed rather than only the retries, because the first call
blocks for up to TIMEOUT_US by itself and the total is what holds audio up. The
retry count and per-attempt timeout are unchanged.

Detect head units whose Bluetooth is an external module

Some head units do not use android.bluetooth for Android Auto at all. A teardown
of the OEM ZLink build one reporter's unit runs shows it gating its entire AA
RFCOMM listener on isBuiltInBt(), which returns false when any of /dev/rf_serial
or /dev/zj_bt_serial exists, or rw.zlink.bt.type / rw.zj.bt.type reads "extra".
On those units AA Bluetooth goes through a vendor daemon to a separate chip, and
the phone bonds to that chip -- so nothing this app writes over RFCOMM can reach
it, however correct the protocol is.

That matches what the reporter's HCI trace measured: fifteen complete AA RFCOMM
sessions on DLCI 17, credits granted both ways, flow control clear, and zero
payload frames in either direction across all of them. The radio transmitted SDP
responses and control frames in the same capture, so the loss is in software
before frame generation, and the external module explains why.

ExternalBtPolicy implements the same four checks and returns the evidence rather
than a boolean, so the log names which signal fired. Native AA skips the whole
route on a positive, because a route that cannot deliver its handshake is better
declined than left to look healthy and stall -- which is what it did, for two
weeks of the reporter's time and several rounds of ours. The manual
secondary-Bluetooth service override still forces it through: that is the one
case detection cannot see, a unit exposing a second radio under a name nothing
enumerates.

NativeAA: say when a P2P group lands on channel 12 or 13

A group above channel 11 is up and beaconing and still invisible to most
phones: a client in the FCC domain associates on channels 1-11 only and
will not even list the SSID in a scan, so the phone reports nothing worse
than "can't find the network". Below API 29 there is no way to ask for a
channel, so name the condition in the log and in a toast, and point at the
two things that do move it: restarting WiFi, or a country code the driver
honours.

Reported in #757, where the same unit connected 5/5 on 2437/2462 MHz and
0/2 on 2467 MHz a few days later, having reset its country code to 00.

Detect only, no recreate. An earlier revision of this change tore the group
down and rebuilt it up to three times, which does not work and costs more
than it buys:

  - The channel is settled when the WiFi radio initialises, not when the
    group is created. Six recreates on the reporter's unit landed on
    2467 MHz six times.
  - Each teardown opens a window where every requestGroupInfo() returns
    null. Five call sites share one groupInfoRetries counter and each null
    re-posts on its own 1s timer, so several ladders run at once, burn the
    20-attempt budget in ~5s instead of 20, and hit FATAL. That log went
    from 0 "Group info was null" lines to 23 plus one FATAL, and for 13s
    the app did not know its own group: no credentials delivered, no join
    watchdog armed.

So the group is reported and kept. A phone in a regulatory domain that
allows channels 12-13 still joins it normally.

Said once per group, keyed on the SSID. Android generates a fresh
DIRECT-xy- per group, it is populated on the first callback, and it is
never privacy-masked, unlike the interface name (null until an IP is up)
and the BSSID (often 02:00:00:00:00:00 here) - either of those would both
split one group across two identities and merge two groups into one.

Two hazards in removeGroupAndRetryNative5Ghz() are left as they are on
main, since it is back to a single caller: it does not call
onNativeGroupInvalidated(), so the detached credential thread can deliver
a dead group's SSID/PSK/BSSID up to 15s later, and it checks neither
isNativeHandshakeInFlight nor isNativeSessionConnected. The shared
groupInfoRetries ladder is a separate pre-existing bug on every teardown
path and wants its own change.

Hotspot: tell the user when this device will not name its own access point

On the head-unit-hotspot route the credentials come from getSoftApConfiguration(),
reflection over a non-public API that a locked-down device refuses outright. There
is then no network name to hand the phone, and the resolve loop treated that as
"there is no hotspot yet" and kept polling.

Measured on a reporter's unit: the access point was up and found the whole time
(ap0, 192.168.43.1), the loop logged that it could not read its name once a second,
switched on a hotspot that was already on five seconds in, and ran out its budget.
Every handshake sat in AWAIT_CREDENTIALS with SSID=<null>, the phone gave up after
~12s and redialled, and the cycle repeated without ever reaching the first message.
From the car the whole symptom is that Bluetooth connects and nothing happens.

Polling cannot fix it -- the read that failed this second fails the next one -- so
the single "nothing published" outcome is split into the two states it was carrying.
NO_AP_YET is worth waiting for and is what auto-enable exists for; it no longer
fires at an access point that is already up. CONFIG_UNREADABLE ends the resolve and
names the two settings that make this route work on such a device. Toasted once as
well as logged, forced past the show-toast preference: the reporter it is written
for had no reason to open a log, and the alternative is a silent dead end.

The rule itself lives in SoftApCredentialsPolicy with eight cases pinned, because
it cannot be reached on any hardware available to test with -- the rig reads its
own configuration fine, and only a reporter's unit refuses. Including the case
that looks like an oversight and is not: a hand-typed network name with no password
goes out open, because the system configuration is not read at all once the user has
named the network, and pairing their name with a passphrase read off the device
would hand the phone a mismatched pair that fails with nothing pointing at why.

Also budgets the resolve against the run rather than one look. The message saying no
access point could be found was unreachable: beginResolve() stamped its own deadline,
refresh() restarts it, and the handshake refreshes every ten seconds, so thirty
seconds restarted every ten never expired. Measured: an access point down for three
and a half minutes, the loop polling throughout, and nothing said. The polling
continues -- switching the hotspot on by hand is a real recovery and sometimes the
only one left -- but it no longer happens in silence.

Hotspot: get the band right, and stop taking down what cannot be put back

The head-unit-hotspot route worked on cooperative hardware. This is what five
rounds on a unit that refuses almost every soft-AP call turned up.

**The band.** Android Auto completes the handshake over 2.4 GHz and then drops the
projection within seconds -- a failure that reads as "Android Auto starts and stops"
and has cost several rounds of log-reading to recognise. So 5 GHz is requested, with
2.4 GHz only where the radio will not host an access point at all. Trying is the only
way to find out: is5GHzBandSupported() describes the station side, and vendors ship
radios that answer yes there and still refuse to host.

**And saying so honestly.** Plenty of head units refuse setSoftApConfiguration()
outright, and the success line named the band it had asked for rather than one it had
confirmed: measured saying "up on 2.4 GHz" against hostapd bringing the access point
up on channel 149, 5745 MHz, 8.3s later. A reader with only the log would have
concluded the opposite of what the radio did. The band cannot be read back instead --
SoftApInfo arrives on a callback needing NETWORK_SETTINGS -- so the line now reports
whether the request was taken, and where it was not, that the band is the device's own
choice. That also ends the band loop early: a refused request never reached the
framework, so trying the other band starts the same access point again, which is three
startSoftAp calls where one was wanted and two of them tearing down what the previous
one had just brought up.

**The port.** The credentials tell the phone to dial 5288 and nothing checked anything
was listening, which produces the worst kind of log -- a clean handshake, a successful
join, then silence. The handshake now waits up to 3s for the bind and aborts with a
reason instead.

**Releasing the network.** Ending a session did not make the phone leave: it stayed
associated and Android Auto cycled its wireless setup until it throttled. Removing the
network is the only lever an app has -- no public API disconnects a client from your
own access point, SoftApConfiguration's blocked-client list needs the same call these
units refuse, and the protocol has no teardown message.

**And knowing when not to.** That lever assumes the access point can be put back, and
on some radios it cannot: hostapd's channel scan races the driver re-creating the
interface and loses, returning ENODEV. Measured on the teardown and on every attempt
after it, including the auto-enable that was supposed to be the way back and gets one
try -- the access point stayed down three and a half minutes with the phone
reconnecting throughout. Retrying does not beat it: nine asks across three runs, none
recovering, and the one bring-up that succeeded came from a start posted 127ms behind
a failure, a window nothing at this layer can aim at. Nothing answers the question in
advance and probing means performing the act, so the app learns it the only way
available -- by trying once -- and remembers. One stranded hotspot on such a device
instead of one per session.

Restarting rather than leaving it down is still right where it works: measured, a cold
bring-up costs the next connection ~26s with the phone waiting, against seconds nobody
waits through here. The interrupted case no longer unwinds with the network still gone,
which is the one state this must not leave behind.

Also here, because it is what timed all of the above: a first-frame log on the hardware
decode path, which had none. Driven by its own flag rather than from inside
onFirstFrameListener, which is set only while the projection activity is up -- a log
placed there is silent in exactly the sessions worth timing.

release 3.2.3

Audio: stop taking system focus when it silences the phone we project

Dynamic playback focus (shipped in v.3.2.0-beta1) takes AUDIOFOCUS_GAIN_TRANSIENT
whenever an AA audio channel opens, so a local player such as the car radio
pauses while Android Auto plays. On a head unit that is also the phone's
Bluetooth A2DP sink that backfires: AOSP's A2dpSinkStreamHandler answers
AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT with an AVRCP passthrough PAUSE aimed at the source
device, and the source is the same phone feeding the AA stream. The phone
pauses, Android Auto tears the audio sink down, we release focus, the phone
resumes, and it repeats every few seconds.

Measured on the reporter's unit across three captures (issue #744): the media
session went PAUSED 59-661 ms after each grant and Android Auto dropped the sink
3.4-4.1 s later, with playback anti-correlated to our holding focus in every one.
v.3.1.1 never called requestAudioFocus at all on that phone, which is why it
worked. Issue #681 is the same defect on USB, and the freeze reported later in
#744 is this same loop seen on screen: with the media paused Android Auto has
nothing to animate, so it stops sending frames and the picture stops updating.

PlaybackFocusPolicy decides whether to acquire, from a Bluetooth media-link probe
plus a runtime latch, with an Auto/Always/Never override. Always keeps the
behaviour issue #658 asked for, on units where the probe answers wrongly.

The app takes system focus in three places, and all three now ask the policy:

1. AapAudio.onAudioPlaybackStarted, the transient grab when an audio channel
   opens. This is the one the reporters hit.
2. AapService.requestPermanentAudioFocus and CommManager.startReading, the
   permanent AUDIOFOCUS_GAIN that Static Audio Focus holds for a whole session,
   taken at connect before any audio exists. Harsher than the first: a permanent
   AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS makes the sink pause once and never resume, so the expected
   shape is a session that starts silent rather than one that cycles. That
   prediction is read off the AOSP handler and has NOT been measured.
3. AapControl.audioFocusRequest, which asked the system for whatever focus the
   phone requested over the protocol, honouring GAIN as a permanent grab. Gated
   at the call site rather than inside requestFocusChange, because that function
   is also path 2's caller, where the answer is the opposite. RELEASE is never
   gated -- abandoning focus must always work. The always-grant protocol reply is
   untouched; it is what keeps AA routing audio to the head unit at all.

The reporter's log shows only path 1 firing (three acquire/release cycles, no
AudioFocusRequestNotification at all), so paths 2 and 3 are latent rather than
confirmed.

The latch is the backstop for units whose adapter will not report its A2DP state:
two media channels closing within 5 s of a grant and we stop asking for focus for
the rest of the connection. Only the media channel counts, because speech and
system-sound channels are legitimately that short. Replaying the reporter's own
timings through it, the latch trips on the second cut and suppresses every later
grab. It covers path 1 only -- it is armed from onAudioPlaybackStopped, and paths
2 and 3 grab outside any channel's lifetime, so those rely on the probe alone and
need Never by hand on a unit that cannot be probed.

shouldAcquire and shouldAcquirePermanent are exact complements on the
staticAudioFocus axis; a test walks every combination to prove they can never
both take focus, as WifiModePolicy and UserExitHotspotPolicy do.

The settings are not merged: Static Audio Focus also carries the shared
AudioMixer, software ducking and AU2 precreation, which one four-way selector
would hide.

The Bluetooth probe deliberately uses the configured adapter rather than
getAllBluetoothAdapterHandles(): this runs on the AAP transport thread for every
track change, and enumerating system services by reflection there would stall
video alongside audio. An unreadable state counts as "a link is up" -- a radio
playing over AA is an annoyance, silence is a broken app.

Every decision path logs what the probe answered, so one grep covers all three
and a bug report says which way it went and why. Also moves the focus binder
calls out of the activeAudioChannels lock.

Verified on hardware for path 1: forcing Always reproduces the fault on demand,
with the phone pausing 167-234 ms after each grant, and Automatic shows none of
it. Paths 2 and 3 are unexercised so far.

Settings: let the user choose when other audio is paused

Settings -> Audio -> "Pause Other Audio During Playback", an
Automatic/Always/Never segmented control backing PlaybackFocusPolicy.Mode, with a
hint line that changes per selection. Automatic is the default and the stored
zero value, so an unset preference behaves like the automatic detection rather
than needing a migration.

Always exists because the Bluetooth probe cannot be right everywhere: a head unit
that reports no A2DP state still needs a way to get the ducking behaviour issue
#658 asked for, and a unit where the probe reads a link that is not really there
needs a way to override the other direction. Never is the manual escape for the
paths the runtime latch cannot cover.

Shown whenever the audio sink is on, including with Static Audio Focus enabled --
the mode governs static's permanent grab as well as the per-channel one. Under
static it applies from connect for the whole session rather than only while audio
plays, so an extra hint line says that instead of maintaining a second set of
three strings. A segmented control plus an info banner rather than a dialog:
AlertDialog will not show setMessage and setSingleChoiceItems together, and the
explanation is the part users need.

Also registers playback-focus-mode in both of SettingsBackupManager's lists,
which it was missing from while static-audio-focus was in both: export omitted
it, import skipped it as an unknown key, and a restore that changed it never
asked for the projection restart AapAudio needs, since the mode is read once at
construction. INT rather than a new enum type -- Settings.playbackFocusMode goes
through PlaybackFocusPolicy.Mode.fromInt, which already falls back to Automatic
for any value outside 0-2, so a hand-edited or truncated backup cannot produce an
invalid mode.

English strings only, matching how the rest of this feature landed.

Logging: stop a verbose capture costing more than it reports

We routinely ask reporters for a VERBOSE log, so the logging path is part of the
diagnostic tooling and has to be cheap enough not to change what it measures.
Three things in it were not.

AppLog resolved its level through Settings.exporterLogLevel on every call, which
is a SharedPreferences.getInt() -- a lock and a map lookup -- so every discarded
verbose line, and every LOG_VERBOSE/LOG_DEBUG guard, went to preferences first.
That is paid at the default INFO too, by every user, on every thread. The level
is now cached and refreshed in init(), which is already called from each place
the setting can change. format() also called Throwable().fillInStackTrace(),
capturing the stack a second time -- the constructor has already done it -- for
every emitted line. The Class.method prefix stays; it is what makes these logs
readable.

The file backend no longer formats and writes on the calling thread. It used one
lock shared by the AAP poll and send threads, the audio and video threads and the
main thread, with a SimpleDateFormat and a possible disk flush inside it, so at
verbose those threads serialised against each other several times per frame.
Lines are now timestamped by the caller -- the timestamp has to be when the event
happened, not when the writer got to it -- and handed to a bounded queue drained
by one background thread. A full queue drops the oldest line and says how many,
rather than blocking the thread that produced it. close() deliberately does not
join that thread: it runs on the main thread whenever the log settings change.

AapSslContext.decrypt() logged its status inside synchronized(this), and
encrypt() takes the same monitor, so the whole logging pipeline sat between the
poll thread and the send thread once per decrypted packet. The line is now built
under the lock and emitted after leaving it.

Finally, rotateLogs() only ran when a capture started, so a capture left running
grew until the disk did; the writer now stops at 16 MB with a line saying so,
under LogFilesHelper's 50 MB budget for the directory.

The filter stays at *:V. The framework lines it brings in are what identified
issue #744 -- the AudioManager, AudioTrack and BufferQueueProducer lines around
ours are what let a report be read at all.

None of this caused the freeze reported in #744; that was the audio focus loop.
The reporter's capture is what showed the cost, at 200-320 lines/s sustained and
four lines per video frame.

Stop the setup wizard from overwriting the reported manufacturer

The car step wrote the chosen name into vehicleMake and headUnitMake as well as
the display name. Reporting the make "Google" alongside the model "Desktop Head
Unit" is what makes Android Auto list apps installed from outside the Play Store
— that pairing is the entire mechanism, and it is what was added when sideloaded
apps were first made to work.

The wizard is shown to every upgrader, and its input is pre-filled with the
stored display name, so simply pressing Next through the car step replaced
"Google" with the app's own name. Everything else about the session kept
working, which is why this reads as "my sideloaded apps vanished" and nothing
else. The values live in SharedPreferences, so it survives restarts.

Only a real car brand now becomes the reported manufacturer; the app's own name
and "Google" leave it at "Google". Re-running the wizard therefore also repairs
an install that has already lost it.

The manufacturer is not dead weight — it is what puts the car brand's logo on
Android Auto's exit button, which is why the step wrote it in the first place.
So the car step and both Make fields now say what picking a real brand costs
instead of silently trading one for the other.

Native AA: say which Bluetooth record the wake poke touched

The poke's two target UUIDs were bare constants in the handshake manager and
appeared in its logs as raw UUIDs, so reading a capture meant knowing that
0000111f is the phone's hands-free audio gateway -- the record its own calls
ride on -- and 00001112 the older headset one. That distinction turns out to
matter for what a poke costs, and it should not need to be looked up.

Moves both into a pure BluetoothWakePolicy alongside the order they are tried
in, names them in every poke line, and pins the values in tests: one of them
was stored for years under the name A2DP_SOURCE_UUID, which it never was.

Also expands the stub hands-free record's accept line. "HFP connection
accepted" reads like success; it means the phone has attached its hands-free
link to this app rather than to the head unit's own Bluetooth stack, and the
responder behind it answers OK to everything while negotiating neither a codec
nor a SCO link, so it can never carry a call. Whether it ever fires is still
an open question -- no accept has appeared in five rig rounds or any reporter
log -- and the line now says enough to settle it from a capture.

No behaviour change.

NativeAA: stop the wake poke taking down this unit's own hands-free link

A poke that connects takes the phone's single hands-free slot, and this head
unit's own client is dropped to make room. Measured on the rig: its
HfpClientConnectionService logged its disconnect from the same peer 4 ms after
socket.connect() returned, and the link did not come back on its own -- eight
minutes later it was still down, and only a Bluetooth adapter cycle restored
it. What the user sees is a head unit reporting Bluetooth disconnected while
the phone reports it connected, and phone calls coming out of the phone.

An earlier round saw no damage only because every poke in it failed to
connect; a poke that fails cannot take a slot.

So the poke stands down exactly when there is something to destroy -- which is
also when it is pointless, because a live hands-free link is itself the ACL
connection the poke exists to create. Units where the poke is load-bearing
have no such link to read and are unaffected, and an adapter that will not
report its profiles pokes anyway rather than silently disabling a mechanism
some units cannot connect without.

Both records were measured destructive, HFP-AG by the chain above and HSP-AG
by a later round where a successful poke left the link down for three minutes
across a healthy session. A phone serves both from one headset connection, so
which record is asked for was never the lever -- noted in the policy, because
a setting to reorder them is the obvious wrong fix and was in fact built once.

The skip is logged at info the first time and debug after: the retry loop asks
again every ~30 s and would otherwise bury a capture.

Native AA: don't poke an unpaired phone, and don't forget one we cannot read

A poke is a raw RFCOMM connect() to a device we assume already trusts us.
Against an unpaired one the OS starts a new pairing negotiation as a side
effect, so a phone the user has since unpaired makes the head unit ask to pair
again every time its radio comes back.

The check goes in pokeDevice() rather than only where the retry loop picks its
devices, because the manual poke from the device picker reaches pokeDevice()
directly and would otherwise skip it.

Pruning the stored Auto Start MAC is a second, separate question, and it does
not get the same answer. getBondState() returns BOND_NONE when the Bluetooth
service is simply unavailable rather than admitting it does not know, so an
adapter that happens to be off looks exactly like a phone the user unpaired --
and this head unit's Bluetooth is known to cycle itself. Deleting on that
reading takes away the user's configured device, written straight through to
device-protected storage where nothing restores it.

So the two rules are split and pull opposite ways: strict about poking, since
refusing costs a retry seconds later; lenient about forgetting, since a MAC
kept one round too long costs nothing because it will not be poked. Only a
positive not-paired answer from a working adapter, or an address that was
never a Bluetooth address, is forgotten. A test walks every reading and
asserts none is ever both poked and forgotten.

Video: catch up after a link stall instead of replaying the backlog

A wireless link that goes quiet for a few hundred milliseconds hands over
what it owed in one burst. The decoder rendered every frame of that burst,
so the picture walked forward in slow motion and the gap against audio,
which does not queue the same way, never closed. That is the freezing and
audio lag in #755, and it is why the symptom survived every decoder fix so
far: nothing in the pipeline ever shed a late frame.

Measured on the reporter's unit (mt6765, Android 9, 1280x720, AVC), same
drive, 40 minutes apart:

  USB   129 windows  inputWait mean 40ms   max 83ms    dropped 0
  WiFi   16 windows  inputWait mean 2017ms max 4410ms  dropped 0

Same codec and same negotiated config both times, so the codec is not the
bottleneck - it sustains 60fps over USB with an empty input queue. 4410ms
of input wait per 5000ms with nothing dropped is a standing backlog.

Render only the newest frame the codec has finished, releasing the rest
without rendering. Already-decoded frames cost no reference data, so this
is the one place load can be shed without corrupting what follows. Being
ready is not the same as being late, though: releaseOutputBuffer(true)
returns without waiting for vsync, so one frame sitting ahead of the
display is ordinary pipeline depth, and discarding it would halve the rate
of a healthy 60fps stream. Nothing is discarded until a third frame is
ready; at depth two both are rendered and counted.

Move the wait for a free codec input buffer onto its own thread behind a
bounded queue. It ran on the transport's read thread, which carries video,
audio, microphone and control together, so up to 300ms per frame was time
no other channel could be dispatched and the socket went undrained. In the
reporter's verbose log 12-byte control keepalives arrive up to 2923ms late
against a 1s cadence.

That thread has to be able to outlive its own codec safely, because
interrupt() does not abort a MediaCodec call and stop() joins with a
timeout. It checks its own identity against the field stop() clears, so a
thread that overruns the join can only exit rather than waking up to feed
the next session's codec alongside the next thread - two producers on one
input queue interleave frames and invert decode order.

Frames are copied on the way in because the transport reuses its buffer,
pooled so the copy does not allocate per frame, and stamped with their
arrival time so draining a backlog does not collapse a dozen frames onto
one timestamp. On overflow the arriving frame is dropped rather than a
queued one: the older frames are what everything after them decodes
against, and this protocol has no way to ask for a keyframe cheaply.

Reports skipped alongside dropped, which separates a low rendered count
that was deliberate from one where the frames never arrived.

Audio: bound the queue by default so it cannot drift behind the picture

The audio queue defaulted to unbounded. On a link that goes quiet for a few
hundred milliseconds every chunk of the burst that follows is played, so
audio ends up running that far behind the picture and never catches up -
the audio latency reported in #755, whose log confirms the default was in
use (queueCapacity=0). The bounded path, its drop-on-overflow and the
setting itself already existed; only the default was wrong. 0 stays
selectable for anyone who prefers gap-free audio to lip sync.

50 rather than a tighter figure because the bound has to clear the window
we hand the phone: AapControl advertises max_unacked 30 for wireless audio,
so a burst that size is legal and must fit. A chunk is one AAP message and
its duration follows the channel config - roughly 20ms on 48kHz stereo
media, several times that on the 16kHz mono guidance channel - so the
setting cannot be expressed in milliseconds.

The video window is left alone, with a note saying why. Narrowing it looks
like the same idea and is not: that window counts messages, not frames, and
a keyframe fragments into a dozen or more, so a small window stalls the
phone part-way through sending one and caps throughput at window/RTT -
worst on exactly the congested links this set of changes targets. The
backlog is bounded in the decoder instead, where discarding costs nothing.

WifiDirect: report a station link running alongside the group

A unit joined to an ordinary WiFi network while hosting the WiFi Direct
group makes one radio serve both, and on a single-channel chipset that
divides airtime. What it looks like from the app is projected video and
audio going dead together for a few hundred milliseconds at a time, over
and over, with every counter in the pipeline clean.

That is exactly what #755 turned out to be, and it took a USB comparison
run to find, because nothing in the log said the unit was also on another
network. The reporter's unit sits on a dashcam AP at -32 dBm through every
session; the same log shows the group owner up on p2p0.

Log the station's frequency next to the group's when a group comes up, and
say plainly what the pair means: same channel is shared airtime, different
channels means the radio is also retuning between them. Neither frequency
is required for the warning - some units report the group as 0 MHz.

The association is detected from supplicantState, not networkId or SSID.
Those two are redacted by the location gate whenever the caller cannot
satisfy it, which on a head unit is routine because the service runs
without the projection activity in front, so keying on either would report
"not associated" on exactly the Android versions where this diagnosis is
worth having.

The channel 12/13 warning comes out of the Native AA branch at the same
time. The frequency was already computed for every mode and only the
warning was fenced off, so a Wireless Helper user whose group landed
somewhere phones cannot join got nothing. It still runs after the 5GHz
mismatch retry, which returns early: a group about to be torn down and
remade must not first tell the user to restart their WiFi, and the retry
regenerates the SSID that the warning dedupes on.

Input: let the Bluetooth side keep the media buttons, and stop mangling clicks

Settings -> Input -> "Send Media Buttons To Android Auto", an Always/Automatic/Never
segmented control backing MediaKeyRoutingPolicy.Mode, and a rewrite of the key
de-duplication in CommManager.sendKey as a pure, tested KeyDebouncePolicy.

One press of a steering-wheel Next skipping two tracks (#803) is two consumers acting
on one button, not one key sent twice. The reporter settled it by toggling "Media
audio" for the phone inside a single live projection session, both directions: with
A2DP on, one press skips two tracks; with it off, one. Their logs show exactly one
AA=87 press/release pair per press in both states, so the second skip was never ours
to debounce. AOSP's BluetoothMediaBrowserService publishes a media session whose
skip-to-next issues an AVRCP passthrough FORWARD at the source device -- the phone we
are projecting -- which is the same head-unit-as-A2DP-sink topology d2dff1df measured
for the audio-focus pause loop. Play/pause never doubles for the same reporter, which
corroborates it: passthrough PLAY/PAUSE are state-specific and converge, FORWARD adds
up. A fault inside this app would double both.

Nothing arbitrates the two consumers for us. setConnectionPolicy and setActiveDevice
are BLUETOOTH_PRIVILEGED, abortBroadcast() cannot reach the framework's media-button
route because it picks one target rather than fanning out, and taking audio focus to
deactivate the sink's session is precisely what d2dff1df removed. So the lever is
which consumer we leave the key to.

Always is the stored zero value, so an unset preference keeps the behaviour every
existing install has -- defaulting to Automatic would silently disable media keys for
everyone whose phone is merely paired for calls on a unit whose Bluetooth side never
touches these buttons. Automatic covers a phone paired to this head unit. Never covers
the case Automatic cannot see, reported by a second user on a BMW F30: the phone is
paired to the car's own system, so our adapter reports no link while the factory radio
still acts on every press. Non-media keys are never held back in any mode, which is
what that user asked for -- keep the iDrive controller, drop the media buttons.

BluetoothHelper gains a2dpMediaLinkState() returning null for "could not read", because
the two callers resolve that differently: audio focus assumes a link is up (silence is
worse than a car radio playing over AA), key routing assumes none (buttons that quietly
do nothing are worse than a doubled skip). isA2dpMediaLinkActive is now that call with
its old default applied, so its callers are unchanged. The probe is cached for 2s
rather than run per press: it is a binder round-trip and sendKey runs on the main
thread from dispatchKeyEvent. Short enough that toggling media audio takes effect
without reconnecting, which is how this gets tested. The mode is read live per press,
so it is not in projectionRestartKeys and does not raise the reconnect prompt.

The de-duplication rewrite fixes three defects that were reachable before any of this:

- keyStates was latched before the debounce returned, so a dropped press still marked
  the key down and its release was transmitted -- DOWN, UP, UP on the wire, present in
  the reporter's own logs. A press and its release are now dropped as a unit.
- A press whose release never arrived latched the key: every later press matched the
  held state and returned in silence until the next disconnect. That is the shape of
  the long-standing "steering keys stop working until I restart" reports. A held press
  older than 2s is now closed out with a release and the new press goes through.
- Deliveries are deduped on KeyEvent.getDownTime() where callers have a real event,
  which is exact and needs no tuning, instead of guessing from elapsed time. Two
  deliberate presses inside 600ms used to merge into one; they no longer do. The
  600/300ms windows survive only for the proprietary OEM broadcasts that carry no
  KeyEvent. A downTime of 0 -- what a KeyEvent built from an action and a keycode
  alone carries -- is treated as no identity, or every press would look like a
  redelivery of the last.

sendKey takes the event identity and a source label, and every call site names itself,
so a log finally shows how many distinct physical presses there were rather than how
many deliveries. The silent drops are logged too.
