Projection: a relaunch no longer destroys the session it is replacing

Bringing the main screen forward - the launcher icon, any deep link -
destroys a live projection by launch semantics alone, because MainActivity
and the projection activity are both singleTask in one task, and
MainActivity immediately relaunches it. The relaunch works: measured on
hardware, the new instance renders in 354ms. What kills it is the old
instance's teardown, which lands 250-650ms later (framework-ordered after
onDestroy; one main-looper post later still on GLES) and acts on the shared
session as if it were still the owner:

  - its onSurfaceDestroyed releases video focus, which the phone answers
    with a video sink stop and then sends nothing - the reporter's black
    screen with audio still playing, permanent until the app is killed
  - its view's onDetachedFromWindow and surfaceDestroyed stop the singleton
    decoder unconditionally, killing one its replacement had already
    claimed and was rendering with
  - its onDestroy nulls the decoder listeners the new instance registered
  - its view callback stays registered forever, because removeCallback had
    no callers anywhere

The fix is an ownership primitive on the decoder: an identity check against
the current surface, and a compare-and-stop that runs under the same
monitor setSurface() and stop() already hold, so the comparison cannot race
a newer surface claiming the decoder between check and stop. Identity
rather than equality because each teardown path hands back the exact
Surface object it created. Every teardown-side stop - ProjectionView's two
direct stops and the activity's surface callback - now goes through that
gate; the direct stops are converted rather than deleted because they are
the safety net when the activity callback is not registered, and the
residual double-stop on the live path is idempotent, exactly as the old
triple-stop was.

Around the gate, the relaunch cycle is tidied: onDestroy deregisters the
view callback and clears only the listeners that still belong to this
instance, recreateProjectionView deregisters the same-instance variant (a
discarded GLES view posts its destroy after the replacement is up), the fps
lambda becomes a named field so it has an identity to compare, and
MainActivity's three byte-identical copies of the relaunch intent recipe
collapse into one so the flags the ownership gate protects cannot drift
apart.

A legitimate background is unchanged: its surface is destroyed while it
still owns the decoder, so the focus release and the stop proceed exactly
as before, and audio continues as it always did.

The same round exposed a second half of the same failure. The reconnecting
watchdog gated itself on HandshakeComplete - a state the session passes
through once, briefly, before video starts - and returned without
re-posting itself. The steady state for the whole drive is
TransportStarted, so the watchdog died on its first tick of every session,
and everything hanging off it went with it: the reconnecting overlay, the
display-stall recovery, the renderer-confirm offer. After a mid-session
video stop the app logged nothing and asked for nothing, because the one
unsolicited focus gain sent when a surface appears was the only video
request in the entire session. The state check moves to a policy object
with its full table pinned by a test, and the watchdog now re-requests
video focus when the connection is proven live but no frame has arrived for
long enough that its own reconnecting overlay is up - paced by the existing
keyframe throttle, and sharing one throttle clock with the startup watchdog
so the two never double-fire across the overlay transition. The startup
watchdog itself is unchanged: its overlay-scoped re-arm is by design.

Reproduced live on hardware; force-stop plus relaunch - the reporter's own
workaround - recovered it every time, which is exactly the behaviour this
removes the need for.

Part of the fix for #822.

Video: the decoder survives the surface churn a relaunch causes

With the projection activity's own teardown fixed, the decoder underneath
it still walked a healthy stream into permanent failure whenever a relaunch
rebuilt it. Three separate mechanisms, all measured on hardware, all
triggered by the same ordinary surface swap.

The codec flip/latch ladder exists for one case: a hardware component that
cannot decode this codec type at all, which would restart forever without
it. Its evidence was "no frame rendered since the last start" - but every
surface swap stops the decoder and zeroes that timestamp, so a stream that
had rendered for an hour was indistinguishable from one that never worked.
This SoC takes up to ~8s to produce a first frame after a mid-session
reconfigure, against a 2s stall window, so every relaunch burned 1-3 of the
3 restarts that flip the codec type, the flip configured a decoder
guaranteed wrong for the running stream, and three more strikes latched
decoderPermanentlyFailed for the rest of the session. Reproduced across all
three view backends and with audio on and off. Three changes, one per rung:
a session-scoped "this session has rendered" flag, cleared only when the
session ends, gates the ladder, so a proven codec type is never flipped and
never latched however many warm-up restarts a relaunch costs; while the
session has rendered, a codec instance that has not yet produced its first
frame gets a 10s stall window instead of 2s, above the worst measured
warm-up with margin, because each premature restart reset the warm-up it
was waiting on and the 2s watchdog manufactured the very stall it was
detecting; and setSurface() calls stop() unconditionally rather than only
while a codec object exists, since the failure paths release the codec on
their way down and the latch used to outlive it. Cold-start behaviour is
unchanged - a component that has never produced a frame still walks the
same ladder at the same pace. The decision is a pure object with its table
pinned by a test.

stop() could also release a codec the feed thread was still inside. Latent
since the feed thread was introduced, and correlated with surface teardown
rather than random: when the surface goes away the codec stops draining,
its input queue fills, and the feed thread parks in dequeueInputBuffer for
its full 300ms budget - exactly when a teardown calls stop(). stop() joined
for 200ms, shorter than the call it was waiting on, and interrupt() does
not abort a MediaCodec call, so the join could time out and fall through to
codec.release() with the thread still inside. A post-release call either
throws into a silent catch or wedges the vendor component until the process
dies. The dequeue wait now also aborts the moment running clears, so a
stopping decoder waits one 10ms dequeue rather than the full budget; the
300ms patience for a merely busy codec is unchanged, because it was
measured and shortening it is what used to report a full input queue on
every start. The join rises to 500ms so it exceeds the worst case with
margin, with the thread-identity guard as the backstop. The feed thread is
published to its field before start(), since its loop guard proves identity
by reading that field and a thread that won the race read the null a prior
stop() left and exited at birth, leaving every frame to queue where nobody
drains. A codec whose configure() or start() throws is released, not just
dropped: on head units with a single hardware decoder instance each leaked
component makes every later create fail until the process dies.

Finally, stop() cleared VPS/SPS/PPS and the dimensions parsed out of them
for every reason except a decoder restart, so a surface swap threw away the
description of a stream the phone was still sending unchanged, and the
rebuilt codec configured itself from HeadUnitScreenConfig's negotiated size
with no csd-0 at all. Not hypothetical: "Fallback to negotiated dimensions"
appeared exactly once per relaunch, on every backend, in every capture of
the round that looked. The pinned codec type three lines below already made
this argument - these fields describe the stream, not the decoder instance,
and only a real disconnect can change what the phone is sending - so they
move under the same endsSession() test rather than getting a new one.
codecConfigured moves with them, since keeping the parameter sets while
claiming not to have them would just re-scan for config already in hand.
The failure counters stay where they are, because a new surface clearing a
permanent-failure latch is load-bearing and must not regress.

Two log-hygiene fixes ride along, both of which cost real time to diagnose
around. The stall watchdog's "restart suppressed (N/4 used, ...)" report
moves inside the real-stall branch: it sat outside the idle-versus-stall
split, so it also printed on the branch that had just correctly decided the
phone stopped sending and there was nothing to decode - "0/4 used" every
10 seconds for minutes on an idle stream, which read as a stall watchdog
perpetually declining to restart, a decoder fault that did not exist. Pure
control-flow move: the idle branch stays silent and keeps its lastOutputMs
update, and no arithmetic changes. And pendingKeyframeRequest and its block
in decode() are dropped - nothing has set it since the focus cycle it
belonged to was reduced to a gain-only nudge, so it was a dormant second
keyframe path sitting next to the real one, and a dormant mechanism is how
the first one got overlooked.

Projection: a relaunch that stays black asks the phone properly

With the teardown and the decoder both fixed, the picture came back - but
slowly, and only on two of the three view backends. Measured per backend on
a UNISOC MT50, over the real user route (cover the projection with another
app, return via the launcher):

  SurfaceView   0.68-0.80 s
  TextureView   5.4-52.5 s
  GLES          6.8-116.4 s

Splitting each return into relaunch, codec creation and wait-for-picture
puts 97-99% of every slow return in the last leg. The relaunch itself ran
in 384-507 ms and codec creation in 49-308 ms on every backend including
the fast one, so the recreate-on-launcher-tap path is not the cost and
never was.

The difference is which backend makes the phone restart its video sink.
SurfaceView's surface is destroyed by the cover, so its teardown releases
video focus, and the return's gain makes the phone re-run sink setup, which
begins with a keyframe: Media Start Request VIDEO landed after 4 of 4
SurfaceView returns and 0 of 10 TextureView/GLES returns. The other two
never destroy their surface, so focus is never released and the phone is
never told anything - and asking again with the same message does not work,
because an unsolicited gain sent while the phone still believes we hold
focus is not a state change. Dozens go out per slow return, one every 1.5 s
from the overlay watchdog and one per decoder restart from the transport,
and not one of them is ever followed by a picture.

So escalate instead of repeating. WarmRelaunchKeyframePolicy decides, and
its gates are the point: a decoder rebuilt under a surface that has never
shown a frame, on a session that has already rendered, with the phone still
sending, past a window that covers the healthy path's own worst case. Only
then, and once per surface, is video focus released and taken back - the
sequence SurfaceView performs by accident. Releasing focus across a stream
that is rendering is the #755 regression, and every gate here requires the
opposite situation, where there is no picture to lose.

Three details that are not obvious:

  - The release and the gain are 400 ms apart. Back to back the phone would
    see focus return to PROJECTED before acting on the loss, which is the
    no-op this exists to avoid.
  - Anything that would drop the pending gain sends it instead. Focus left
    released is a permanent black screen with audio still playing, which is
    worse than the slow return being fixed.
  - The check is driven from the surface, not from the reconnecting
    watchdog, which first ticks 5 s after onResume - that would have put a
    floor under recovery above the window the policy specifies. The
    watchdog stays as the backstop.

The release makes the phone answer with a video sink stop, so it is marked
via ignoreNextStopRequest - giving that flag its first writer, and keeping
an unrequested sink stop, the decisive line in several hardware rounds,
still readable as one.

The escalation window is 850 ms, and that number is measured rather than
chosen. It started at 2000 ms, set before any of this code had run and with
no measurement of the healthy path it has to clear; at that value the whole
recovery came to a flat 3.0-3.2 s, of which the window was the largest
single term (the rest: ~480 ms relaunch, ~402 ms release-to-retake, ~150 ms
phone response, ~145 ms decode). The path it must clear is now known: the
slowest a surface has ever been measured rendering unaided is 404 ms, a
SurfaceView return whose codec creation took 308 ms and whose first frame
followed 96 ms later. 850 ms is twice that ceiling. Only the window moved -
the gates that keep a focus release away from a live stream are untouched,
and the phone-alive gate is in fact stricter at 850 ms than at 2000 ms on
the SurfaceView path, where the phone has stopped its sink and so has not
sent recently.

The boundary test is relative to the constant and would stay green at any
value, so the ceiling is recorded as HEALTHY_FIRST_FRAME_CEILING_MS and a
second test holds the window at twice it. Firing early is not a harmless
false positive, and a constant that drifts under the healthy path should
fail with a test that says why. That test is also why the value is 850 and
not a rounder 800: doubling the measured worst case is the rule, and 800
sits under it.

Measured against the same build with this commit's policy removed, same rig
and same day: GLES went from 30.8 s, 74.8 s, one cycle that never rendered
at all, and 49.3 s to 2.08 / 2.06 / 2.00 / 2.03 s, and TextureView to
1.87-1.99 s. SurfaceView, whose teardown already does all of this, fired
the policy zero times and stayed at 0.62-0.76 s.

Video: a surface that dies mid-configure stops restarting into itself

decode() checks the surface is valid before configuring, but the framework
tears surfaces down on the main thread and no lock of ours covers the
window between that check and MediaCodec.configure. When it lands there,
start() throws "Surface not valid" and schedules decoder_start_failed - a
restart that can only fail exactly the same way until a new surface
arrives.

That would be merely wasteful if the retries were local, but they are not.
Every restart reaches onDecoderError, which asks the phone for a keyframe.
Caught in full on a SurfaceView run: the failed restart fired during a
backgrounded window, the phone answered with an unsolicited video sink
start while no surface existed at all, and the session's next genuine
relaunch then needed a full focus cycle to recover from the state that left
behind - 3.2s instead of the 0.7s every other cycle in that run managed.
Pre-existing rather than new: both log strings are present verbatim in the
commit before this one.

The fix is to schedule nothing when the surface is what failed. decode()'s
existing surface guard already idles the path, and setSurface() rebuilds
when the replacement lands, which is the same route every ordinary surface
swap takes. Detected from the surface itself rather than by matching the
exception text, so a genuine start failure that happens to mention a
surface still restarts.

Everything else in the catch is untouched, including the codec release -
that one is load-bearing on head units with a single decoder instance.

The race then fired twice in the following hardware round and was caught
both times, with zero decoder_start_failed restarts and no unsolicited sink
start; both affected cycles were among that round's fastest, so this
removes the slow cycle at its source rather than recovering from it
afterwards.

No policy object: the decision is one framework-coupled predicate with
nothing to decide away from Android, so there is nothing to extract.

Stop discovery opening a second connection to the head unit server

Android Auto's "Start head unit server" developer option binds itself to one
connection and never rebinds for the life of its process. Anything it accepts
that nobody follows through leaves it deaf to every later attempt, recoverable
only by stopping and starting it on the phone -- which is what the reporter has
been doing before every drive.

Four paths opened such a connection and walked away.

onAvailable did stop(); startScan(). stop() is cooperative, so that is a race
rather than a restart: the second sweep starts beside the first and both probe
port 5277. It fires the instant the head unit joins the phone's network,
exactly when a drive starts. Plain startScan() is a no-op while a healthy scan
is in flight, which is what this wanted all along -- a scan is running, so the
network is already being looked at. onAvailable also fires per network and
again on re-validation, hence the debounce.

startDiscovery() answered every request by stopping the old NetworkDiscovery
and constructing a new one. The replacement's scanJob is null, so its guard saw
no scan to wait for and probed while the discarded instance still had a probe
in flight -- and cancelling cannot stop that, because Socket.connect() is not
interruptible. One press of the WiFi button logs "Starting scan... / Scan
interrupted / Starting scan..." four milliseconds apart, because
startWirelessServer() and the ACTION_START_WIRELESS_SCAN handler each call it.
In the reporter's capture "Found Headunit Server" fires 13 times against 10
"Auto-connecting to Headunit Server": three sockets opened to 5277 and
abandoned. The instance is reused now, which lets the guard do the job it was
written for, and it serialises on a class-level job because the resource being
protected is process-wide and the two racing callers were different instances.
A real mode change still gets a fresh instance: stopWirelessServer() nulls it.

A cancelled scan could still be holding a connected socket. Handover runs on
the main thread, so cancellation threw out of withContext before the listener
ran and left the socket behind, and nothing checked for cancellation between
deciding to probe and connecting. The socket has exactly one owner at every
point now, and a cancelled scan closes it rather than delivering it:
cancellation means stop working, and connecting is work.

CommManager.connect(socket) refused a socket handed to it during a connect in
flight and returned without closing it. Discovery gives ownership up at that
call, so nobody else was going to.

isConnected excludes Connecting by design, which is how a rescan reached that
guard at all: the connect-and-handshake window is twelve seconds at worst.
isBusy answers the question discovery actually has -- "will this connection be
followed through" -- and gates both the scan and the handover.

oneShot moves from the listener closure onto the scan, since one instance now
serves callers that want a single sweep and callers that want the re-arm. A
continuous request arriving during a one-shot promotes it rather than being
dropped, which would otherwise end discovery entirely.

DiscoveryModePolicy records which configurations reach this path at all. It is
worth naming because "Headunit Server" (mode 1) and "Wireless Helper / Phone
Hotspot (Host)" (mode 2, strategy 3) look like unrelated features in the
settings screen and are the same code underneath, which is why this defect has
read like two separate reports.

One user-visible consequence: pressing WiFi while a connect is in flight now
does nothing rather than starting a sweep. That sweep could only ever have
produced a socket that was refused.

Fixes #773

Back off from a head unit server that has stopped answering

Once that server is bound to a connection nobody follows through it stays
bound: closing the offending connection does not recover it, and neither does
waiting. So the 10 s discovery loop cannot succeed however long it runs, and it
is not free -- every attempt strands another socket on the phone, which never
reaps them either.

AapTransport can tell that case apart from a broken link of our own. Every read
timed out rather than failing, the peer sent no byte at all, and none of our
sends failed: that is PEER_SILENT, the one handshake failure that says
something about the peer rather than about us, and the only one the user can
act on -- the fix is on the phone, in Android Auto's developer settings.

The count lives in CommManager, in the same continuation that discovers the
failure, rather than in a ConnectionState.Error collector. That state is not
observable: connectionState is a MutableStateFlow, so collection is conflated,
and startHandshake() emits Error and then calls disconnect() -- not a suspend
fun, so .value moves on straight away -- with no suspension point between them.
The value has already reached Disconnected before any collector resumes. In the
reporter's own log the same when-block's Disconnected branch logs four times
and its Error branch never, across 11 handshake failures.

UnresponsivePeerPolicy then slows the rescan and explains, once, what is wrong
and what the user has to do about it. Backing off rather than stopping matters:
the user can fix this from the phone at any moment, and an app that had given
up for good would not notice.

The explanation is gated on the endpoint being the head unit server. The phone
dialling our own server on 5288 and the Nearby helper can both reach the same
branch, and sending their users into Android Auto's developer settings after a
switch they never turned on would be worse than saying nothing.

Also noted, not fixed: onHandshakeFailed() hangs off that same unobservable
Error state, so the USB accessory re-enumeration it performs has presumably
never run either. That predates this and wants its own change.

Close the session while the link still works, when the system warns us first

A peer that vanishes without closing wedges the head unit server exactly as an
abandoned probe does, and nothing above touches that case -- we leak nothing
there, the interface simply goes away underneath an established session. A
session that closes properly does not wedge it, which is the difference between
a drive that ends with the app disconnecting and one that ends with the power
being cut, and it is the only account that fits the reporter saying 3.1.0
worked across drives.

The one lever available is timing, so this takes the losses the system warns us
about first:

- ACTION_SHUTDOWN, already received and until now only logged. A car being
  switched off is the common case.
- WIFI_STATE_DISABLING, not previously listened for at all, which is also a
  user toggling WiFi.

Driving out of range, an access point restarting and a power cut with no
orderly shutdown still arrive with no warning and are not fixable from here.

LinkLossTeardownPolicy decides which sessions a station-WiFi loss applies to. A
P2P group and a soft AP are separate interfaces that outlive the toggle on
several chipsets, so tearing a Native AA session down there would cost a 45-90s
reconnect to prevent nothing; a test asserts the answer is the exact complement
of the two routes that own their own network, so no combination is claimed by
both or missed by both.

It asks the session for whether that link is even the one in use, rather than
the settings. wifiConnectionMode is stored and describes what the app would do
next time: a USB session is live under whatever wireless mode happens to be
selected, and mode 1 is the default the auto server users sit on. Deciding from
it sent a ByeBye and closed a USB drive whenever anything switched WiFi off,
which head units do on their own. CommManager already knows -- the connection
is a SocketAccessoryConnection or it is not -- and the policy takes it as a
parameter rather than inferring it, because the settings genuinely cannot
answer the question and a policy object that quietly guesses is worse than one
that asks. DEVICE_SHUTDOWN stays unconditional: everything is going anyway, and
a USB session that vanishes wedges the phone's server just as a wireless one
does.

The teardown is deliberately not disconnect(). That one means "the user pressed
Exit": it marks a user exit, which suppresses the reconnect, and it honours
killOnDisconnect, which would finish the activities and stop the service on a
WiFi toggle the user expects to come back from. disconnectForLinkLoss() sends
the ByeBye, closes the socket and blocks until that has happened, since the
whole point is that the close goes out before the interface does.

A failed send is now logged. It is how "the ByeBye went out" and "the link was
already gone" tell themselves apart.

Say why the discovery loop stopped, and do not sweep a network that just went away

Two consequences of the changes above, neither of which shows up in a test.

The loop can now end at two guards that return without a word: startDiscovery()'s
isBusy check, and the re-arm at the end of a sweep. Both are correct -- a
connection is live or being set up, so probing would only produce a socket that
gets refused -- but a discovery loop that stops for no visible reason is the one
thing a submitted log cannot be read for. There is no error, no scan line, and
nothing to grep. Both now say which of the two it was, at INFO, so it survives
the default log level users capture at.

The other is a real waste. A link-loss teardown ends the session, and the
ordinary answer to a disconnect is to restart the discovery loop two seconds
later -- on a WiFi network that is, by construction, on its way down. What
getSubnet() then finds is whatever interface enumerates first, usually a modem
bridge, so it sweeps a subnet the phone was never on, every ten seconds, until
WiFi returns. It costs little and it cannot wedge anything, but it reads in a
capture exactly like discovery probing the wrong network for real, and misread
logs are expensive here.

So the WiFi trigger leaves discovery down and lets the network's return revive
it: onAvailable already calls startScan() on the instance, which is still there
because a teardown does not stop the wireless server. The shutdown trigger does
not set the flag -- the device is going with it, so the two seconds do not
matter -- and Nearby and WiFi Direct keep their restarts, since they bring the
phone to us over transports a station toggle did not take away.

Video: feed the codec whole frames, and hold enough of them

Two ways the feed path shed reference frames, both fixed here, because
both are the same mistake: giving the codec less than a whole frame, or
giving up on one the thread in front was still waiting for.

A frame larger than the codec's input buffer used to be split across
buffers - fill one to capacity, restore the limit, loop for the rest.
Each piece reaches the codec as its own buffer, and with no
partial-frame flag on this API range every buffer is parsed as a
complete access unit, so the pieces corrupt the picture as surely as
the loss they were trying to avoid, and did it without even touching
the drop counter. The reference decoders all refuse to do this:
ExoPlayer skips an oversized sample outright and Moonlight treats one
as fatal. Drop the whole frame instead. The check stays inside
feedInputBuffer because that is the only place the real buffer capacity
is known - codecs are free to allocate more or less than the
KEY_MAX_INPUT_SIZE the format asked for - and the dequeued buffer goes
straight back empty so the codec's pool is not depleted. With splitting
gone a frame is fed in exactly one call, so the chunking loop collapses
into a single call returning FED, NO_INPUT_BUFFER or DROPPED_TOO_LARGE,
which also removes a second partial-AU path nobody asked for: a
mid-frame input-buffer timeout used to leave the already-queued pieces
behind in the codec.

The other half is a plain inconsistency. feedInputBuffer waits 300ms
for the codec to free an input buffer; the queue behind it held twelve
frames, "around 200ms" by its own comment. On any codec stall between
those figures the queue was shedding frames the feed thread had not
given up on. One number was chosen against touch latency and the other
against codec behaviour, and nothing reconciled them. Both now live in
VideoFeedQueuePolicy, with the depth derived from a 500ms window
against fpsLimit - 30 frames at 60fps - and a test asserting the queue
always holds more video than the thread in front of it waits for. The
floor exists because fpsLimit is the user's cap rather than a rate
negotiated with the phone; the ceiling bounds pooled memory, and a test
pins the rate at which it starts deciding the depth instead.

A deeper queue is not the latency it looks like: the backlog drains in
milliseconds once the codec unblocks, and the output thread then
discards all but the newest decoded frame, which breaks no prediction.
The exception is a decoder persistently slower than the stream, where
nothing ever drains - the forced software-decoding path, already a
deliberate choice by someone whose hardware decoder does not work.

Measured on hardware (round 6), same rig and an identical transient
CPU-burst lever on both builds: dropped=0 skipped=110 against the
twelve-frame queue's dropped=4 skipped=95, with both of those drops
escalating into a full recovery cycle. That is the trade this change
is for - a prediction-breaking input drop becoming a prediction-safe
output skip.

Video: repair a shed reference frame in seconds, not a GOP

Every frame the feed path still sheds is a reference some later frame
predicts from, so the picture drifts washed-out and blocky until a
keyframe arrives. #830 photographed exactly that: the map still visible
under a white wash, macroblocking on the media card, self-healing
"after a minute or so", on USB and wireless alike. The minute is not a
coincidence - the phone runs a fixed encoder GOP measured at ~69s
(round 4: eight gaps, median 69.4s, spread under 2s, unmoved by sixteen
probe messages), so one lost frame costs ~35s of corruption on average.
That is the reporter's minute, derived without their log.

Both drop sites - queue overflow on the transport thread, input-buffer
exhaustion on the feed thread - now route through one helper that asks
the phone for a keyframe, throttled to one request a second so a
sustained backlog does not cost one per frame. It stays silent until
the codec has rendered a frame: a warming codec sheds frames while
perfectly healthy, which is the startup false positive that burned
#757, and that window belongs to WarmRelaunchKeyframePolicy, which must
not have a second decider reaching for the same lever underneath it.

The ask itself is a gain-only unsolicited focus notification, and it
does not work. Rounds 1 and 2 fired it 419 times under sustained drops
and round 4 reproduced the result on a clean stream: in every round the
median wait to the next keyframe came out at half the natural keyframe
interval, which is what a random observer of a periodic process gets -
the arithmetic of no causal link. It is kept as the first response
because it costs one message, does not disturb a running stream the way
a release can, and has only ever been tested against one phone.

So it escalates. AAP has no keyframe-request message at all - verified
against the protobuf definitions extracted from Google's own Android
Auto binary, which end at MEDIA_MESSAGE_AUDIO_UNDERFLOW_NOTIFICATION
(0x800B), and against the Head Unit Integration Guide, which never
mentions keyframes. VideoConfiguration has no keyframe-interval field
either, so the GOP is not ours to negotiate. Round 4 measured the
cheaper candidates and none of them is cheaper: an UpdateUiConfigRequest
is acknowledged by the phone and changes nothing (16 of 16), and
VIDEO_FOCUS_NATIVE_TRANSIENT produced a full sink stop and a new
session on all five fires. The release/regain focus cycle is the only
lever that exists, and it produces a keyframe 0.52-0.78s later.

KeyframeCycleEscalationPolicy holds the gates, pure and tested. The
trigger is how long the picture has been *unrepaired*, not how long a
drop episode has run: a single lost frame is an episode of length zero,
so anything counting drops or measuring an episode could never fire for
the fault this exists for. A shed frame starts the clock and
VideoKeyframeScanner stops it by reading the NAL type of what actually
reaches the codec - against the pinned codec type, never a user
preference, which is what made 66e59b2c's latch stick for a session,
and gating nothing, so a miss costs one extra request rather than a
frozen picture. Budget: three cycles a session, sixty seconds apart.
Releasing focus across a rendering stream is the precondition of #755,
and seven clean cycles on one rig with one phone is evidence, not proof.

Measured on hardware (round 5): 2.672s and 2.678s from shed frame to
keyframe on both fully-captured cycles, against the ~35s median the
same drop cost before. Budget capped correctly at three with eight
refusals correctly deferring to the phone's own keyframe, spacing
65.3s, and Codec initialized: at zero across every cycle - no #755
signal. Round 6 reproduced the chain at 2.57-2.69s.

Also corrects two comments that claimed things measurement has since
disproven: that the notification trailing UpdateUiConfigRequest brings
a keyframe forward, and that WarmRelaunchKeyframePolicy is the only
policy allowed to reach for a focus release.

Native GPS: send the head unit's own fix, at the only point the phone accepts it

Reported as the Native GPS setting not actually overriding the phone's own
location (GitHub issue #832).

The send point was wrong. A SensorEvent only goes out once the phone's
SENSOR_STARTREQUEST for that type has been processed, and the request for LOCATION
arrives ~1-1.7s after TransportStarted, behind DRIVING_STATUS and NIGHT. Anything
flushing at TransportStarted is structurally too early - the phone cannot have sent
that request before our own read loop, which TransportStarted marks the start of -
and lost the race every time on device. AapControlSensor.sensorStartRequest now
sends the current fix as soon as it answers the phone's own request, mirroring what
NIGHT already did, which is the earliest point a send can succeed. Both outcomes
log: the send with its on-wire result, or that no recent GPS fix existed to prime
with.

What it sends is narrowed to this head unit's own GPS. The obvious accessor,
LocationHolder.currentLocation, falls through to getLastKnownLocation over GPS,
NETWORK and PASSIVE, and whatever came back would travel as SensorType.LOCATION -
the car's own position. That misfires hardest on a unit that has a GPS chip but no
antenna attached: it passes every gate, never locks, and would hand Android Auto a
network fix frequently derived from the very hotspot or P2P group we created.
currentGpsFix reuses the same last-known lookup restricted to GPS_PROVIDER, keeps
the fed fix only when the GPS produced it, and returns null on a unit that has
never locked - which is the right answer: the phone then keeps using its own
location. Its staleness check accepts a future-dated fix on purpose: system clocks
on these units routinely lag GPS time, and a negative age means clock skew, not
staleness. currentLocation keeps its wider behaviour for geofence and the map
picker, which ask a different question.

LocationData.accuracy is now always set. It is a proto2 `required` field, so a fix
reporting no accuracy left it unset and threw UninitializedMessageException out of
build(); inside the control-channel dispatcher that surfaces as a HandleException
and takes the session down.

Native GPS: keep a parked head unit emitting, and stop covering for a dead one

requestLocationUpdates asked for 400ms AND 5m. Android ANDs those two gates and
only advances its previous-location marker on an accepted delivery, so a stationary
head unit received exactly one fix and then nothing - and Android Auto, which
prefers the car's GPS but falls back to the phone once the car's signal looks
interrupted, fell back. Asking on time alone fixes that at the source. 1Hz is the
automotive GPS norm and what Android Auto's navigation is tuned for; the old 5m
gate was delivering a fix every ~0.4-0.6s at driving speed anyway, so this is fewer
updates while moving and a steady stream instead of a single fix while parked.

The fan-out cost of that stream is paid at the sink, not by starving navigation:
the receiver now skips the stored-location write when the coordinates have not
changed, since a parked unit repeats the same position every second and each write
rewrote the whole preferences file.

A periodic resend of the last real fix stays as a backstop for a chip that only
emits on change, bounded four ways. It only fires for a beat the chip actually
missed - while real fixes arrive on schedule it does nothing, so it never
duplicates the live stream. It is skipped when the user has chosen the phone as
the GPS source, where it could never reach the phone anyway. It stops once
the last real fix is older than a minute, measured on the monotonic clock because a
resend bumps Location.time by design - without that bound a GPS that dies mid-drive
(tunnel, garage, antenna knocked loose) looked exactly like a parked car forever,
and Android Auto would stay pinned to a stale position rather than falling back. A
confidently wrong position while moving is worse than the stall the resend exists
to prevent. And it only ever republishes a fix from onLocationChanged, so it cannot
mislabel a network or passive fix as this head unit's real GPS.

The log gains what diagnoses a unit end to end, and no position: which gate refused
when no subscription was made, the first fix and how long the lock took, the point
where a stale fix stops being resent, and - verbose only - a bare per-fix cadence
line. That last one is what a parked verbose log needs to show whether the chip
honours a time-only subscription, i.e. whether the resend backstop is still earning
its keep on real hardware.

stop() clears every field start() and the resend depend on, and onLocationChanged
ignores a callback dispatched after stop(), so a re-armed instance cannot republish
a fix from the previous connection.

Sensors: report a dropped event once, not once per event

AapTransport silently discarded a sensor event when the phone had not started that
sensor type - the two branches that would have said so were commented out. With
LOCATION now arriving about once a second, the case most worth diagnosing (the
phone never sends SENSOR_STARTREQUEST for LOCATION) would have produced either
nothing or a flood.

It reports now: the first drop of each sensor type immediately, then a per-type
count at most every 30s for as long as the condition lasts. The bookkeeping is
synchronised - and startSensor with it - because sensor events are sent from the
main thread while the AAP poll thread fills startedSensors, and the report line
iterates that set.

CommManager's connection-state gate stays as it was: events arriving before
TransportStarted are the pre-handshake window the priming fix already covers, and
AapTransport's report is the one that carries the diagnosis.

Vehicle info: colour the dialog note with a call that exists below Android 6

Tapping Vehicle ID or Make under Head Unit killed the app on Android 5.1. The
dialog those fields open shows an explanatory note, and the note's colour was
read with Resources.getColor(int, Theme) — an API 23 method, on an app whose
minSdk is 16. Below Android 6 the method is simply absent:

  java.lang.NoSuchMethodError: No virtual method
    getColor(ILandroid/content/res/Resources$Theme;)I in class
    Landroid/content/res/Resources;
      at VehicleInfoFragment.showTextInputDialogWithMessage
      at VehicleInfoFragment$updateSettingsList$5   (Vehicle ID)
      at VehicleInfoFragment$updateSettingsList$7   (Head Unit Make)

Fields without a note pass messageResId = null and skip the branch entirely,
which is why Display name, Model and Year were unaffected and why the report
reads as two specific fields rather than a broken page. Since 8dda5c19 gave
Vehicle Make a note as well, 3.2.4 onward has a third crash site on the same
devices; one line covers all three.

DialogUtils already had the correct form of this same helper, so this only
brings the private copy in VehicleInfoFragment into line with it.

Neither CI workflow ran lint, and abortOnError is off, so NewApi had no way to
fail anything — hence a third job that runs lint and fails on NewApi alone.
Other lint findings stay non-blocking; an API above minSdk is not a warning,
it is a crash on a user's head unit.

DPI picker: let the keyboard close, and keep the number that was typed

Tapping the DPI value in the setup wizard opened the keyboard with no way to
put it away: not the keyboard's own check key, not the wizard's buttons. Back
lowered it, and then Next saved the previous DPI rather than the typed one.

Two faults, both in the shared picker.

The check key did nothing because the editor-action listener returned true.
Consuming IME_ACTION_DONE skips TextView's own handling of it, and that
handling is the thing that lowers the keyboard. It now dismisses explicitly,
which is what this codebase already does elsewhere for the head units that will
not close a keyboard on their own; it also accepts IME_NULL, for hardware Enter
and the OEM keyboards that send no action id.

The typed value was dropped because the only paths that folded the field into
the picker were that dead handler and a focus-loss listener. Back leaves focus
on the field, and buttons take no focus in touch mode, so neither the wizard's
Next nor the DPI screen's Save moved it — the value stayed in the text field
and dpi kept reporting the slider. Both call sites now commit first, and the
picker commits itself when it stops being visible, so a step change or the
Automatic switch cannot strand a value or leave the keyboard up.

Settings -> DPI was worse than the wizard: Save is enabled from the change
callback, so a typed value left it disabled and could not be saved at all.

The commit is a separate call and not part of the dpi getter on purpose. As a
getter it would recurse without bound: commitInput -> applyDpi -> onDpiChanged
-> a listener reading dpi -> commitInput.

Also drops the slider's step from 2 to 1 so a typed 175 stays 175 instead of
snapping to 176 — invisible until now only because typed values never survived.
The Kotlin constant and android:stepSize have to move together: applyDpi
assigns slider.value, and a Slider throws IllegalStateException for a value
that is not valueFrom plus a whole number of steps.

Video: rebuild the projection pipeline from the stream instead of from a guess

Reassembly, allocation, decoder configuration and the keyframe wait, which were
five branches and then sixteen commits and then four before this. Folded here as
one because they are one change: every part of the path from a video message to a
rendered frame stops assuming what the phone will send and reads it instead.

 - AapVideo reassembles fragments against the declared total the protocol carries
   on flag 9, which the old code discarded, so a lost middle fragment is now
   visible rather than silently decoded as a holed access unit.
 - Buffers are sized from the device rather than from a constant, behind
   DeviceMemoryProfile, because the 1 GB units in the reports could not hold what
   the constant asked for.
 - The decoder is configured from the stream's own parameter sets, and the codec
   is chosen through DecoderConfigLadder and DecoderCapabilityReport instead of
   from a name match.
 - A codec rebuilt mid-session resumes on a P-frame and can render nothing until
   an IDR, and the phone's GOP is around 69 s. DecoderStallCausePolicy names that
   case and asks for a keyframe rather than rebuilding again. AAP has no keyframe
   request, so the lever is a video-focus cycle; FocusCycleLever makes the two
   implementations of it mutually exclusive.

Validated on hardware (UNISOC MT50): the failing case ran 2 faults, 2 rebuilds,
2 focus cycles, keyframes 0.544 s and 0.557 s later, and rendered was never zero
in any window. A control run with the focus cycle swapped for the inert mode 4
reproduced the pre-fix wedge at full severity, so the escalation path is
measured load-bearing rather than assumed.

Reproduces the tree of 1b962591 exactly.

Video: an idle screen is not a fault, and a keyframe repairs only when it decodes

The second half of the same work, kept separate because it is about what happens
after the pipeline is right: telling a quiet wire apart from a broken one, and
proving a repair worked instead of assuming it. Folds b7bc0367, e77e6ba0,
a22c84e9 and 3ec512ea.

 - Android Auto sends no video when nothing on screen animates, so a still
   picture is not a lost connection. ProjectionWatchdogPolicy now requires the
   link itself to have gone quiet before it says so, and DecoderStallCausePolicy
   refuses to rebuild a codec that is merely receiving nothing. The two are
   independent layers and neither gates the other; recovery in both is still
   driven by the frame gap, so a real stall is still repaired.
 - A read that loses bytes ends the session. Skipping after a short read leaves
   the socket desynchronised and unrecoverable, so AapReadRecoveryPolicy stops
   rather than resynchronising into a stream that already lost framing.
 - KeyframeRepairTracker closes the loop: a keyframe counts as a repair only once
   a frame decodes, so a request that changed nothing no longer reads as success.
   AuditRecoveryPolicy carries the framing audit's finding through to the repair.
 - A relaunch onto an idle screen can still ask for the picture back
   (WarmRelaunchKeyframePolicy), which is the black-screen-on-return case.
 - videoCodec is a preference expressed to the phone, not a command to the
   decoder, so an announced codec that the phone declines no longer rebuilds a
   decoder against a stream in the other codec.

One file here is not video: twelve lines in WifiDirectManager raise the discovery
loop's only log line to INFO and say whether a session is live while the peer
search runs. It sits with this work because it is an instrument for the same
investigation, and because the level it was at is one no reporter is ever asked
to capture.

Reproduces the tree of 3ec512ea exactly.

WiFi Direct: ask for the band we want, and let a stopped manager start again

Three things about the group this app hosts, all in WifiDirectManager and its
policies. Folds b79a2b69, 7ec828ba, 38e56a1f and f925199f.

The band. Nothing in the reports records which band a group came up on: below
API 29 getGroupFrequency returns 0 and the reflection over frequency/mFrequency
finds nothing, so "Freq: 0 MHz (unknown)" is every capture. Two levers follow
from that. NativeGroupBandPolicy lets the test rig host on 2.4 GHz deliberately,
so the band can be a variable instead of an assumption. P2pOperatingChannelPolicy
and WifiP2pChannelCompat give pre-Android-10 units the only band control they
have: setWifiP2pChannels is hidden but present, and an operating channel of 36
becomes setDisallowedFrequencies around 5180 MHz. Off by default, because a unit
whose P2P firmware cannot host a 5 GHz group owner would fail to form a group at
all; it clears the restriction and retries once if that happens, releases it once
the group forms, and clears it on teardown, since the list lives in the
supplicant and would otherwise outlive this app.

Channel 14 sits at 2484 MHz, not on the 5 MHz grid. P2pChannelPolicy already knew
that and converts the other way, so the constant is now shared and a round trip
through both objects is asserted.

The lifecycle. stop() unregistered the P2P receiver but left isReceiverRegistered
true, so it never registered again and CONNECTION_CHANGED stopped arriving; it
also left checkGroupAndCreateInFlight latched, so no group was ever created
again. In-flight ActionListener continuations could create a group after stop(),
defeating a user-exit teardown, and the detached credential-delivery thread never
revalidated its group, so a dead group's SSID and passphrase could overwrite the
live one and the phone was handed a network that no longer exists. A generation
counter and a credentials epoch close all four, and the join watchdog is now
armed once per group rather than on every group-info callback.

Reproduces the tree of f925199f exactly.

Native AA: bind the wireless server so it can rebind, and read credentials once

Two defects on the handshake path, both in main rather than regressions from the
work below.

ServerSocket(5288).apply { reuseAddress = true } sets SO_REUSEADDR after the
constructor has already bound, where it does nothing. While the previous peer is
in TIME_WAIT the rebind throws, so the phone is woken by the poke and then handed
nothing at all. Binding explicitly after setting the flag is the fix.

The four credential fields were plain vars written by the group-info thread and
read by the handshake thread: a torn read hands the phone a mismatched SSID and
BSSID, which Gearhead rejects as WIFI_INVALID_BSSID, and the null check could
pass before a field was cleared and then fail on the !! as "Handshake error:
null". They are one immutable snapshot behind a single volatile now.

Also: the manual poke button woke the phone with nothing listening, because
start() could not reopen listeners that closeAaListeners() had closed. It now
re-inits when the manager is not active rather than assuming it is.

Reproduces the tree of 828bada5 exactly, so this branch's tip is byte-for-byte
the stack it replaces.

Native AA: a wireless server that failed to bind can now be repaired

A reporter's head unit hosted its network, woke the phone over Bluetooth, handed
out credentials, and then aborted every handshake with "nothing is listening on
port 5288", about every four seconds, for as long as the capture ran. Everything
upstream worked: 5 GHz group up, BSSID accepted, credentials delivered three
times per group, the phone arriving over Bluetooth each time.

Two things made that state permanent and invisible.

**It latched.** startWirelessServer() opened with `if (wirelessServer != null)
return`, which reads "assigned" as "running". The bind happens asynchronously
inside the coroutine the server launches; if it throws, or the accept loop exits,
the finally clears the listening flag and closes the socket but leaves the object
in the field. Every later call then returned immediately and nothing rebound.
Only a full initWifiMode() cleared the field, so the port stayed dead for the
life of the mode.

**It was silent.** Of the four ways this can go, two printed nothing at all: a
start skipped by that guard, and a coroutine cancelled before it bound (the catch
logs only `if (isActive)`). So "never started", "started and skipped", "started
and threw" and "started and cancelled" were indistinguishable, which is why two
otherwise complete reporter captures cannot attribute this failure. That is the
larger half of this commit.

WirelessServerRestartPolicy decides between leaving a server alone, starting one,
waiting for one that is still binding, and replacing one that died. The middle
case is load-bearing: assigned-and-not-listening is normal for a second or so
while the bind retries, and treating it as dead would tear down a server about to
succeed, whose replacement would then race it for the same port. SO_REUSEADDR
does not help there - it covers TIME_WAIT, not a live listener. `job?.isActive`
is what separates the two. Rebuilds are bounded (3 per 60 s, 10 s apart, budget
cleared by a successful bind) because the caller is a handshake that retries
every few seconds, and a port that can never bind would otherwise become a
rebuild loop worse than the stall it replaces. A live session is never disturbed.

The repair is narrow on purpose: it replaces the WirelessServer object only, and
must never call stopWirelessServer(), which also sets activeWifiMode = -1 and
would make the poke and auto-start paths force a full re-init, tearing down the
P2P group and minting a new SSID in the middle of the handoff being rescued.

NativeAaHandshakeManager now asks for that repair before aborting, so a server
that died once no longer stays dead. The ensure marshals onto Main because every
other caller of startWirelessServer() runs there; without it this one arrives
from Dispatchers.IO and can pass the same check as initWifiMode() and both bind.
Its wait is deliberately short, since awaitWirelessServerListening() delays
without pumping the session's inbound channel.

Also: the bind is retried three times rather than dying on the first exception,
and every outcome now prints, including a line before the launch so a coroutine
that never runs is visible by the absence that follows it.

Does not prove the reporter's root cause. No bind failure is recorded in either
of their captures, and neither is a successful start; what this changes is that
the next capture says which.

AapRead: probe the phone before calling a quiet link dead

A socket read that returned empty ended the session outright: one 15 s
window with no traffic logged "connection lost" and returned -1, which
tears the transport down and costs a full handshake and the "Android is
starting" screen to recover.

That window is not evidence of a dead link. A stall that long is ordinary
on WiFi -- a scan, a power-save wake, a retransmission burst, or a head
unit busy enough not to service the socket for a moment -- while a link
that has actually gone is rare. The file's own comment above the read said
as much ("the phone can be idle for minutes and that's normal") while the
code below it assumed the opposite.

The USB path already gets this right: on a timeout it returns 0 and keeps
reading, and only gives up once the connection itself reports it is down.
That test has no equivalent here, because a TCP socket whose peer has
vanished goes on reporting isConnected == true -- the flag records that
connect() once succeeded and nothing more. So the socket path could not
tell idle from dead, and resolved it by assuming dead.

Stop inferring and ask. The protocol already carries a ping, which this
app answers for the phone but never sends. A silent window now costs a
PING_REQUEST rather than the session, and only a peer that ignores three
consecutive probes is treated as gone -- roughly a minute, against the one
window it used to take. Any inbound byte resets the count, including the
response to a probe still in flight, so a busy link never approaches the
limit and a dead one cannot escape it.

Add a side-by-side diagnostics build

Chasing an intermittent fault on a device meant replacing the working app
with a debug one, and capture defaults to off, so the first reproduction
-- the drive where it actually dropped -- produced nothing and had to be
hit again with the setting turned on.

The debug variant now installs as a separate package (".dev" suffix,
"Open Headunit Dev" in the launcher) and starts capturing to a file at
DEBUG on first launch. A file rather than logcat because the ring buffer
has long since wrapped by the time a mid-drive drop is read; DEBUG rather
than VERBOSE because verbose emits several lines per video frame, and on
a device slow enough to be dropping the connection that load is itself
something the investigation would be measuring. These are defaults only
-- a choice made in the settings UI is stored and wins.

Two things do not follow applicationId on their own and had to be made to:

- The NAVIGATION_UPDATE signature permission. A permission belongs to
  whichever package declares it first, system-wide, so sharing the name
  with an installed store build is INSTALL_FAILED_DUPLICATE_PERMISSION
  and the debug build will not install at all. It now comes from a
  manifest placeholder, defaulting to the canonical name, with the send
  site reading the same value from BuildConfig so the two cannot drift.
  A release declares exactly what it always did.

- android:targetPackage in shortcuts.xml, which is a literal in a resource
  file. Left inherited, every shortcut on the debug build launched the
  store app instead -- the one case where two installed builds actively
  mislead, because the shortcut looks like it worked.

The trace was attached only when the logger was Logger.Android, so a

gets read afterwards, and the throwable is the whole reason these call
sites pass one.

error" followed by a blank line. With the trace kept it reads
java.net.BindException: EADDRINUSE at AapService.kt:3084 -- a second head

rather than a symptom.

Nearby: build the tunnel whichever callback arrives last, and say why one failed

Two Nearby callbacks decide whether a stream tunnel gets built, and nothing
orders them. onBandwidthChanged reporting HIGH before onConnectionResult had
recorded the endpoint was discarded against an activeEndpointId that was still
null -- and Nearby does not report the upgrade again. The decision now lives in
maybeBuildTunnel(), fed by recorded state, so either callback can complete it.

The same class of race lost the phone's stream payload: a null-safe assignment
dropped it when it arrived before our own socket existed. The phone does not
send it twice, so the tunnel stayed half-open until Nearby gave up ~16s later
with nothing in the log connecting cause to effect. An early stream is now held
and attached when the socket appears.

That 16s was spent parked on an unbounded latch.await() in NearbySocket, which
made "the phone never answered" indistinguishable from "the phone is slow". The
wait is bounded at 12s and throws; recvBlocking already maps IOException to -1,
so it degrades into the ordinary disconnect path.

Captures from a Note8 show the two remaining failures are also indistinguishable
from inside NearbyManager and need opposite responses: across seven attempts
with one tablet the head unit's own Wi-Fi was torn down and rebuilt four times
while Nearby negotiated its upgrade, and no payload ever arrived; across two
attempts with a phone that works, zero drops and both tunnels completed. So the
active network is recorded at connect and compared on failure, and the log now
carries the conclusion -- peer never answered, or this radio cannot hold the
access point link while forming the peer-to-peer group -- instead of a symptom.

Also stop logging one line per failed 5289 probe. A single /24 sweep wrote 254
of them and four sweeps buried an entire connection fault under 60% of the
capture. scanSubnet reports the tally, which says more than the lines it
replaces: "253 probed, 0 responded, 253 silent on 5289 (last:
SocketTimeoutException)".

The Lint (NewApi) job added in 8bec136d does not complete. The last run sat in
./gradlew :app:lintGithubDebug for 2h 16m and its final output was

with no lintReportGithubDebug after it, so it stalls inside the analysis task

This was already known. .github/workflows/README.md carries a "No lint job
(yet)" note recording the same hang and the same guess at its cause, and

The likely cause, worth writing down for whoever tries again: the eight
generated protobuf files under aap/protocol/proto/ total about 107k lines of
Java and are checked into the main source set rather than build/generated, so
lint cannot skip them as generated. It parses all of it, and NewApi then does

What this gives up is real. lint { abortOnError = false } means no lint finding
blocks anything, and on a minSdk 16 app NewApi is not a style warning: it is
the crash 8bec136d fixed, a NoSuchMethodError on Android 5.1 from an API 23
call (#858). Until a lint job can run, changes touching framework APIs need the
API level checked by review.

Merge upstream/main, and withdraw the idle probe that #861 disproved

The branch and #861 changed the same read loop, and the conflict is not a
textual one: the two commits answer the same question in opposite ways.

This branch argued that a silent read window is not evidence of a dead link,
so it sent a PING_REQUEST and waited three unanswered probes -- about a
minute -- before giving up. That rested on an assumption never measured here:
that windows of that length are ordinary on WiFi.

#861 measured it, and the assumption is wrong. LinkGapMonitor records that
the phone sends a CONTROL Ping Request once a second for the life of the
session, so fifteen seconds of total silence is fifteen missed pings, not a
stall. A link that quiet is already outside anything a working one does, and
there is nothing left for our own probe to establish.

The cost of being wrong is not symmetric either. AapReadRecoveryPolicy has a
capture of what follows a short read: 69 WRONG FLAG lines and 63 SSL decrypt
failures within four seconds, because the byte stream cannot resynchronise
once an unknown number of bytes are gone. Waiting a further minute does not
recover that session; it only delays the reconnect that would.

So the probe is removed rather than merged -- IdleLinkProbePolicy and its
test, AapTransport.sendIdleProbe, and the PING_RESPONSE arm in AapControl
that is now unreachable because nothing sends the request. Both read files
are taken from upstream whole.

What survives is what #861 does not touch: the Nearby tunnel race, the
AppLog trace that is still dropped whenever the logger is not Logger.Android,
and the side-by-side debug build.
