Diagnostics: see a media-only outage, an idle screen, and the station state

Five captures from a 1 GB MediaTek head unit put the same fault in front of
three instruments and none of them reported it. A 2x2 of codec against the head
unit's WiFi station being joined to a network shows the station is the variable
and the codec is not: joined, no dropout longer than 0.65s in 138s and zero
audio underruns on H.265, and on H.264 a 69s clean stretch with zero underruns;
unjoined, the picture gone for four to eight seconds every ten and a half,
thirty underruns in two minutes, both codecs alike. What follows is what the app
needed in order to have said so itself.

PER-SERIES GAPS

LinkGapMonitor measures silence on any channel against 1200ms, and the phone
sends a CONTROL Ping Request about once a second for the life of the session, so
a link carrying nothing but pings scores healthy while both media channels are
gone. It printed twice across the five logs, both times naming a gap of 1.6-1.8s,
including in windows that each held three six-second blackouts. So the same
measurement now runs per series, the all-channel monitor untouched plus video and
the three audio sinks, because reading the three together is what separates a
dead radio, which silences all of them, from a stalled media path, which is what
the captures show: video and audio dying in the same window twelve times out of
twelve while control ran on.

The media series need more than a gap count before they speak, and hardware
answered that rather than a design assumption. Three untouched minutes on a
stationary Google Maps screen with no navigation printed four video-gap lines on
a rig whose session was clean by every other measure. The assumption had been
that Android Auto sends no video at all while nothing animates, one long silence
per window, which a two-gaps-minimum floor would suppress. What it actually sends
is a trickle: an isolated packet every few seconds, a clock tick or a location
pulse, and every one of those arrivals closes a gap and opens the next. Measured:
four windows, 2-5 gaps in each, dead=95%, 99%, 96%, 99%, intervals scattered from
3.3s to 17.9s. The floor suppressed none of it.

What separates that from the fault is not how many gaps there are but how much
picture runs between them. The reporter's waveform is 4-8s of silence every 10.5s
with video at 45-55 fps in between, dead around 55-60% and 22% on the milder
capture, against 95-99% for a screen nobody is touching. Nothing measured has ever
landed between, so the media series require both two gaps and a window no more
than 85% dead. A window past that is not a stuttering picture, it is a stopped
one, and a stopped picture already has instruments: the projection watchdog
decides when to call it a lost connection and the decoder reports the rate. The
link series keeps no ceiling, because a link that quiet really is dead.

THE UPLINK

UplinkStallMonitor adds the half no inbound series can supply. The media channels
are flow-controlled by max_unacked, twelve frames on video and thirty on each
audio sink, so a head unit whose MediaAcks stop leaving the socket stalls video
and audio together and leaves control alone, which is the observed shape. The
send handler serves one socket from one thread, so the write's own duration is
the time the uplink refused to drain.

THE STATION STATE

logStationCoexistence told the user that one radio serving both the station link
and the group can stall video and audio together, and to disconnect the other
network. It said so on a comparison it had just described as unavailable:
WifiP2pGroup.getFrequency() arrived in API 29, so every unit below that reports
the group frequency as zero and the advice went out anyway. On this unit it fired
on all three station-joined runs and on neither unjoined one, and joined was the
configuration that worked. It then fired again on a second rig with both
frequencies known and 260 MHz apart, during ten minutes at 45-55 fps with no gap
on any channel. That is two units, and no measurement anywhere in which
disconnecting the station helped, so StationCoexistencePolicy keeps a
prescription for nothing: the retune is real and worth naming in a log, telling
the user to act on it is not supported, and the line describes and stops.

It also returned silently whenever the supplicant was not associated, so only one
arm of the comparison ever printed. A capture with no coexistence line in it
meant either "not joined to any other network" or "the read threw", and nothing
could tell those apart. That cost this work directly: a test brief asserted the
rig had no station association, when it has been joined to a 5500 MHz network
throughout, which made the unjoined arm of a planned run untestable and was only
found when the joined arm printed something the brief said was impossible.

describeNotAssociated() is a new function rather than a flag on describe(): every
existing branch presumes association, and a zero station frequency there already
means "associated, frequency unreadable below Android 10", which must not
collapse into "not associated". A test pins the property the change exists for,
that the two arms are separable by a single grep. The dedupe key now carries the
association state alongside the group, so a station that drops or joins part-way
through one group says so once more instead of standing on whatever it said
first.

A MUTED HEAD UNIT LOOKS LIKE A BROKEN ONE

With enableAudioSink false the media and speech channels are never declared, so
the phone never opens them and never sends audio. Nothing said so anywhere. The
log of a deliberately muted head unit is identical to the log of one whose audio
has broken: no channel setup, no media messages, every audio instrument reading
zero, and no cause in the file. It has already cost a test round, spent on an
audio run that could not have produced audio, before the setting was found by
reading the device's settings.xml rather than the capture. One INFO line on the
else branch, following the pattern the Bluetooth service already uses eleven
lines below, and worded so a reporter can act on it rather than in terms of the
setting key.

THE ONE CHANGE THAT IS NOT DIAGNOSTIC

maybeRecoverFromDisplayStall rebuilt the projection view and the decoder in the
middle of a link outage, about 1.7s more black screen plus a forced focus cycle,
for a fault no rebuild can fix, and two defects in its long-frame counter made
that inevitable. The baseline is never seeded: the check survives its gates only
when the picture has been still for over two seconds while video arrived within
the last one and a half, which happened once in two minutes on this link, and
subtracting a baseline of zero charged the session's entire fourteen long frames
to that one tick, tripping a floor of ten on its first evaluation. And the window
counted slots rather than time, while the check returns early whenever video is
not arriving, so five surviving ticks could span two minutes. Each slot now
carries the clock reading it was written at, only slots inside the window are
summed, and a tick with no recent baseline re-baselines and charges nothing. A
consumer that is genuinely collapsing keeps ticking, because video keeps arriving
throughout, and loses only its first tick; the escalation ladder and the frozen
branch are untouched.

Nothing reads either monitor's report.

Offline VPN: give it an owner, a session lever, and a teardown that works

The dummy VPN was stopped from the last line of stopWirelessServer(), which
initWifiMode() runs on every mode change. A #839 reporter described the VPN
icon disappearing on their second connection and the audio stutters coming
back with it; their log shows the mechanism outright:

  03:28:00.278  AapService.initWifiMode | Initializing WiFi Mode: 3
  03:28:00.281  VpnControl.stopVpn      | Stopping DummyVpnService

Three milliseconds. The wireless server never owned the VPN, so it stops
deciding. DummyVpnPolicy holds the ownership rules: SELF_MODE or SESSION, and
a VPN with no owner is never touched. Only the teardowns that own it call
stopDummyVpn(), and there is deliberately no Reason for a wireless re-init.

Removing that stop cost the one cleanup it did by accident, so startSelfMode()
now arms a 120s watchdog: Self Mode with no phone takes the tun back down
rather than leaving the unit without IPv4.

A second reporter on different hardware saw the same periodic outage go quiet
while the VPN happened to be up, which is what the new setting is for. It is
off by default and gated twice. keepDummyVpnDuringSession is the trigger, and
shouldStartForSession re-tests the connection mode at the point of use: the
toggle only renders inside the Native AA block, so a preference turned on there
and then hidden by a mode change would otherwise put a blackholing tun on a USB
session. The mechanism it claims is a working theory, not a measurement, and
the setting's own description says so.

A session VPN also has to leave this app's own sockets alone, which Self Mode's
never had to. An Android VPN captures its own app's traffic too, and this one
routes 0.0.0.0/0 into a descriptor nobody reads, so every socket opened after it
comes up is dropped, including the one a reconnect needs. The session owner
therefore establishes with addDisallowedApplication(packageName); Self Mode
still must not, because its whole purpose is a non-null activeNetwork for our
own process.

The flavor seam is the second half. Google does not allow the fake VPN this app
uses for offline Self Mode, so the playstore flavor must ship none of it.
isVpnAvailable() was the seam meant to say that, but the only copy of
VpnControl hardcoded true and lived in app/src/github/, which is why the flavor
could not compile at all. The reason nobody ever added the missing copy is one
line of .gitignore: "playstore/", sitting next to "cert/" and clearly meant for
a root-level store assets folder. The pattern is unanchored, so it matched
app/src/playstore/ too and silently swallowed anything put there.
!app/src/playstore/ re-includes it.

app/src/playstore/.../VpnControl.kt now answers no to everything, and main stops
touching android.net.VpnService and DummyVpnService directly: VpnService.prepare
moves behind consentIntent() and isPrepared(), so Self Mode and the new session
toggle go through the same seam. The prepared check is short-circuited on
isVpnAvailable() so the playstore path cannot reach a prepare() call at all. The
seam covers the copy as well as the code: the keep_dummy_vpn strings live in
app/src/github/res/values/strings.xml, so the words are absent from the Play
Store APK, and main reads them through VpnControl's resource ids, which the
playstore copy answers 0. Both copies must keep identical signatures.

The last part is the teardown, and it is the part that was never working at all.
A rig round on an Android 14 unit ran the session VPN through two teardowns.
Both of them logged exactly what they were supposed to:

  releasing the dummy VPN (owner=SESSION, reason=SESSION_ENDED)
  VpnControl: Stopping DummyVpnService (GitHub Build)

and neither did anything. tun0 stayed <POINTOPOINT,UP,LOWER_UP> from the first
establish() through the end of the round, the service's createTime never
advanced, and dumpsys showed why: Client AppBindRecord{... system/1000},
hasBound=true. The framework binds to a VpnService the moment establish()
succeeds, so stopService() clears the started flag and stops there. A bound
service is not destroyed, onDestroy() never runs, and the descriptor stays open.
Only killing the process took the tun down. The cost is the one the app
announces when it brings the VPN up, that other apps on the unit have no IPv4,
and it was being paid from the first session that raised the tun until the
process died rather than for the session that asked for it. Self Mode's teardown
goes through the same call, so this was never confined to the new setting.

Asking the service to stop through an Intent is not the answer either: starting
a non-foreground service from the background throws on O+, which is precisely
where the teardown runs, since AapService.onDestroy() calls stopForeground(true)
on the line before stopDummyVpn(). So the stop does not go through an Intent at
all and closes the descriptor on the running instance directly. stopService()
stays behind it for a service that was started but never established, where
there is no instance and only the started flag to clear.

onRevoke() was unhandled next door, with the same shape of silent failure:
after the user or another VPN app takes the slot, vpnInterface stays non-null
and startVpn()'s idempotence guard refuses to establish a new tun for the rest
of the process's life. It now clears that state. Since a revoke arrives on a
binder thread and the close can now come from any caller's thread, startVpn and
stopVpn are synchronized.

Native AA: one session at a time, and credentials the phone can use

Three faults on the wireless bring-up path, all of which leave a unit that looks
healthy in its own log and never connects a phone.

THE WIRELESS STACK RAN UNDERNEATH A USB SESSION

Wireless bring-up is driven entirely by the stored wifiConnectionMode and never
asked what the live session is riding on. initWifiMode() runs from onCreate()
before USB is even probed, and onConnected() stopped nothing, so a wired session
carried all of it alongside.

A reporter's USB capture has every piece of it at once, on Native AA:

  03:00:33  Native AA recovery (no phone joined within 60s): recreate attempt 2/4
  03:00:33  Standard createGroup SUCCESS!            group up 10s before USB connects
  03:00:43  SSL handshake complete                   USB session live
  03:00:47  Stopping poke retry loop (session=true)  4.1s after the handshake
  03:01:35  Native AA join watchdog fired but a session is already connected
  03:01:49  NearbyManager: Stopping discovery ...    only at user exit
  03:01:49  User exit with wirelessServer active     :5288 bound throughout
  03:01:51  WifiDirectManager: Stopping and cleaning up

The P2P group, the RFCOMM listeners, Nearby, the :5288 server and the join
watchdog all ran for the full session, and none of them can succeed while USB
owns it: no phone can join a group it is not looking for. The watchdog only
avoided tearing the group down mid-session because of a guard added for a
different reason.

The poke loop is the half with teeth. It does refuse to poke once a session
exists, but it only asks at the top of each iteration and an iteration is a 15s
hold plus a 15s gap, so 4.1s here and 30s worst case are spent opening RFCOMM
connections into a live link. Each one raises an OS-level ACL_CONNECTED that
AutoStartReceiver reads as the user's phone arriving, and the answer to that can
be initWifiMode(force = true), which rebuilds the P2P group underneath a session
that is already up.

So:

- onConnected() asks commManager.isWirelessSession, not the settings, and on a
  wired session stops NetworkDiscovery, Nearby, the Native AA handshake manager
  and the P2P group. Stopping NetworkDiscovery matters beyond the re-arm: the
  isBusy gate stops the next sweep, while the one in flight keeps probing 254
  addresses on two ports each.
- The poke loop is now cancelled on the connect event rather than polled, for
  every transport, via NativeAaHandshakeManager.onSessionEstablished().
- initWifiMode() refuses to arm while a wired session is live, so the Bluetooth
  auto-start path cannot walk the stack back up behind it.
- No HIGH_PERF WiFi lock for a session whose bytes are not on the radio.
- Disconnect re-arms with one initWifiMode(force = true), which subsumes the
  mode-3 reset and the user-exit teardown; running those as well would race a
  stop() against the re-arm's createGroup. Re-arming on a user exit too, because
  unplugging has to return the unit to its configured mode either way.

Taking the group down here is safe precisely because no phone can be on it, and
it is never reused: the re-arm creates a fresh one, so the never-reuse-a-P2P-group
rule holds by construction. UsbSessionQuiescePolicy states the rule and the
quiesce/re-arm symmetry, with tests. A stack taken down with no way back is how a
long-lived manager ends up unable to re-arm.

THE HOTSPOT TRANSPORT DROPPED THE CREDENTIALS IT RESOLVED

On the head unit hotspot transport, a unit whose access point is already up never
wakes the phone. Everything the app is supposed to do it does, and then it stops.
From a reporter's capture, in 60 ms:

  19:49:11.893  Native AA on the head unit hotspot - resolving credentials
  19:49:11.899  NativeAA: Starting Bluetooth Handshake Servers
  19:49:11.916  NativeAA: ACTIVELY LISTENING on Android Auto UUID
  19:49:11.937  SoftApCredentials: SUCCESS - Providing credentials from wlan0:
                SSID=..., IP=192.168.43.1, BSSID=<a real one>

and then, for the remaining 2m40s, no "Received WiFi credentials from manager",
no poke delay, no poke attempt and no accepted connection.

onNativeCredentials logs at INFO unconditionally on both of its branches, so
neither line printing means onCredentialsReady was null when publish() invoked
it. onCreate started the provider by way of initWifiModeWithOptionalWait and
wired the listener fifteen lines later. start() launches its resolve on IO, and
with the access point already on it publishes on the first poll iteration, 44 ms
later, while the main thread is still inside onCreate. The delivery hit a null
field.

It is unrecoverable for the run rather than merely late. publish() returning
PUBLISHED makes beginResolve return, so the loop never polls again and there is
no second delivery to catch. The handshake manager's credentials stay null, so no
poke is ever scheduled and there is nothing to put in a type 3 response even if
the phone dials in by itself. The unit holds a working access point and an open
Bluetooth listener and looks, in the log, exactly like one idling. WiFi Direct
shares the wiring order but does not lose the race, because startNativeAaQuietHost
goes through the async P2P framework and takes seconds.

The listener block moves above initWifiModeWithOptionalWait, next to the manager
construction it belongs to. Every setter is a field assignment and every lambda
reads its managers at invoke time, so this is only an ordering change, and it
covers both transports. CredentialsHandoff then carries the value from whichever
side arrives first, so the class cannot throw away the one delivery a run makes:
latest-value, not a queue, because older credentials describe a network the phone
can no longer join. And publish() says so when nothing was listening, since until
now the log of a unit that never woke its phone was identical to a healthy one
waiting for the user.

Measured on a UNISOC MT50 with the access point already up before launch on both
arms: baseline 0 "Received WiFi credentials from manager" and 0 pokes, candidate
1 and 1. The gap between "Native AA on the head unit hotspot" and "SUCCESS -
Providing credentials" was 52 ms on the baseline and 58 ms on the candidate, so
the window was genuinely open on both and the arms are comparable. The reordering
is what does the work: "the access point resolved before anything was listening
for it" appeared zero times on the candidate, so CredentialsHandoff covers a
timing this rig did not produce rather than the one it did.

THE ANSWER ARRIVES WHEN NOBODY CAN ACT ON IT

Most reports that call the hotspot transport dead are a head unit that could not
read its own hotspot name and password, so the credentials handed to the phone
were empty and nothing ever joined the network.

The app already detected this exactly. SoftApCredentialsPolicy.decide returns a
dedicated CONFIG_UNREADABLE verdict meaning "there is an access point and this
device will not name it, and waiting cannot change that", the provider stops
polling and logs the remedy, and the overrides that fix it have had settings rows
all along. What was missing is reach, not detection: the verdict is produced
during a handshake, and every string naming the remedy is phrased as "if the log
says the name could not be read". The failure is reported to the audience least
able to act on it, and the values that would fix it sit unset a few rows below.

So the same question is now asked when the user picks Native mode or switches the
transport, which is when they are already in Settings with a keyboard.
NativeCredentialsPreflightPolicy is pure and answers per field: supplied by the
user, available from the device, must be entered, or unknown.
NativeCredentialsPreflight gathers the facts and decides nothing.

Two properties keep it from becoming noise.

Only certainties are reported. The hotspot name and password are answerable with
the access point down, because getSoftApConfiguration reads the stored
configuration and a refusal there is a permission refusal, so a no now is a no at
handshake time. A MAC is not: it has to be read off an interface that exists, so
it is reported inconclusive whenever there was nothing to read from, and unknown
is never prompted for. The hotspot probe also refuses to answer while the
framework says no access point is running, because pickApInterface will otherwise
land on a cellular bridge and report confidently about the wrong network, which is
the trap NativeCredentialsPolicy.shouldPublishCredentials already exists for.

Nothing is asked for that could not work. The WiFi Direct route reports the BSSID
and nothing else: its network name and passphrase are generated by the framework
per group and read back off WifiP2pGroup, so a name the user typed could not
match the group the phone is told to join, and no setting for one exists. Where
location services are off, the toggle is offered instead of a MAC, because a
static override outranks every automatic source afterwards and so outlives the
problem it was entered for.

No new settings rows. The check hangs off handleNativeAaSelection, which already
ran a compatibility gate on mode 3 and showed a dialog, and the prompts reuse the
same entry dialogs and the same copy as the rows themselves.

Two fixes on the path this feeds, which it cannot ship without, since its whole
purpose is to get more users hand-typing MAC addresses. WifiDirectManager took the
static BSSID verbatim whenever it was anything other than the unset sentinel "0";
a mistyped address won the chain, did not match the masked-string test below it,
suppressed all six fallbacks, and surfaced 30 s later at Type 3 time as a message
blaming location services. It now goes through SoftApBssidPolicy.choose, which is
what the hotspot route has used since the same bug was found there, and the value
is validated where it is typed rather than accepted and dealt with later. And a
P2P group that came up with no network name was dropped with no else branch and no
log at all, reaching the reader only as the handshake's generic "No WiFi
credentials available after Ns wait", which points at the credentials wait rather
than at the group that never named itself.

17 unit tests pin the outcome table. Two cover a blanked hotspot configuration,
which arrives as a present pair of empty strings because HotspotConfigReader's
pre-Q branch returns the fields with no emptiness check. Testing nullness there
asked only for the name, and setting a manual name is what makes
SoftApCredentialsPolicy.resolve stop consulting the device, so the check would
have walked the user into the open-network trap that policy exists to prevent.

Native AA: keep the reason a connection failed, and say it on the main screen

The app already works out why a wireless connection failed and says so exactly.
What it does not do is keep the answer. The verdict is produced mid-handshake and
written to a log nobody reads from the driver's seat, so by the time the user is
in front of the app with a keyboard nothing anywhere says what went wrong, and
the main screen that MainActivity deliberately returns them to after a failed
attempt says nothing at all.

THE RECORD

Each condition is now recorded where it is detected and cleared where it is
disproved. Three conditions, one stamp each, independently cleared, because they
are independent: a user who has set a manual hotspot name gets credentials
published while the configuration is still unreadable.

Wall clock rather than elapsed realtime, unlike every other stamp on this route,
because these outlive a reboot and get rendered as a time. The suffix on the
property names is the reminder. Nothing here is cleared by a manager restarting,
a mode change or a user exit: those change what the app is doing, not what the
hardware did.

The third condition is new. A handshake where the phone opened the channel, our
write returned and nothing ever came back had no user-visible signal at all, and
it is the one that matters most: a stack that accepts the write and airs nothing
logs every send exactly like a healthy one, so the log reads as a session waiting
for the user. It reuses the predicate already driving the handshake backoff
rather than inventing a second one, because that predicate already excludes the
aborts that are ours rather than the radio's.

That predicate needed a fix to be true. spokeToPhone was set when the version
request and the start request went out, but not when the credentials themselves
did, and not for a ping response. With the version exchange off by default the
phone can open the exchange itself, and then the only thing we send is the
credentials, so the flag stayed false through exactly the case worth recording.
It is now set after every write returns, which also means such a handshake counts
against consecutiveHandshakeFailures where it did not before. That is the reading
the counter's own comment asks for.

A test pins the precondition the flag depends on: with the version exchange off,
SocketReady emits nothing and the phone's request is accepted against a unit that
has written nothing yet. If that ever changes so we always speak first, the flag
stops separating "we transmitted and got silence" from "the phone went first",
and the record would start accusing units never given the chance.

THE BANNER

One banner, naming the condition and what fixes it, tappable straight through to
the setting that fixes it.

In activity_main.xml rather than fragment_home.xml because the home screen has
two layout variants, a landscape constraint chain and a portrait grid, and a
banner in there would mean two of everything and two ways to get it wrong. The
root here is already a frame holding four sibling overlays over the nav host, so
this is a fifth, and both orientations get it.

One at a time, most recently raised, because these panels are commonly 1024x600
and often 800x480 and three stacked warnings would be the screen. Dismissable per
occurrence rather than permanently: the stamp is compared against the next raise,
so dismissing hides what has been read and the next failure brings it back on its
own.

Never beside a live session, and never in front of the wizard. The first is not
cosmetic: in picture-in-picture the main screen is deliberately left in front of
a running projection, so an unguarded banner would sit next to a connection that
is working perfectly well.

Deliberately not driven by CommManager.connectionState. Its Error value is never
delivered to a collector, since the flow is conflated and startHandshake
overwrites Error with Disconnected before any collector resumes. The overlay
observer next to this has an Error branch that cannot fire, which is the trap.
This reads stamps instead, and refreshes on resume, which is when somebody comes
back from a failed attempt.

The tap seeds the settings search rather than using EXTRA_DESTINATION, which
targets a whole screen. All three remedies are rows inside one list, and search
is the only thing that overrides the Basic and Advanced filter. Static BSSID is
Advanced-only, so a Basic-mode user sent to Settings any other way would arrive
at a list that does not contain the row the banner just named.

The look is the existing info banner with a warning tint, forked rather than
reinvented, amber rather than red because these are conditions a user can usually
fix and a red panel on a dashboard reads as a fault in the car.

The decisions are a pure object with tests, next to the rename notice's, because
each one is a way of being wrong in front of somebody: a warning beside a working
session, one that outlives its own remedy, one that cannot be dismissed, one that
names a route the user is not on.

WHAT THE HARDWARE ROUNDS CHANGED

The first round passed, and then found four ways the banner told somebody to do
something that was not going to help.

A record does not apply to every route. HOTSPOT_CONFIG_UNREADABLE showed on the
main screen while WiFi Direct was selected, a transport that never resolves
credentials from our own access point and cannot produce that condition at all.
Each condition is now filtered by where it is raised, rather than by a looser
notion of what a route touches: the two handshake conditions need Native AA,
BSSID_UNAVAILABLE needs WiFi Direct because the hotspot transport survives a
masked address by sending an empty one, and HOTSPOT_CONFIG_UNREADABLE needs the
hotspot transport because nothing else constructs the provider that raises it.
That is a suppression and not a clear, so the paragraph above about a mode change
still holds: the stamps stay, and are only hidden while they cannot be the reason
the last attempt failed.

A record whose remedy is already in place is worse than no record, so
remedyApplied() hides one whose override is set.

The tap reached one of the two fields it needs. It seeded "Hotspot name (manual)"
and the settings search is a plain substring match, so the password row was
filtered out. That row is not optional: once a manual name is set the device's own
configuration is never read, so a blank password goes out as an open network the
phone refuses rather than falling back to the real one. Both rows now carry one
shared phrase as a search keyword and the banner seeds the same string resource,
so the two sides cannot drift and a translated build matches on the translated
phrase.

And "WiFi address" is not a term anybody would search for. A BSSID is the access
point's MAC address, and the row the banner points at is called Static BSSID.

A WORKAROUND IS NOT A DISPROOF

The second round found the retire rule was wrong, and the measurement is exact.
publish() reached its SUCCESS line and cleared the persisted stamp
unconditionally, four lines after warning that an empty passphrase is an open
network the phone will refuse. So with the hotspot name set and the password
blank, the run that showed the banner deleted the record behind it, and it could
never come back: decide() returns CONFIG_UNREADABLE only when the resolved SSID
is empty, so a name that is set is a name that resolves. A user who did half the
remedy lost the instruction permanently.

With both fields set the clear also fired, but the device still will not name its
own access point. The record describes the hardware, so only the device naming
its own access point retires it, and a hand-typed name is a way round the fault
rather than proof it is gone. remedyApplied() is what keeps the surviving record
off the screen, which makes it load-bearing rather than cosmetic.

Keeping the record is not sufficient on its own, because dismissal is per
occurrence and a stamp that never advances is hidden for good after one
dismissal. The publish site therefore raises rather than merely keeps when the
credentials going out are not joinable, which also gives a device that names an
open access point its first signal of any kind. The same shape was latent on
BSSID_UNAVAILABLE behind a static override, and that clear is now gated on a real
disproof and on the WiFi Direct transport, since the hotspot route cannot raise
the condition at all. The predicate and remedyApplied are exact complements and a
test asserts it.

ONE SURFACE

A forced toast and a three-condition notification carried these same verdicts for
a while, and both are removed here. Both predate the record: the toast is gone in
seconds, the notification the moment somebody swipes it, and neither answers the
question the user actually arrives with. The durable record does, the settings
preflight asks the same questions before the user ever connects, and three places
to say one thing is three places to keep in step. The toast was also posted past
the user's own show-toast-messages preference, so it was the only unmuteable one
on the route.

Wireless settings: let the user pick the band, and show each lever where it is read

Both Native AA transports could already land on 2.4 GHz, and on neither of them
was that a choice anybody could make. The two now carry the same Auto / 5 GHz
only / 2.4 GHz only selector, and the rows around them are shown where they are
read.

THE HEAD UNIT HOTSPOT

The hotspot transport reached 2.4 GHz three ways: the [5 GHz, 2.4 GHz] fallback
sweep in HotspotManager, the device refusing the band request and hostapd's ACS
then picking whatever it likes, and the user's own hotspot being up already.
SoftApBandPolicy.attemptOrder(prefer5Ghz = false) returned [BAND_2GHZ] and had no
production caller at all since it was written, no setting and no UI.

So the boolean becomes HotspotBandPreference (AUTO, FORCE_5GHZ, FORCE_2_4GHZ),
backed by Settings.hotspotBand and in the backup allowlist, and it is rendered on
both routes that reach the sweep: Native AA's hotspot transport and Helper
strategy 4.

The KDoc that drove the old shape said "5 GHz is what the link needs", which
over-states what was measured. 2.4 GHz held 800x480/30 for 308 s on the rig and
only failed at 1080p/60. The wording is why the fallback had no off switch and
why the log offered no remedy, so the hint now says what the measurement says and
tells the user to lower resolution and frame rate along with the band.

HotspotManager's break warning named attemptOrder().last() unconditionally, so it
could tell the user that "trying 2.4 GHz would start the same access point again"
about the band it had just tried. That was live before this change, and forcing a
single band would have made it the common case.

This half is unverifiable on the rig available, which refuses
setSoftApConfiguration() for both bands, so the request never reaches the
framework and the sweep breaks on the first band. Coverage is SoftApBandPolicy's
own tests.

WIFI DIRECT

WiFi Direct had three levers for the same question and none of them was that
choice: a rig-only 2.4 GHz debug flag, an opt-in for the pre-Q operating channel,
and the UNII-1 versus UNII-3 sub-choice. The first two collapse into
Settings.wifiDirectBand and P2pBandPreference, mirroring the hotspot enum
exactly, with values migrating on first read; the sub-choice stays.

On API 29 and up the preference drives the band request. Auto is today's default
unchanged, and 5 GHz only differs from it in one place: the create-failure
exhaustion no longer falls through to a no-band createGroup, because a session on
2.4 GHz can connect, look entirely healthy and show nothing, which is harder to
diagnose than a group that never forms. Choosing 2.4 GHz disarms the band
mismatch retry for free, since shouldRetryFor5Ghz already requires that 5 GHz was
what was asked for, and leaving it armed would tear the group down as soon as it
succeeded.

Below API 29 there is no band request, so the app asks for an operating channel
through hidden setWifiP2pChannels, which is a disallowed-frequency list rather
than a preference. That is the hazard: a unit whose firmware cannot host a group
owner on the band it names is not left on the other one, it is left with nowhere
legal to put a group and fails outright. What shipped cleared the restriction and
retried once, letting the driver pick, and nothing ever requested 2.4 GHz.
attemptChannels() makes it a ladder instead, channel 36 then channel 6 then
unrestricted, so a wrong answer costs a round trip rather than the connection.

That ladder is also what makes 5 GHz safe to try by default there. It was an
opt-in precisely because a wrong default cost every pre-Q unit its connection;
with somewhere to fall back to, that reasoning no longer holds. Pre-Q cannot read
a group's frequency back, so the outcome is unverifiable on the device either way,
and the rig runs Android 14 and takes the real band request. Coverage for this
half is NativeGroupBandPolicy's and P2pOperatingChannelPolicy's own tests.

One long-standing log line said ", forcing 2.4GHz" where the code called
standardCreateGroup with no band request at all. It now says what happens.

WHERE EACH LEVER IS SHOWN

The three WiFi Direct band levers were gated only on pendingWifiConnectionMode ==
3, so they rendered on the hotspot transport too, where createQuietGroup, the only
thing that reads them, is unreachable. WifiModePolicy.usesWifiDirect is the wrong
gate for them despite what it is normally for, because it also claims mode 2
strategy 1, which does not reach that function either.

The mirror fault was worse. autoEnableHotspot was never rendered on Native AA with
the hotspot transport, although that route reads it twice, so the setting
governing the route was unreachable from the screen that selects the route.

Static BSSID had no gate at all: it was added after every mode block closed, with
Advanced-only as the only thing limiting it. Its read sites mean mode 3 on both
transports and mode 2 strategy 1, so it is gated on exactly that. Not
usesWifiDirect, which would drop mode 3 on the hotspot transport, a route that
does read the override. The banner's remedy deep-links here by searching the row
title, and search bypasses the tier filter but not construction, so a stricter
gate would land that remedy on an empty result. The row is also relabelled Static
BSSID (MAC Address), matching the banner's own wording.

Both band selectors are in the Basic tier, since the question they answer is one
a user hits before they know Advanced exists.

THE EXPERIMENTAL TAG

The hotspot transport's note loses it, after two hardware rounds. The Auto-Enable
Hotspot dialog keeps its own, which is a different feature: the reflective
hotspot-on call, which the test rig still refuses outright on both bands.

That note is also trimmed from 204 characters to 106. The clause it loses told the
user to enter the network name below if it could not be read automatically, and
that failure now has a main-screen banner naming it and tapping through to both
override rows.

Untranslated English copies of the strings this touches are deleted rather than
left behind, so a change to the default actually reaches those locales. Only
values-de and values-ko were ever real translations, and both are updated in
place.

WHAT THE ROWS SAY, AND WHERE THEY SIT

Both band hints were written as the argument for the default rather than as help
text, and ran to 584 and 612 characters on panels that are commonly 1024x600.
They are now two sentences each: the fallback order, the ceiling, and on WiFi
Direct the pre-Q clause, which is the one thing a reader cannot infer from the
options themselves.

The hotspot hint stated its evidence in the form it was measured in, a 1080p/60
session dying and an 800x480/30 one holding. It now says 2.4 GHz is reliable up
to 720p. That figure sits between the two measurements and was never itself
tested, which is deliberate and is written down in SoftApBandPolicy's KDoc beside
the numbers it rounds: quoting both would ask a user to work out where their own
panel falls between them. The raw measurement stays in the KDocs, in the
Settings comment and in HotspotManager's retry log line, where the audience is
somebody diagnosing rather than choosing.

The WiFi Direct block also moves above the three rows shared by both transports,
the Bluetooth adapter, the secondary Bluetooth service and the version exchange,
so it sits directly under the transport selector the way the hotspot arm's rows
already do. The band is the first thing to try when a wireless session connects
and shows no picture, and it was fifth. In Basic it barely moves, since those
three rows are Advanced-only; in Advanced it goes from fifth to first. The move
is a pure relocation of 33 lines, gate and comment included, and the dependent
upper-5-GHz toggle travels inside it.

AAP: stop dropping the last fragment of a video frame

The AAP flag byte is a bitfield and only a message with bit 0x01 set
carries the 2-byte message type at offset 0. decrypt's guard rejected
every payload under two bytes on every channel and flag, so a legal
1-byte flag-10 tail (any access unit whose size mod 16384 is 1) was
discarded, costing the whole frame and every P-frame that references it.
Measured seven for seven across a reporter's 3.2.5 and 3.2.6 logs: each
"Decrypted payload too short: 1" is followed within 21ms by "Previous
frame was truncated", with the framing audit silent because it counts
fragments before decrypt.

The guard now applies only to messages that carry a type. The crash it
was written against (fb47a323 read two bytes out of an exactly sized
one-byte array) can no longer happen: the plaintext buffer is pooled and
never smaller than 131080 bytes, and the only reallocation grows it.
Every consumer of a 0- or 1-byte continuation was checked: the video
path appends from offset 0, the assembler reads no bytes, and the
decoder rejects empty units.

The "Decrypted payload too short" line now carries channel, flags and
enc_len so the next capture says which stream and which framing state
produced it. AapMessageFraming names the bit semantics in one place,
with tests, so the next guard reads the flag instead of assuming a type.

Also records why the sustains=false decoder-capability WARN on the
reporter's unit does not justify revisiting the 1440p rule: their
throughput windows show fed equal to rendered with inputWait at 3
percent, which exonerates the decoder.

Video: a corrupt access unit reaches the focus cycle, at every budget position, all drive long

Three fixes to one lever, the only repair AAP allows (there is no
keyframe request; the release/regain cycle produces one in 0.52-0.78s).

AapVideo's corruption callback was armed with escalatable=false, so a
wire truncation got only the gain-only nudge, measured inert across four
rounds, and armed no clock. Measured in a reporter's 2h21m session: the
one event that escalated repaired in 2.78s, the three that could not
stayed broken 27.5s, 11.2s and 19.2s. The path now passes the same
hasRenderedThisSession gate the dropped-frame path uses, and wire
corruption is its own parameter rather than the inverse of escalatable,
because the lastWireCorruptionMs stamp had to survive the flip. Rig
validated: truncation-to-repair 2682/2673/2687ms against 68.65s and zero
escalations on the previous build.

The wire-quiet gate then checked the last-cycle hold before the
isolated-fault exemption, so a lone truncation arriving with one cycle
left waited a full quiet window: ~15.5s instead of ~2.4s, on exactly the
event the reserve exists for. The exemption now leads and covers every
budget position; the hold and the deferral ceiling apply only once
corruption has continued past the arm. All four prior last-cycle tests
hold unchanged.

And the 3-cycle session budget was sized for a bad patch, not a drive: a
multi-hour session meeting an isolated fault every half hour spends it
on the first three and meets the fourth with nothing. A spent cycle now
comes back after five unbroken minutes of quiet on both clocks, one per
window, capped so lifetime spends can never exceed 8 per drive. The cap
is an invariant on potential (spends so far plus what the refreshed
budget could still spend), because capping on spends alone double counts
unspent headroom and allows a ninth; a greedy spend/refund property test
converges on the ceiling exactly. Nothing comes back while the picture
is unrepaired, so the held last cycle stays held, and five quiet minutes
cannot occur under any injection cadence, so rounds measure it inert.

Video: return the input buffer when the feed throws

feedInputBuffer's catch lost the dequeued input buffer index: anything
throwing between dequeueInputBuffer and queueInputBuffer left the codec's
input pool permanently one buffer shallower. Enough throws and every
later feed times out with NO_INPUT_BUFFER, which the stall watchdog then
answers with a rebuild the codec never earned - a stall whose cause looks
like backpressure and is actually attrition. The null-getInputBuffer path
leaked the same way.

The catch now hands the buffer back empty, the way the too-large drop
path always has, and reports the new FeedResult.ERROR so the loop's
answer is a keyframe request rather than logFeedDrop's 'Input buffer
full' - the one label the case is not. A throw after queueInputBuffer is
told apart and stays FED: the codec holds that frame, and reporting it
shed would spend a keyframe request on a picture that is not broken.

Logs: say which build produced a capture, and when SSL unwraps nothing

No exported log ever named the build, the device or the settings that
produced it; telling 3.2.5 from 3.2.6 in one reporter thread meant
fingerprinting which log lines existed. A one-line banner now prints at
WARN (reporters run there) from both export paths: after the logcat pipe
starts, and before the ring-buffer dump, so it is present even when no
capture was running. Verified on hardware through both paths.

And a zero-produce SSL unwrap printed only at DEBUG, so on reporter
captures the story of a desync started at the disconnect instead of at
the cause. A single one is legal TLS (a record can carry only handshake
or alert bytes), so the line goes out at WARN through the same refilling
burst-then-summary budget the framing audit uses; built under the lock,
emitted outside it, like the status line beside it.

Video: split the watchdog clocks the concealment window will race

Behaviour preserving, twice over, so the mechanism that needs both
lands as its own diff.

lastOutputMs (the sync_stall watchdog's clock) now stamps on every
dequeued output buffer; lastFrameRenderedMs (the display watchdogs'
instrument) stamps only when a frame reaches the surface. The two were
one fact only while every dequeued buffer was also displayed; anything
that legitimately holds a decoded frame off the screen must not read as
a codec that stopped decoding, because that classifies STALLED and
rebuilds the codec into a P-frame, the exact wedge
DecoderStallCausePolicy was written to break.

The 5s display-freeze deadline and the 2s watchdog tick move from
private vals in the projection activity to named constants on
ProjectionWatchdogPolicy, beside FRAME_GAP_MS and LINK_QUIET_MS,
so a unit test can pin anything racing them. Note the tick sets
detection granularity only: a condition is seen up to one tick after
its threshold, never before, so a racer's margin belongs under the
threshold itself.

Video: hold the last good frame instead of melting it after a lost access unit

A lost access unit has never been fed - the assembler discards damaged
units - but every P-frame after it references a picture the decoder does
not have, and showing them is the melt reporters describe. Even a
successful escalated repair leaves that on screen for a measured 2.7s,
and in every state where the escalation is refused it runs to the
phone's ~69s GOP.

The output thread now answers a corruption report by releasing buffers
unrendered, so the surface keeps the last good frame; the window closes
on the frame KeyframeRepairTracker confirms as the repaired picture,
which is itself shown, or on a 3.5s cap sized above the slowest measured
escalated repair and a full second under the display-freeze teardown,
both pinned by tests. An expired window disarms concealment until the
next confirmed keyframe, so sustained loss buys one freeze and then the
honest smear, never a strobe. Third attempt at hiding corruption, first
to meet every constraint the two removed ones set: the feed is untouched
(the 66e59b2c latch starved the codec for 16.5s), the keyframe signal
uses the pinned codec type via the tracker, the bound is wall clock held
once per output-loop turn even when the phone goes idle mid-window, and
a lost window stamp fails open. The policy has no absorbing state; a
property test walks every state to a rendered frame inside the cap.

The one damaged unit still fed - a missing middle fragment, invisible to
the reassembler and caught only by the framing audit's byte accounting -
is now discarded instead, behind a 256-byte floor over the channel's
learned expectation because the audit's history is false positives and a
discarded keyframe costs a whole GOP. The one-shot verdict travels on
the poll thread ahead of the completing fragment and is consumed by the
next process() whatever its action.

Reported from AapVideo above the wire throttle so a swallowed report
still conceals; backpressure drops deliberately do not report (marginal
hardware would strobe-freeze). Window edges print at WARN through the
shared refilling budget, and the throughput line carries concealed= so a
capture can tell a window from a wedged decoder.

Rig validated end to end: hold/restore pairs at 2651-2683ms across
truncation, holed-run and orphan faults, one millisecond from the
pre-concealment repair on the same fault shape; the previously wedging
holed-run mode left "Configuring decoder" at 1; a 30-fault storm
produced exactly one freeze; 121 clean-control windows all concealed=0
with zero watchdog reactions.

Merge upstream/main: drop the lint job that never finishes

Upstream removed the CI lint job in #866 because it hangs on a hosted

Drop the side-by-side diagnostics build

Review on hardware found the second install is not free, and the cost lands
on the sessions it was meant to help diagnose.

Two copies of this app cannot coexist. The WiFi Direct group is device-wide
and torn down unconditionally, so launching the second build destroyed a
running session on the first within about 16 ms -- a tester chasing an
intermittent fault would lose the capture they were there to take. Both
copies also register the same RFCOMM/SDP UUID and NSD service name, so each
starves the other's handshake and neither settles.

The rest compounds it. The `.dev` package gets its own SharedPreferences, so
it re-runs first-time setup and captures logs describing codec, resolution
and DPI values that are not the ones the fault occurred under. Nineteen
locale-qualified strings.xml files override the "Dev" label, so most users
would see two identically named icons. DEV_DIAGNOSTICS routed logging to
file exclusively, leaving logcat empty in the one build a tester would
expect to be loud.

The navigation permission change is the part that would have shipped. It
moved the broadcast guard from the contract constant to a BuildConfig value
under a different package name, which silently cuts off third-party
navigation consumers in release builds -- a shipped behaviour change,
untested, carried in on a debug convenience. Reverted to the contract
constant; whichever name becomes canonical deserves its own PR.

Every one of these is fixable, and fixing all of them to keep a developer
convenience is not worth it. Removed instead. dev-note8.ps1 goes with it and
is ignored by name, as deploy_old_tablet.sh already is.

Nearby: fix the defects review found in the tunnel and the sweep summary

Seven findings against the two files this branch touches, all confirmed by
reading against a hardware run.

The failure explanation was guarded by its own inverse. `describeTunnelFailure`
exists to name the canonical case -- socket built, phone never registered its
stream -- but the guard asked whether the socket was *absent* or a stream was
*pending*, and both are false in exactly that state. The one case it was
written for was the one case it stayed silent for. The test is whether the
inbound half ever attached, which is what "built" means here; asking whether
anything is pending cannot work either, because a completed session has
nothing pending too.

A quality of HIGH survived a failed attempt. `lastQuality` is keyed by
endpoint id and Nearby reuses ids across attempts, so a HIGH left behind by a
connection that then failed satisfied the tunnel precondition on the retry and
tunnelled over whatever medium Nearby actually held -- skipping the upgrade
wait that exists to prevent that. Cleared on every non-OK result and before
each new attempt.

The stream wait could not report. `NearbySocket` waited 12 s for the phone's
half while the handshake budget is 10 s, so the handshake always abandoned the
attempt first and the message explaining why never printed -- the whole reason
the wait is bounded rather than indefinite. Now 8 s, inside the budget. A
working phone answers in well under a second.

`NearbySocket` also never closed. The `close()` overrides belong to the
wrapper objects handed out by `getInputStream`/`getOutputStream`, and
`Socket.close()` does not call them, so both Nearby streams survived every
teardown. Overridden to close each independently.

A STREAM payload with nothing readable behind it was stored anyway, under a
log line claiming the stream was held; the wait then timed out against a
message asserting the opposite. It now says what happened and leaves the slot
alone.

The tunnel coroutine re-read the volatile socket instead of the one it had
just built, so a stop() and a fresh upgrade in between could attach this
tunnel's pipe to the next session's socket. It uses the captured reference and
bails if it is no longer current. `activePipes` and `pendingInboundStream`
gained the @Volatile their siblings already had, for the same reason.

The sweep summary lost the gateway scan twice: the subnet sweep zeroed the
counter on entry, and on the path where the gateway scan succeeded the sweep
never ran to print anything. Each phase now owns and reports its own tally,
with probed and responded alongside the failures so the three can be checked
against each other on any path.

Native AA: credentials on the hotspot route, and the port they point at

Two halves of the same failure: on the head unit hotspot transport, mode 3
resolved an access point and then did nothing with it.

The provider's two callbacks were registered inside setupWifiDirect(), which
only the WiFi Direct arm of start() calls. On the hotspot arm the provider was
started with no listener attached, so it published its credentials onto a latch
nobody was reading and, having found its network, stopped looking.
updateWifiCredentials() was never called, no poke ever fired, and the ten-second
refresh the handshake asks for republished into the same latch. The unit held a
working access point and an open Bluetooth listener and looked idle.

That wiring used to sit at service creation, above a comment recording the same
delivery-before-listener fault being fixed once already. It is now in its own
setupSoftAp(), called for every strategy and before either transport starts.

hasWirelessServer() was gated on the strategy as well, so the hotspot route bound
nothing on 5288 at arm time. The handshake's own repair does start it, late, but
only once credentials exist, so every attempt paid the port wait first and logged
a genuine-failure line that is not one; a phone reconnecting on credentials it
already had found nothing listening. The credentials name port 5288 whichever
network carries them, so both transports need it.

WifiLauncherCapabilityTest covers all three predicates across every mode and
strategy, since a wrong answer here is a route that never starts rather than a
compile error.

Session lifecycle: a user exit can be recovered from, and the hotspot comes back down

Three faults, all from the same cause: WifiLauncherManager.stop() nulls `active`,
and decisions taken from `active` afterwards can only answer no.

The Native user exit stops the launcher, which takes the P2P group with it. The
ordering guard below it then read `active?.hasWifiDirect()`, got false, and never
awaited CommManager. So the interface came down while the ByeByeRequest and the
socket close were still in flight, which is exactly what the comment above that
guard says must not happen. The await now runs before the stop, and the guard
works from a value read before it.

The Bluetooth auto-start re-arm had the same shape and worse consequences: it
tested `active is WifiLauncherNative`, which is null in the one state the branch
exists to recover from, so after a user exit the mode stayed dead for the life of
the process however often the phone came back. It asks the setting now. The
handshake checks still go through the launcher, where a null one correctly
answers "nothing running".

The soft-AP arm of the disconnect was dropped entirely, leaving
UserExitHotspotPolicy, HotspotManager.restart and hotspotTeardownProvenUnsafe
with no caller at all. On the head unit hotspot routes, both native and helper
strategy 4, ending a session left the phone associated with Android Auto
retrying its wireless setup until it throttled. Restored, asked of the settings
rather than the launcher for the reason above, and reaching the credentials
watcher through the stop sequence the launcher already defines for it.

UserExitHotspotPolicyTest gains the half of "exact complements" that catches
this: "never both" survives deleting an arm, "always one, for a route that hosts
the network" does not.

Wireless services: the VPN is not the server's to stop, and a one-shot scan stays one

Four things the move out of AapService changed by accident.

stopWirelessServer() now calls VpnControl.stopVpn(). The code it replaced carried
a comment saying not to, and why: the dummy VPN belongs to Self Mode or to the
session that asked for it, this runs on every mode change, and doing it here is
what took a user's VPN down three milliseconds after it came up. The owning
teardowns already call stopDummyVpn(). The comment travels with the fix this
time, since it has now been lost once.

startLocalDiscovery() took a oneShot flag, used it in its own guard, and then
called startScan() with no argument. Both callers that ask for a single sweep -
the Auto-mode retry after an unclean disconnect, and the scan button - were
getting the self-rescheduling loop instead.

forceStartDiscoveryScan() stopped the running scan before starting one, which is
the stop-then-restart the comment at its call site forbids: stop() is
cooperative, so the pair ran two sweeps side by side, and two sweeps probing the
head unit server's port at once is how that server ends up bound to a connection
nobody owns. It also returned true whenever a discovery object existed, so the
caller's rescanWithoutWaiting fallback fired only when there was nothing to scan
with, never in the in-flight case it was written for. It now reports the three
outcomes apart: started, already running, and no discovery loop to kick.

The guard refusing wireless bring-up under a live wired session was dropped with
initWifiMode(). Every automatic entry point lands in setActive(), including the
Bluetooth auto-start one of our own pokes can raise, so without it the stack
walks back up under a USB session that has no use for it - on the Native route
recreating the P2P group and restarting the poke loop beside a live one. It is
back, as UsbSessionQuiescePolicy.shouldRefuseBringUp so the three conditions are
stated once and tested.

LinkLossTeardownPolicy now takes a nullable launcher. Null is a real state, not a
missing argument: a wired session quiesces the wireless stack, and the call site's
`?: return` meant a shutdown in that window skipped the orderly teardown entirely,
leaving the phone's head unit server holding a peer that never came back.

Self Mode and Nearby: act on the session that exists

Self Mode projects this device's own Android Auto over the loopback address. It
needs port 5288 bound and nothing else, and that is what it used to do. Arming
the Native launcher instead replaced whatever wireless mode the user had
configured, created a P2P group and opened the RFCOMM listeners and poke loop it
has no use for, could be refused outright by the boot-loop guard, no-opped
entirely for a user already in Native mode because it did not force, and on the
hotspot strategy bound nothing at all while the magic intent a few lines below
still points Gearhead at 127.0.0.1:5288. It starts the server directly again.

That leaves the server running with no launcher behind it, which
WifiLauncherManager.stop() used to return early on, so the port stayed bound
after the session ended and after onDestroy. The early return is gone: the shared
services can be up without a mode being armed, and each of their stops already
copes with being called when nothing is running.

The Nearby connect action replaced the active launcher before connecting. That
stopped the running advertiser, and stopDiscovery() with it, then handed the
endpoint id the user had tapped to a brand new client that had discovered
nothing, so requestConnection() was asking about an endpoint it had never seen.
It also switched a user in Auto or Native mode over to Helper/Nearby without
being asked. It now connects on the advertiser that found the endpoint, and only
builds a launcher when Nearby is not the transport that is running.

Video: pace the transport thread instead of shedding reference frames

A decoder running at its ceiling - decoding and rendering continuously,
just slower than the phone sends - filled the feed queue, and the
enqueue answered every arrival burst by shedding the newest access
unit. Every unit in this stream is a reference frame, so each shed one
cost a washed-out, blocky picture until the phone's own keyframe, tens
of seconds away. The escalation ladder's 3-cycle budget cannot outrun a
fault that recurs every second.

Measured on the reporter's unit in #875 (MT6735, Android 5.1, 1920x720
panel, AVC at 1080p60): fifteen minutes clean at 50-60fps, then the
codec's drain falls to 42-58fps against a 60fps stream, inputWait jumps
from ~130ms to ~4000ms per 5s window, and the queue sheds 36-56 frames
per window. Two focus cycles repaired the picture and the next burst
broke it again; the session then died with the uplink 52% blocked. The
same unit ran the same 1080p60 negotiation artifact-free before the
feed queue existed, because the synchronous feed blocked the poll
thread and the phone's ack window throttled it.

Margin is what makes this reachable, not the hardware. That unit
sustained 59.8fps arriving at 0.46ms of input wait per frame across
fifteen minutes, so it decodes 1080p60 with slack; inputWait per fed
frame is a threshold rather than a capacity measure, reading ~0.5ms
whenever the codec has any headroom and about one frame period once the
queue is full. A pipeline running on single-digit-percent headroom
crosses that line on any transient, and the only question is what
happens when it does. Two 30fps drives on the same unit and the same
build, 522 windows over 44 minutes, shed nothing at all.

Restore that flow control, bounded. When the queue is full, decode()
now waits for a slot in 50ms slices up to 1s (VideoFeedThrottlePolicy)
instead of shedding: the paced read thread stops acking, the phone's
16-message unacked window closes, and the phone slows to the codec's
real drain rate. In steady state at the ceiling the wait per frame is
one frame period. The wait sits outside the decoder monitor so stop()
is never held behind it, and aborts within one slice of running being
cleared. The link-stall backlog path never blocks here at all - the
phone is silent while the queue drains - so the catch-up behaviour this
queue was built for is unchanged.

Budget expiry still sheds the frame and asks for the keyframe: the feed
thread frees a slot every 300ms by giving up on the frame it holds, so
outlasting 1s means the codec took nothing for the whole wait - a
wedge, which is the sync_stall watchdog's case, not a pacing one.

The throughput line grows an enqueueWait counter, appended after the
existing fields, so a paced session is visible in a reporter log:
backpressure working reads as enqueueWait high with dropped=0, where
the old shedding read as dropped high with the picture melting. Both
outcomes of a wait are counted, the admitted and the expired, because
counting only the admitted ones would zero the longest waits the path
can produce and make a wedge read as a session that never waited at
all. A throttled "Feed queue full - pacing" line marks the onset.

A debug setting holds the feed thread for a fixed interval after each
fed frame, so a codec slower than the stream can be produced on working
hardware - this path is otherwise reachable only on a unit we do not
have. The hold is applied after the feed rather than inside the codec
wait, so inputWait stays honest; it is read once at feed-thread start
and announced loudly there in the fault injector's convention, coerced
to at most 250ms, off by default, and sits in the debug settings next
to the injector.

Validated on hardware with that lever. At a 40ms hold the pre-fix build
sheds in every one of ~123 windows, 30-164 frames each, with visible
macroblocking and the vendor decoder reporting an unintentional loss of
picture; this build sheds nothing in any window over the same route,
with enqueueWait rising to a ~4.5s plateau and rendered matching fed
throughout. An H.265 arm with the hold off is untouched: 122 of 122
windows at enqueueWait=0ms and no pacing line. A teardown under pacing
completes in 345ms.

Never dropping decodable input is where the mature clients have landed
too: Moonlight blocks on dequeueInputBuffer indefinitely and drops only
decoded output, ExoPlayer retries a full input queue and never discards
on timeout. Neither has a keyframe-request channel to make an input
drop recoverable, and neither do we. Dropping only non-reference frames
instead would be a null strategy here: Android Auto negotiates H.264
Baseline, where every P-frame is a reference, and its H.265 stream
shows no temporal layers.

AAP: let an exhausted escalation budget recover once the fault allows it

A session that spent all three focus cycles with the picture still
broken latched dead in two interlocking ways. The refund refused to
grant anything while the picture was unrepaired, on a rationale - a
held last cycle stays the last cycle - that only protects a reserve,
which an exhausted budget does not have. And even a granted refund
would have been unspendable: escalateIfStillUnrepaired() stops
re-arming its check once the budget is spent, and every later fault
returns early on the armed clock, so nothing was left pending to spend
it. The end state was one inert focus-gain nudge per second for the
rest of the session, with the phone's own keyframe a GOP away as the
only exit.

Traced in the state machine rather than caught in a capture. #875's log
reaches two of the three cycles before the link dies, so that fault can
reach this latch but did not reach it there; the inert stretch is
bounded by one GOP either way, since any keyframe reaching the codec
also clears the clock.

Two narrow changes. The refund's unrepaired hold now applies only
while a reserve remains, so an exhausted session earns one cycle per
five quiet minutes back - sustained wire corruption still blocks
refunds through its own stamp, faults that stamp none run the window
from the last spend, and the drive ceiling of eight binds as before.
And a refund granted while the clock is armed re-posts the unrepaired
check itself, so the earned cycle is spent at the next check instead
of waiting on a keyframe that the broken stream is what delayed.

MAX_CYCLES_PER_SESSION stays 3; the burst behaviour is untouched.

One existing test pinned the old blanket hold with the budget at
exactly the exhaustion point; its intent - the reserve is not diluted
mid-hold - now runs over every reserve-holding budget position, and
the exhausted position has its own tests, including the quiet-gate and
drive-ceiling bounds on the new path.

Logging: stop asking the ROM about logcat on every app launch

Settings.logSource resolved its default by spawning `logcat` and blocking in
waitFor(). Because the default was computed before getOrElse, that ran even
when the stored preference already answered the question, and App.onCreate
reaches it through AppLog.init, so it ran on the main thread at every process
start. On Android 13+ each spawn raises the system log-access consent dialog,
which `pm grant READ_LOGS` does not suppress: a test rig measured it firing 55
times across scripted relaunches on one device, once taking SystemUI down with
it and once leaving the app alive with no log output for 90 seconds.

The getter goes back to a plain prefs read. The probe and its two remaining
call sites go with it, because the useful half of bae47b23 does not need one:
launchLogcatPipe already detects a ROM that refuses logcat from the capture
that actually ran, and that auto-switch stays. A user with capture off now
spawns nothing at all, and one with capture on spawns it once per session from
Dispatchers.IO.

The auto-switch no longer writes exporterCaptureEnabled = true beside the
source change. That branch is only reachable from a capture the user already
enabled, so the write was redundant, and it is the line that would have turned
capture on behind a user's back if that ever stopped being true.

Self Mode: a launch that is still in flight is not a launch that failed

The 2500 ms watchdog added with the launcher refactor called emitError, which
disconnects. On the AA < 17.4 route that removed the two things the phone still
had to arrive on: onDisconnected takes the dummy VPN down, and the VPN's
Network object is what we hand Gearhead as PARAM_SERVICE_WIFI_NETWORK, while
scheduleReconnectIfNeeded stops the wifi launcher and closes the port 5288
server. Gearhead needs 15 to 20 seconds on that route and
SelfLauncherLegacy.runWifiLauncher already spends up to one of them waiting for
the VPN to become the active network, so the deadline expired on every attempt
and killed sessions that were working. The reporter saw it as Self Mode failing
with VPN errors that 3.3.0-beta1 did not have.

SelfLaunchTimeoutPolicy holds the two rules with tests behind them: a deadline
each route can meet, and no route may disconnect on a timeout. CommManager
gains reportError for that, which says the same thing as emitError without the
teardown. A phone arriving after the deadline still connects, because
connect(socket) guards on Connecting and not on Error.

The permission trampoline had the opposite defect and always fired downstream
of this one. Its own comment says AA's permission activity closes at once when
everything is granted, and onActivityResult then treated any return under a
second as a failure, so a healthy check produced "Failed to start Android
Auto" every time. A returned result now means permissions are not the problem
whatever it cost; the only failure the trampoline can observe is not being able
to start the activity, and that is the one case that still runs the
installed / system-app diagnosis.

The dummy VPN is deliberately untouched. It is how Self Mode gets a non-null
activeNetwork for our own process, which is why DummyVpnPolicy.Owner.SELF_MODE
exists.
