Logging: make the exported file usable on Android 13+, and say which build wrote it

#887 added READ_LOGS so the in-app capture could return system-wide logs on
older Android. From API 33 it does the opposite. platform.xml maps the permission
to the log group, so a granted READ_LOGS makes the app a privileged logd reader,
and logd then routes every capture through LogcatManagerService: the system
log-access consent dialog while the app is foreground, a silent downgrade to
own-UID logs while it is a background service. No pm grant, property or setting
suppresses it, verified against the android14 logd and LogcatManagerService
sources. maxSdkVersion=32 keeps the permission where it pays off for free, pre-13
where there is no LogcatManagerService, and drops it where it only costs. Without
it the app is an ordinary reader: logd serves its own UID's lines, Java and
native, immediately and with no dialog, which is how 3.2.x behaved. The only
lines it loses are other processes', and anyone who needs those uses adb logcat.

That dialog is also what turned the export button into an ANR.
saveLogToPublicFile fell through to a ring-buffer dump that ran
Runtime.exec("logcat -d"), copyTo and waitFor synchronously, and both callers are
fragment click handlers, so all of it ran on the main thread. An untapped dialog
means waitFor never returns: the app ANRs with Input dispatching timed out, and
the logFile.delete() below the wait is never reached, so a 0-byte HUR_Log is left
behind. Measured on a UNISOC head unit. The dump moves to Dispatchers.IO behind a
10 s bound, served by destroy() rather than by cancelling the wait because copyTo
blocks where coroutine cancellation does not reach, and the file is removed on
every path that returns nothing rather than only the one that used to be
reachable.

The file that comes out now says which build wrote it. sessionBanner carries
BuildConfig.FLAVOR and VERSION_NAME but reached the file through AppLog, so on
the two logcat paths the line had to travel logd, the logcat process and the
pipe's writer thread while the export returned the capture file eleven lines
later. It lost that race in two independent #897 captures, from a build that had
carried the banner since 504a2b1a, and identifying that build took a full pass
over release tags when one line in the file would have answered it. appendBanner
writes it directly: a single small write is atomic against the pipe because both
streams are opened O_APPEND, so it lands at the end whatever the capture is
doing. The AppLog call stays, since it is the only one that reaches AppLog's own
file on the APPLOG_FILE path.

startCapture is deliberately untouched. Writing the banner there would defeat
launchLogcatPipe's zero-byte test, which is how a ROM that refuses logcat
outright is detected. The continuous capture is untouched for a similar reason:
it already runs its pipe on a daemon thread, and it was only the export's
fallback that ever blocked a caller.

Self Mode: a duplicate launch is not a second launch, and loopback needs no network

Two independent faults on the same path.

auto-start-self-mode and an explicit ACTION_START_SELF_MODE are two doors to the
same room. HomeFragment guards the setting behind hasAutoStarted and isConnected,
but the intent reaches AapService directly and nothing downstream stopped both
firing. On the AA 17.4+ route that costs a session rather than a retry: there is
one launcher, it dials 127.0.0.1:5277, and the request that runs out of launchers
calls emitError, which disconnects. Measured: the first request reported All
launchers failed and tore the projection down while the second's socket was
connecting, and the run collapsed to nothing connected within 10000ms. The USB
session established line in that capture is the same event seen from another
angle, since isWirelessSession asks what _connection is and the teardown had
already cleared it. The legacy route absorbs the duplicate because it has three
launchers and a slower path.

SelfLaunchCoalescePolicy holds both rules with tests behind them: one launch at a
time, and running out of launchers is reportable only while nothing has
connected. The second is not redundant, it is what stops a duplicate that reached
the launchers some other way from ending somebody else's session. launchInFlight
is cleared by the launch and by clearLaunchInFlight beside isActive, because this
manager is stopped and re-armed within one process and a flag set in one
direction would strand Self Mode after a stop that landed mid-launch.

Separately, SocketProjectionConnection.connect picks an interface before every
outbound socket: a synchronous sweep of allNetworks for a WiFi transport, then a
NetworkCallback with a 1500 ms latch, then bindSocket. Self Mode dials 127.0.0.1,
which never leaves the device, so there is nothing to choose and on a phone with
no WiFi the latch always waits out its full timeout. Measured on the #897
captures, on every attempt in both: 12:11:08.037 to 12:11:09.545, and
15:00:57.365 to 15:00:58.880, between "Connecting directly to Headunit Server"
and the socket options line. If a WiFi network had existed it would have been
worse than wasted, since bindSocket would have bound a loopback connection to it.

LoopbackBindPolicy gates the whole block, both the modern arm and the legacy
requestRouteToHost one. It answers for localhost, ::1 and the whole of
127.0.0.0/8 rather than the single literal, because a hand typed address anywhere
in that range is still local. Everything that reaches a real link is unaffected
and runs the identical code. This does not fix #897: the phone is silent for its
own reasons and this only stops us paying 1.5 s a try to find out.

Silent head unit server: name the cause the APK shows, not the one we assumed

A peer on 5277 that accepts and then sends nothing made us tell the user their
head unit server was bound to an earlier connection and to stop and start it in
Android Auto's developer settings. #897 shows that advice failing: the reporter
force stopped Android Auto, started the server again, and the first connection
into a brand new Gearhead process was accepted and answered with nothing, ret=0
on all three reads with the version request written each time. A new process
cannot be holding an earlier connection.

The 17.5.663204 APK explains it. DeveloperHeadUnitNetworkService is a proxy, not
an AAP server. It binds ServerSocket(5277) on 0.0.0.0, and on accept it logs
"Head unit connected", makes a socketpair, starts both pump threads, and then
calls IConnectionController.startDuplexConnection into the :car process, binder
transaction 11 with flags 0, fully synchronous. There it fires a START_DUPLEX
activity carrying the fd and waits with no timeout until the setup state machine
reaches transferForHandoff. Until that happens our bytes sit in the socketpair,
the reverse pump is parked in read(), and nothing is written back or closed.

So the bind is not permanent, the accept loop is serial: a(Socket) ends in
join() on both pumps, so while one connection is parked every later one sits in
the kernel backlog and is completed by the kernel alone. Same observable,
different cause, and it is why stopping the server changes nothing. That path
closes only the listening socket and never interrupts a parked a(Socket), so
killing the process is what clears it.

Both messages now say that, and UnresponsivePeerPolicy's KDoc carries the
mechanism rather than the assumption. The threshold, the backoff and the tests
are unchanged: the behaviour the policy describes is real, and the teardown
explains why retrying cannot help rather than refuting it.

Two gates worth recording as absent, checked instruction by instruction across
the whole path: no ConnectivityManager or network-state check of any kind, and
no car mode, since requestProjection is reached only inside transferForHandoff,
downstream of answering the socket.

Chore clean aap

aap/ had become the default home for anything written during an Android Auto investigation,
protocol or not, and decoder/ had grown to 23 files with audio and video mixed together. This
files every one of them by what it is about. aap/ goes from 50 files to 29, and each of those
handles an AAP message, decides to send one, or orchestrates the session carrying them.

Packages after the move:

  aap             the message pump and framing, SSL, the channel handlers (AapVideo, AapAudio,
                  AapMediaPlayback, AapControl, AapNavigation), the fragment audit, the link
                  instruments, AapService and AapProjectionActivity

  decoder/audio   5 files: AudioDecoder, AudioMixer, AudioTrackWrapper, MicRecorder,
                  PlaybackFocusPolicy
  input           new: KeyCode, TouchCoordinateMapper, ProjectionKeyPolicy, MediaKeyRoutingPolicy
  app             the auto-start and boot-loop policies, beside the receivers that trigger them
  connection/*    the wireless and USB policies, each beside the manager that calls it
  utils           AuditReportPolicy (a log-rate limiter), DummyVpnPolicy, ExternalBtPolicy

Tests now live in their subject's package. That covers the ones this change moves and about a

while testing classes that had been under connection for some time. The legacy
com.andrerinas.headunitrevived path held one last test and is now gone from app/src entirely, so

USB: the native symbols still name the package UsbNative left

379d355e moved UsbNative from connection to connection.usb and did not rename
the ten JNI entry points in usbhelper.c, which still export
Java_com_andrerinas_openheadunit_connection_UsbNative_*. There is no JNI_OnLoad

Only libusb mode reaches them. use-libusb defaults to false and every
connectAndSwitch call site passes it, so the AOA switch fails for the users who
turned it on and nobody else notices. UnsatisfiedLinkError is an Error rather
than an Exception, so UsbAccessoryMode's catch around openDevice does not cover

The same class of change was made correctly one commit ago: the reorganisation
renamed the HEVC decoder's symbols with it and retargeted the proguard keeps.
Checked the whole tree by comparing each JNI class's Kotlin package against the
symbols in cpp: UsbNative was the only one left behind, and both match now.

This cannot be caught by a build. The names only matter at runtime, and the
library compiles and loads either way, so it needs a unit with a real USB
accessory path and use-libusb on.

Video: a directly uploaded YUV frame now counts as a drawn frame

The GLES YUV sink has two upload paths. The staged one sets pendingYuvFrame and
drawYuvFrame stamps lastFrameDrawnMs as it consumes it. The direct one uploads
on the GL thread and clears that flag, so the stamp never ran and the value
stayed 0 for the whole session.

The display-stall watchdog reads it, so with the bundled FFmpeg HEVC decoder
feeding the sink it read a frozen view off a picture rendering at ~48 fps and
rebuilt the projection view four times, ten seconds apart, stopping the decoder
each time, until its recovery budget ran out. Measured on the rig with
force-software-decoding on. The hardware path is unaffected: it stamps in
onDrawFrame's OES branch.

Video: measure what the decoder and the panel actually do, and read the codec's own answers

One thread runs through all of this: the project could not say what rate the
panel showed, what the component's decode delay was, or whether a low-latency
key did anything, and it had recorded a log line as a rejection. The decoder
configuration decisions that were resting on that evidence are here too.

rendered= counts every buffer released with render=true, and the surface holds
one of them per pass, so it runs about 1.6x the rate a driver actually sees,
measured over 619 samples on #875's unit. Every fps figure quoted on #839, #875
and #886 is a rendered figure and overstates the picture. presented= is the real
one, and the GLES backend now reports it too. SurfaceView still cannot, which is
worth knowing before reading a capture from a unit on view:SURFACE.

DecodeLatencyMonitor puts the component's decode delay on the throughput line
for one subtraction per frame: input buffers already carry the frame's arrival
time as their presentation stamp and the component hands it back on output, so
no side table and nothing threaded through. Median and p95 rather than a mean,
because ten slow frames in a hundred are the whole signal and a mean hides them.
A component that does not carry stamps through reports unreadable rather than a
number, since a number gets quoted.

That is the instrument the low-latency work has been missing. A configure that
does not throw proves the key cost nothing, not that the component acted, and
the format cannot be read back for an answer: ACodec builds its input format
from its own bookkeeping rather than re-asking the component, so an ignored key
round-trips exactly like an honoured one, and the units where this matters
predate the CCodec that would answer honestly.

MediaCodecInfo's FEATURE_LowLatency only exists from API 30, so
advertisesLowLatency() returned a hard false on everything older, and that false
printed in the capability line beside real verdicts, where it reads as "this
decoder cannot do low latency". On #886's unit it says exactly that and is wrong
twice: the unit is API 28, so the feature is unaskable rather than absent, and
the MediaTek spelling of the same feature was in fact being accepted, nine
configures across two drives, all optionalKeys=vendor [vdec-lowlatency], zero
rejections. Capability.lowLatency is nullable now and prints unknown, matching
what sustains has always done. The ladder is unchanged: unknown routes to the
vendor rung, which is right for every component too old to have the official
feature.

The ladder also caught every exception out of configure()/start() and logged it
as "Decoder rejected optionalKeys=<tier>", including a surface released between
the loop's own validity check and the configure call. Across three captures and
41 configures on that unit exactly one "rejected" line exists, and it reads "The
surface has been released", logged 80ms after onSurfaceDestroyed during a device
shutdown. Anyone grepping for whether the key works would have found that line
first and concluded the opposite of what the other 40 configures say. The catch
now checks the surface, says what happened, and stops laddering, releasing the
component on that path because the loop otherwise only releases at the top of
the next rung and a unit with one hardware decoder instance fails every later
create if this one leaks.

KEY_PRIORITY and KEY_OPERATING_RATE come back, on the ladder's optional rungs.
They were removed on the reasoning that a rejected key takes the session, which
is sound, but the evidence behind it was a misreading: ACodec's setPriority and
setOperatingRate log the component's refusal and then return OK, and
configureCodec adds a second "err = OK; // ignore error" at both call sites, so
the -1010 those keys drew could never have failed a configure. Verified in
android-9.0.0_r61, the platform of the unit in #886. Media3 sets KEY_PRIORITY=0
unconditionally on every API 23+ device.

MediaTek gets a rung above the measured-good one carrying vdec-no-record and
use-clearmotion-mode=0, its output-reorder switch and its motion interpolation,
which adds latency rather than removing it. Those are the only levers found
anywhere that attack a component's pipeline depth below API 30, where the
official key does not exist. They get their own rung so a component that
dislikes them falls back to vdec-lowlatency alone, which nine configures across
two drives on #886's unit accepted without complaint, rather than to nothing.
Neither key is prefixed vendor., so on a component that does not know them they
are never read: setVendorParameters, the one call configureCodec checks the
result of, only looks at vendor.-prefixed keys.

MediaCodec has said since API 21 whether a failure is transient or recoverable,
and the output thread read them all alike. A component saying it was busy spent
one of three strikes; a component saying it could not recover waited out two
more strikes and 100ms of sleep before the restart it was always going to need.
On units with one hardware decoder instance a restart is the most expensive
response available, and it costs a GOP of keyframe starvation on top.
DecoderExceptionPolicy splits the three cases; anything unclassified keeps the
shipped path, because a policy that made an unrecognised failure less likely to
be repaired would be a regression.

Two things were sized or worded once and should not have been. The feed queue
and the memory reading were fixed at construction, and VideoDecoder is built
once per process, so changing fpsLimit resized nothing until the app was killed:
the 30 fps workaround this project has been asking reporters to try was never
actually exercised by anyone who did not force-stop afterwards. Both are
re-derived per session now. And hideReconnectingOverlay() logged "frames
resumed" unconditionally, though two of its four callers are teardown paths, the
20-second reconnect timeout and the finish path, so both reporters' logs claim
frames resumed on a session that was ending. The reason now comes from the
caller.

The low-latency setting itself moves from Debug, where it sat below the FPS
counter, to Video, where every other setting that decides how the decoder is
configured already lives. Same key, same immediate-apply behaviour, same search
keywords.

Tests: the two new policies, and the ladder's existing cases restated, that the
hints ride on the offered rungs rather than costing one, that an unknown
component is still never guessed at, and that the two low-latency spellings are
still never combined.

Log capture: keep the tail of a long drive, and declare the debug levers

A capture stopped dead at 16 MB and kept the first 16 MB. At VERBOSE that is
reached in minutes, so a fault at minute 30 was unrecordable: one reporter hit
exactly that ("Verbose not record after 10 minutes"), which is why every log
on two open issues is INFO and why sub-second frame pacing has never been
measured on that hardware.

The capture now rolls at 8 MB and keeps the two newest segments, so the
retained window is the last 8-16 MB and the total on disk is what it was
before. An export joins both segments into one file, because a reporter
attaches one file. Both segments are left in place, so exporting cannot cost a
capture that is still running.

The session banner also carries the settings that make the app behave unlike
itself. Video fault injection deliberately corrupts the stream, and #886's
pre-fix capture ran a whole drive with DROP_MIDDLE_FRAGMENT at 1-in-10 and 137
injected drops. The only thing that said so was a disclaimer printed mid-log;
that capture was nearly read as evidence of a real fault. The banner now reads
debug=none when nothing is on, so a clean capture says so.

WiFi Direct: ask the radio whether it has a 5 GHz band, and believe a no

Two issues spent weeks arguing about a band nobody could establish. #886's
unit is 2.4 GHz only and said so in a comment; #839's has a working 5 GHz
radio and was read as if it did not, and forcing 2.4 against 5 on it made no
measurable difference. Neither fact ever reached a log, so no capture could be
sorted into the right arm.

WifiManager.is5GHzBandSupported() has answered this since API 21 and this app
has never called it. It is read per bring-up, printed beside the band lines,
and passed to the two policies that choose what to ask for.

Only a false is acted on. SoftApBandPolicy already records why: the call
describes the station side, and vendors ship radios that answer yes there and
still refuse to host anything on it. A no means the band is absent, which is
hardware and safe to build on.

What changes is AUTO, and only on a radio that reports no 5 GHz band: it asks
for 2.4 GHz rather than spending the 5 GHz rung first. That rung is not free.
The pre-Q request is a disallowed-frequency list, so a band the unit cannot
host leaves it with nowhere legal to put a group rather than on the other
band, and the ladder only advances on that failure. Above Q the request fails
outright, and the band-mismatch retry cannot clean up after it either, because
shouldRetryFor5Ghz only fires on a group that came up on the wrong band and no
group came up at all. Either way the user is left finding the 2.4 GHz toggle
by hand, which is what #886's reporter had to do.

FORCE_5GHZ is untouched. The setting exists for a driver that surprises this
call, so the capability must not be able to overrule it, and a test pins that.
describePreference() now says which band AUTO is about to try, so the line
cannot contradict the request logged after it.

AAP: measure what arrives, and say when the band and the frame rate disagree

Two additions, both to the inbound side, both diagnostic except the second
which is advice.

InboundRateMonitor reports video, audio and other in kB/s over the same 30s
window LinkGapMonitor uses, so the two lines land together. It reports on
every window including the healthy ones, because a rate only means something
next to the rate beside it.

It exists because the other two inbound instruments cannot answer the question
these issues keep asking. A picture that sags without stopping leaves every
gap series silent, and a gap that is named still does not say whether the link
was full or the phone was holding back. Measured on #886's two driving logs,
28m13s and 32m30s on 3.3.0-beta1: dropped=0, skipped=0, concealed=0 and fed
close to rendered in all 714 throughput windows, zero decoder restarts, zero
UplinkStallMonitor reports, zero AudioTrack underruns, and inbound video quiet
17 times against inbound link quiet once. So our decoder, our renderer and our
uplink are all exonerated and the phone stopped sending video while 48kHz
stereo PCM kept arriving on the same socket. That last comparison is the one
nothing could make in numbers, and it is what this line is for. The test
replays it.

NarrowBandProfilePolicy names the one configuration known to be a bad pair: a
radio with no 5 GHz band being offered 60 fps. The protocol has no bitrate
field - control.proto's VideoConfiguration is resolution, 30-versus-60 fps,
margins, density, aspect ratio and codec - so frame rate is one of only three
levers, and the app has never mentioned it. Measured on a 2.4 GHz access
point, a 1080p/60 stream died having sent no frame at all where 800x480/30
held indefinitely.

It describes and changes nothing, and says so in the line itself.
logNegotiatedCodecCapability already refuses the same move on a capability
verdict, and the one unit where 2.4 against 5 GHz was actually run as an A/B
showed no difference, so there are no grounds to overrule the user's setting.
Three gates, each ruling out a different false positive: a wired session does
not care what the radio can do, a unit already on 30 has taken the advice, and
only a false from the capability read means the band is absent.

The evaluation is wrapped: service discovery must not fail over a diagnostic.

Audio: ask for system audio focus until the phone is seen refusing it

A head unit that routes its amplifier from system audio focus has been silent
under Android Auto since the automatic focus mode arrived. AUTO declined the
grab whenever a Bluetooth media link was connected, which is any paired phone,
so the app asked for focus zero times where it previously asked once per track.

The decline was a guess at harm. The harm it guesses at is real - our focus
grab makes an A2DP sink AVRCP-pause the phone we are projecting - but a link
that is merely connected does not cause it, and the detector that observes it
happening already exists and was unreachable behind the same decline.

- AUTO now takes focus and stops only once the self-defeating detector has seen
  the phone cut its own playback twice.
- That verdict is written to settings, so a unit that behaves this way pays for
  the trial once instead of at every connect. Re-picking the focus mode clears
  it, which is the way back from a false positive.
- Static mode is unchanged and still declines on a connected link. It grabs once,
  outside any channel's lifetime, so there is nothing there for the detector to
  observe.
- The Bluetooth probe leaves the dynamic path entirely, taking two binder
  round-trips per track change off the transport thread.
- The decline log line now names which gate said no instead of printing the
  inputs to be re-derived.

Measured on the reporting unit: four captures, zero requestAudioFocus calls
against three abandonAudioFocus, with the vendor AudioManager logging both. The
same unit plays correctly once its own media player has opened the hardware
path, which stays open until reboot.

The Automatic hint string is rewritten for the new behaviour; its translations
still describe the old one.

Self Mode: keep the projection in front when a call covers it

In Self Mode the phone is both the head unit and the phone, so answering a
call buries the projection under the phone's own call screen. Two rounds on
hardware root-caused it and it is not ours to fix: Android Auto never enables
its car-mode in-call service on Android 13+, so Telecom's swap - the only
thing in AOSP that suppresses the Dialer during projection - cannot fire, and
`pm enable` of that component is refused even to adb shell.

What the same rounds measured is that Android Auto's own call UI is live on
the projected surface the whole time, so the picture underneath the call
screen is already the right one. This puts the projection back on top of it.

Bounded so it never turns into a fight. onUserLeaveHint separates a call
screen covering us from the user pressing Home, so leaving on purpose is
never argued with. Three attempts per call and then silence, which is also
the escape hatch for anyone who wants the phone's call screen. A relaunching
call screen cannot buy a second budget. One last attempt a second after the
call ends, for the report that the projection never came back - Android
normally reveals the still-paused activity itself, measured at 17 ms, and
that second is there to let it.

The call itself is read from AudioManager.mode, which needs no permission and
covers VoIP, with our own microphone uplink excluded because it sets
MODE_IN_COMMUNICATION for SCO routing.

Self Mode only, and on a setting. Everywhere else the call screen lands on
the phone while the projection is on the head unit, so there is nothing to
do; gating it there is also what keeps a re-raise away from real head units.
The raise itself goes through the service's existing overlay trampoline, the
same route the call screen used to cover us, and is a task reorder onto the
live singleTask instance, so no surface is torn down. The full-screen-intent
fallback is refused on this path: it would compete with the call screen's own.

The "raise finished" line prints from closeCallRaiseEpisode rather than the
tick's DONE branch, because on the path that always happens - the raise
landing on the first attempt - onResume ends the episode before the tick that
would report it can run. A round showed the raise going out with nothing
saying it worked, on all four call cycles.

The stale active flag is fixed here because the raise would inherit it.
SelfLauncherManager.isActive is set in start() and cleared in exactly one
place, the Disconnected transition in AapService. Two paths end a Self Mode
attempt without ever producing that transition, and both leave the flag true
for the life of the process. The service can be destroyed with the flag set:
onDestroy never touched it, and the manager is process-lived, so the next
session created in the same process reads a stale true. ServiceDiscoveryResponse
then drops the media and speech audio sinks from the announcement of a USB or
wireless session that has nothing to do with Self Mode, and the raise would arm
itself the same way. The launch timeout is the second path:
SelfLaunchTimeoutPolicy.mayDisconnect answers false on every route, on purpose,
because the report must not tear down the wireless server the phone may still
arrive on, but reportError emits Error without disconnecting, so no Disconnected
ever follows. Clearing beside handleNeverConnect and in onDestroy closes both.
The branch of the failure report that skips emitError because a session is
already connected is deliberately left alone: the connected session may well be
the Self Mode one, and its flag is still true for a reason.

The two new strings ship in all twenty locales rather than English-only, in
step with the recent sync that completed the missing translations, using each
locale's established name for Self Mode.

Measured on hardware (POCO X3, Android 15, AA 17.5.663204): six raise cycles
across incoming and outgoing calls, every one landing on attempt 1, with
1927-2124 ms from the Dialer's START to our onResume, mean 2076. A Home press
mid-call raises nothing. With the setting off the old behaviour is exact.
dropped=0 in every throughput window and one decoder configure in the whole
capture, at session start, so the reorder costs no picture.

Video: the keyboard keeps video focus, and a gray frame is not a picture

Two defects, fixed together because the first one's return path depends on
the second.

Tapping the phone-keyboard key in Android Auto opens its keyboard as a plain
opaque fullscreen activity pinned to display 0. On the SurfaceView backend
that cover makes the framework destroy our surface, and the teardown has
always answered with VIDEO_FOCUS_NATIVE. Android Auto reads that as the
projection being over and tears the session down, which takes the keyboard
with it: measured on a reporter's unit, Gearhead logged "Asked by projected
IME to detach" 49 ms after our release, and on a second unit 28 ms after. The
keyboard appears and vanishes and the user is left with no keyboard at all.

The teardown is not ours to prevent. surfaceDestroyed is a notification, not
a veto, and z-order, an overlay host and PiP were each assessed and rejected.
The release is ours. The TextureView and GLES backends never lose their
surface to a cover, never send it, and keep the keyboard - which is the
difference two reporters found for themselves by switching backends, and
which two arms of a hardware round confirmed by holding the keyboard for
29.8 s and 17.4 s across the same pause.

The release cannot go in general: it is what makes the phone re-run sink
setup, worth 42-96 ms to a picture against seconds without it. So
VideoFocusReleasePolicy withholds it for one cover shape only - opaque, live
session, arriving within 3 s of a touch we forwarded - and the return is
carried by the warm-relaunch focus cycle already in the tree. Home,
notifications, alarms, the Dialer and every real teardown keep the fast path
untouched.

Withheld rather than deferred, which is the form this was drafted in once and
withdrawn: a release posted to fire later can land after a keyframe cycle has
completed and leave the phone released with nothing pending to take focus
back, which is a black screen with audio still playing. Nothing is queued
here. The phone keeps streaming while we hold focus: decode() discards the
bytes on an invalid surface, and acks are sent independently of what the
decoder consumed, so there is no unacked-window wedge.

The second defect is what made that return work at all, and it was visible on
its own in a live backend switch from Quick Settings, which left the screen
gray for a long time: measured 11.0s TEXTURE to GLES, 32.4s or more SURFACE
to TEXTURE, and 66.5s GLES to SURFACE, which is a whole GOP. Throughput was
healthy throughout, 49-54fps with dropped=0.

recreateProjectionView stops the decoder with a surface-lifecycle reason, so
endsSession is false and the cached parameter sets survive. The codec
reconfigures and starts on a P-frame, the component emits output from it
anyway, and lastFrameRenderedMs is stamped 173ms in. From that instant every
gate that asks "has a frame rendered on this surface" reads a working picture
and stands down: the warm-relaunch escalation answers NONE at 850ms, the
reconnecting watchdog only reaches that escalation while lastFrameRenderedMs
is zero, onDecoderError never fires because a surface stop is not a restart,
and DecoderStallCausePolicy sits behind a stall gap that output at 50fps
never opens. Nothing is left to ask, so the picture waits for the phone's own
next keyframe.

The question those gates need answered is whether a keyframe accounts for
what is on screen. KeyframeRepairTracker already tracks that per codec
instance; PictureCredibilityPolicy turns it into the boolean the gates read,
and the parameter is renamed in both of them because the old name is how this
comes back. Two rows carry the reasoning: the bundled software HEVC path
keeps no keyframe accounting, so a rendered frame is the only evidence it
has, and a keyframe still working its way to the output is given 2s before
the picture stops counting - twice the tracker's own confirm-by-count
fallback at the lowest plausible frame rate.

The escalation also now runs on every watchdog tick rather than only before
the first frame, so the 850ms check is no longer the only attempt. It answers
NONE on a healthy stream. No new lever and no new budget: recovery is the
existing focus cycle, one per surface, which a backend switch creates exactly
one of. Charging it to the session budget instead would put a 60s cooldown
between two consecutive switches, almost exactly the 66.5s this removes.

"First frame rendered (hardware decode)" is qualified for the same reason. It
fires once per codec instance, so on a warm rebuild it announces the gray
P-frame and reads as a working picture when there is none. The prefix stays,
so the landmark greps still match, and the line now says when no keyframe
accounts for the frame.

Measured on hardware (POCO X3 NFC, Android 15, AA 17.5.663204, Self Mode,
1920x1080 H.264). The keyboard: held 23 s and 108 s across two runs, ended by
the operator, with zero focus notifications during the hold and zero "Asked by

never dropped. The control: a Home press still releases focus in the same

and 1615 ms, paid only on the covers that are withheld. The backend switch:
gray to picture 1648, 1634 and 1555 ms on the three transitions that were

Self Mode: the projection stays in front of a call, and the Android Auto keyboard stays up

Audio: playback starts full, the drain ends, and a paused sink is not an outage

- Preroll: AudioTrackWrapper started the track inside init(), before the playback loop had written
  a byte, so the hardware began consuming an empty buffer. Audio arrives at real time, so the writer
  can never fill faster than the mixer drains and the opening deficit is never recovered. Measured on
  a Spreadtrum sp7731e over sixteen minutes: all five 48 kHz media-stream starts underran 588-960 ms
  after their Media Start Request, five of that capture's seven underruns. The media track is rebuilt
  on every pause, resume and assistant session, so it is heard as a stumble each time. Same race is
  why a deep audioLatencyMultiplier bought so little: a buffer started empty stays near empty.
- AudioPrerollPolicy decides when enough is banked: 200 ms of playback, capped at three quarters of
  the track's real capacity so the write that triggers the start still fits, with a 300 ms deadline
  so a notification blip shorter than the target is still played. Capacity from
  getBufferSizeInFrames() where the API has it, since setBufferSizeInBytes is a request the framework
  may clamp and that margin is the only thing keeping a write off a not-yet-playing track from
  blocking the thread that would start it. Deadline runs from the first write, not construction: a
  track precreated at Media Sink Setup can sit idle for minutes.
- Drain: cleanup() polled playbackHeadPosition against framesWritten after stop(), and neither exit
  could fire. stop() zeroes the head, and the stagnation escape was guarded on pos > 0. Measured
  2525 ms, 2603 ms and 2522 ms, the full budget on every clean teardown, on an URGENT_AUDIO thread
  and long enough to overlap the next track's start. The head is sampled before stop(), so the wait
  is computed and capped at a second. An interrupted drain is a restart rather than a failure and no
  longer logs a stack trace at error into logs reporters attach to bug reports. A track torn down
  before it reached its pre-roll is started first, so what it holds is played rather than discarded.
- MicRecorder gains a capture summary on stop: source, elapsed, bytes against expected, empty reads,
  peak amplitude. A microphone delivering pure silence logged identically to a working one, because
  read() returns a full buffer either way and no error path fires, so an assistant that could not
  hear the user left nothing to read. Its capture thread moves to urgent audio priority, the last
  audio thread still at default.
- Diagnostics: Android Auto stops the media sink for every assistant session and every pause, and the
  audio gap series counted those deliberate silences as outages. One window read "inbound audio quiet
  3 times in 30220ms: dead=10937ms (36%)" when all of it was a fourteen-second assistant session.
- That matters beyond tidiness. Whether audio went quiet at the same time as video is what separates
  a dead radio from a stalled media path, and the all-channel series cannot answer it: the phone
  pings once a second on CONTROL, so a link carrying nothing but pings scores healthy while both
  media channels are dead.
- LinkGapMonitor.skipExpectedGap() excludes a silence the caller expected and shifts the window past
  it, so what the window has already measured survives and its percentages stay against live time. A
  reset would have restarted the 30 s window on every sink cycle, and a series stopping and starting
  faster than that would never report at all. A gate on the feed would have hidden any stream that
  arrives without a start request, which is the worse failure for this instrument.
- AapTransport tracks which audio channels are open, so guidance on AUDIO1 opening and closing inside
  an assistant session cannot discard the media window running underneath it.
- VideoFeedThrottlePolicy records that the thread it paces carries audio too. One read thread serves
  the session and the budget is the same order as the audio sink's own depth, so a codec at its
  ceiling can push audio into the drop path rather than merely delaying it. Unmeasured, because the
  units that stutter are link-starved and never take the wait, but anyone raising that budget is
  spending audio headroom as well.

Mic uplink: a message type, one sample rate, whole messages, and a reply

- Framing: AapMessageFraming states the rule, a message whose flag byte has bit 0 set carries a
  2-byte message type at payload offset 0, and the receive path obeys it twice. The microphone uplink
  set flags 0x0b and wrote no type at all. sendEncryptedMessage encrypts from byte 4, so the phone
  was handed [timestamp:8][PCM] where it expects [type:2][timestamp:8][PCM].
- It parsed only by accident: a millisecond elapsedRealtime has two leading zero bytes, which read as
  message type 0. The phone then consumed six real timestamp bytes plus the first PCM sample as its
  timestamp and started the audio one sample late, on every message of every session, with the
  timestamp jumping by up to 65535 in either direction with the audio content.
- Never right. The original layout put the timestamp at byte 2, where the length field overwrote its
  first two bytes; moving it to byte 4 fixed that half and left the type unwritten. Both degrade
  rather than fail, which is why the microphone works for most users.
- MicUplinkFrame writes the layout and nothing else, pure, no Android, no logging, so its test is the
  record of the offsets and asserts them from both ends: it decodes the frame back with the same
  rules the inbound path uses and checks the first PCM byte lands at payload offset 10. The timestamp
  moves from milliseconds to microseconds, the unit every other AAP media producer stamps with,
  guarded because the nanosecond clock is API 17 and this flavor's minSdk is 16.
- Rate: the service announced a hardcoded 16000 Hz while MicRecorder opened AudioRecord at whatever
  the Mic Sample Rate setting said, with no resampler anywhere on the input path. Choosing 48000
  handed the phone 48 kHz PCM under a 16 kHz declaration, three times too fast. Three reporters found
  this independently and all arrived at the same remedy, putting the setting back to 16000.
- Android Auto validates the announced configuration: 16000 or 48000, 16 bits, one or two channels,
  everything else rejected with a teardown reason naming a bad microphone config. Google's head unit
  guide is narrower and requires PCM 16 kHz 16-bit mono for speech. So four of the six rates the
  picker offered, 8000, 24000, 32000 and 44100, could never have worked at any layer.
- MicCaptureFormat owns the format and the announcement and the recorder both read it, so the two
  cannot drift again. The wire is always 16 kHz mono. The setting survives as a capture-side
  compatibility control for a device whose AudioRecord will not open 16 kHz, which the existing
  getMinBufferSize probe already detects. Its list drops to 16000 and 48000 and a stored value from
  the old list migrates in the getter.
- 48000 is the only fallback worth having: it is a whole multiple of 16000, so MicPcmDecimator
  converts it by averaging whole sample groups with no filter to design, where 44100 would need a
  low-pass nobody here can measure. The averaging is deliberate, since picking every third sample
  folds everything above 8 kHz back into the band speech recognition listens to.
- Reply: MicrophoneRequest has a defined response, Android Auto names it in its own protocol enum,
  and this head unit only ever started or stopped the recorder and sent nothing back. A phone waiting
  on that reply before opening its speech pipeline looks exactly like a microphone that is heard but
  never understood.
- The status is real rather than decorative. MicRecorder.start() returned zero even when AudioRecord
  had thrown and left nothing recording, so success meant "we tried". A failure is now sent to the
  phone instead of leaving it waiting on a stream that will never arrive. The session id is whatever
  a MediaStart left behind, zero on every captured session because the phone opens this channel
  without one, and if a Start ever does arrive the right id appears with no further work.
- Stop: mediaSinkStopRequest branches on Channel.isAudio and the video channel, and isAudio
  deliberately excludes the microphone because it is a source. Widening that predicate would make the
  head unit claim audio focus and precreate an AudioTrack for a microphone. So a stop on channel 7
  fell through both arms and the recorder kept running and kept sending after the phone had asked it
  not to. It has its own arm now.
- Request contents: anc_enabled, ec_enabled and a flow-control window were all parsed and discarded,
  and the line that prints them sat at DEBUG where no reporter log reaches. It is at INFO now.
  Honouring the flags and gating on the window both wait on seeing real values first, since a window
  implemented against acks that may never come would silence the microphone.
- Permission: PermissionChecker reports a granted permission whose app-op a ROM has revoked as
  denied, and the log said only "No RECORD_AUDIO permission". That cost one reporter weeks, because
  their permission really was granted and the remedy was in the ROM's privacy settings, not in this
  app. The two now read differently. The microphone effect descriptions gain the same honesty:
  Android Auto expects gain control and single-microphone noise reduction off and applies its own.
- Chunking: Google's guide gives the microphone a 2048-frame buffer and requires messages to be a
  multiple of it, and Android Auto's own audio classes use the same number. AudioRecord hands back
  whatever the device feels like, 640 and 768 frames in reporter logs, and the sender dropped any
  read of 64 bytes or fewer without a word, so a short read became a hole in what the phone heard
  rather than a wait for the rest.
- MicChunkAccumulator gathers reads into fixed messages and holds the remainder. A chunk is stamped
  with the capture time of its first byte rather than of the read that completed it, because a chunk
  is 128 ms long and stamping at the end would put every message that far out and undo the timestamp
  fix. The tail left when capture stops is discarded rather than padded: zero padding injects silence
  the microphone never heard into a speech stream, and a short final message breaks the
  multiple-of-2048 rule. At most one chunk is lost, after the user has stopped speaking, and the
  uplink report counts those bytes so the cost is visible rather than assumed.
- The capture buffer grows to hold two whole messages, scaled by the decimation factor when the
  fallback rate is in use, so assembling one never becomes the reason a read overruns. This costs
  128 ms of uplink latency, which is what the guide specifies and what real head units do. If the
  assistant turns out to feel sluggish, 1024 frames is the experiment, but it is a deliberate
  deviation from a stated requirement, not a fix.
- MicUplinkMonitor: nothing had ever said whether microphone bytes left the head unit, so a reporter
  log shows AudioRecord being initialised and then silence, and a microphone routed nowhere and an
  uplink that sends nothing read identically. Paired with the capture summary the two lines separate
  them: capture peak zero means the input is routed nowhere, capture healthy with no uplink line
  means we heard it and never sent it. It reports per microphone session rather than per window,
  because a session is a few seconds, and it counts the phone's acks, which nothing had ever done on
  a stream the phone really does flow-control. Diagnostic only, nothing reads the report.

Mic: a setting that leaves the microphone to the phone

- Two reports asked for the same thing from opposite directions: a motorcycle dash whose Bluetooth
  helmet intercom loses its microphone the moment this app takes it, and a phone-as-head-unit whose
  own microphone is far worse than the one the user's real phone is already connected to.
- Shape: declare the service exactly as before, decline every request, send nothing. The physical
  microphone is never opened, so an intercom keeps it, and the phone is left to fall back to its own
  recorder. Omitting the service was rejected here because Android Auto's required-service check was
  read as refusing a head unit that declares no microphone service. That reading is corrected later
  in this branch and the service is withheld instead.
- MicrophonePolicy holds the decision so the two places that read it cannot disagree, and it names
  the reason rather than returning a bare boolean: a microphone the user handed to the phone is not a
  fault and the log has to say so, the same way the audio-sink skip does, while a device with no
  usable capture is a different sentence for a different person. The transport never wires the
  recorder when the policy declines, so AudioRecord is never constructed at all.
- Depends on the microphone response landing first. Without a reply, declining a request would leave
  the phone waiting on a stream that never arrives, with nothing to tell it otherwise.
- The toggle lives at the top of the microphone screen, which is where someone looking for microphone
  behaviour goes, and the rest of that screen collapses behind it since none of it applies when
  nothing is recording. The main settings search finds it too.
- Copy: the toggle promised that Android Auto would use the phone's own microphone. It does not.
  Gearhead picks its recorder once, at projection start, and picks the phone's own only when the head
  unit declared itself a motorcycle and the car audio service reports no input configuration. Every
  other head unit gets the car recorder for the life of the session, and nothing sent in reply to a
  MicrophoneRequest can move that choice, because the choice is already made by the time the request
  exists.
- This head unit sends no vehicle type at all, so the phone records VEHICLE_TYPE_UNSPECIFIED and the
  fallback is unreachable. With the setting off the phone waits on a microphone that never sends and
  times out with no answer. Measured twice: by a test round, whose two spoken attempts both timed out
  rather than falling back, and by hand afterwards. The half that does work is the one the motorcycle
  requests asked for first, since nothing opens AudioRecord and a helmet intercom keeps the
  physical microphone.

Service: claim the microphone foreground type only while capture is open, and fill in the Bluetooth address

- Foreground type: with targetSdk 36 a foreground service that captures audio needs the microphone
  foreground-service type, and this one declared only connectedDevice and mediaPlayback. The effect
  is a microphone that returns silence with no error whenever the projection activity is not the
  visible foreground, which is Self Mode or the screen simply showing something else, and that is
  exactly the case the capture summary was written to detect and cannot explain.
- The type is while-in-use, so holding RECORD_AUDIO is necessary and not sufficient. A service
  started in the background is refused with "the app must be in the eligible state/exemptions" even
  with the permission granted, and this one starts from the boot, USB and Bluetooth receivers.
  Measured on a background Bluetooth auto-start: five starts, five SecurityExceptions, every one of
  them in onCreate.
- The cost was wider than the microphone. onCreate's catch calls stopSelf and returns, so
  fillBluetoothAddressIfUnset, setupCarMode, setupNightMode, observeConnectionState and
  registerReceivers never ran, while onStartCommand went on to form a full AAP session anyway. Every
  background-started session with the microphone enabled therefore ran unpromoted and without its
  receivers.
- So the start claims no while-in-use type at all, which is what main did and what cannot be refused,
  and the microphone type is added at the moment capture opens. By then the projection is on screen
  and the app is eligible. It is dropped again when capture closes, so it is held only while it is
  true rather than for the life of the service.
- Since Android 14, calling startForeground with the microphone type while RECORD_AUDIO is not
  granted throws. An unconditional claim would turn "the user declined the microphone permission"
  into "the app does not start", on the default path, for a much larger population than it helps.
- ForegroundServiceTypePolicy splits into baseTypeMask and withMicrophone. It exists because the two
  startForeground call sites are more than a thousand lines apart and have already been edited
  independently. Its earlier typeMask gated on the permission and the setting, which are the right
  questions asked at the wrong moment, and that was the bug.
- MicRecorder owns the claim because it owns the capture lifecycle and already returns codes its
  caller declines on. A refusal is ERROR_NO_FOREGROUND_TYPE, which AapControl answers with the
  STATUS_INTERNAL_ERROR it already sends when capture will not start, so the phone is told rather
  than left waiting. The seam is a companion-held interface because the service is a singleton and a
  MicRecorder is not.
- Prophylactic: no reporter has demonstrated this fault and it is hard to demonstrate positively.
  What it changes is a silent, unexplained microphone into one that either works or fails for a
  reason.
- Bluetooth address: two reports say phone calls never reach the head unit. Neither is a defect in
  this app. Google's head unit guide routes in-call audio over a Bluetooth hands-free link and never
  over the projection connection, Android Auto's own build agrees since it names a telephony audio
  stream in an enum and has no code anywhere that produces one, acquiring call audio over Bluetooth
  instead, and its user-facing text says to connect the phone to the vehicle over Bluetooth. There is
  nothing on the projection side to fix.
- What is fixable is that this app only tells the phone where to connect. The service discovery
  response announces the Bluetooth service, with its hands-free pairing method, only when the
  Bluetooth address setting is non-empty, and that setting is typed by hand, so most installs
  announce nothing at all. Meanwhile BluetoothHelper has resolved the real address for years through
  the adapter, reflection and OEM system properties, and used it only to build description strings.
- The service now fills the setting in at startup when it is blank and the hardware can be read, so
  the announcement actually changes rather than waiting for someone to open Settings and press Save.
  It never overwrites what the user typed, since a hand-entered address is usually there because the
  detected one was wrong. The line that reports the omission also says what it costs, because a
  reporter grepping their log is the fastest way to find this.
- No new banner. The main-screen banner carries hardware verdicts from ConnectionIssues, and a blank
  settings field is a configuration fact, not something the hardware did.
- Also: the microphone announcement is 16 kHz and the comments now say why 48 kHz is not an
  alternative. AudioConfiguration is one message shared by every audio service, so the validator
  accepts the union across all of them and 48 kHz is in that set for the media channel's stereo
  stream. The guide names one rate for the microphone.

Protocol: HeadUnitInfo under the numbers Android Auto reads, and a vehicle type the user picks

- Field numbers: the eight fields were numbered head_unit_make first, but Android Auto reads this
  message as make, model, year, vehicle_id, then head_unit_make, head_unit_model,
  head_unit_software_build, head_unit_software_version. Every value has been arriving under the wrong
  name. Nothing failed loudly because all eight are strings.
- Recovered from Gearhead 17.5.663204: the branch that fills this message from the deprecated
  top-level ServiceDiscoveryResponse fields copies them one at a time, and each copy sets a presence
  bit whose index is the field's declaration order. Cross-checked against both messages'
  protobuf-lite schema strings, which give the field numbers and types directly. The phone prefers
  this message over the deprecated fields whenever it is present, so what it stores today is the
  scrambled set.
- It costs a head unit its identity once: the phone keys its per-head-unit update records on
  HEAD_UNIT_MANAGER_<make>_<model>_<year>_<vehicle_id> and matches vendor workarounds against the
  same values, so an already-paired unit looks like a different one on the next connection.
  Common.java regenerated with protoc 25.1; the descriptor block also changes escaping style, from
  octal to the short forms, and the decoded descriptor bytes are unchanged.
- Vehicle type: HeadUnitInfo has a ninth field, an int32 vehicle type, that this head unit has never
  sent. Unset reads as car, measured, rather than the unspecified the field name suggests. It is now
  a Car / Truck / Motorcycle setting the user picks in Vehicle Information, using the segmented row
  the wireless and dark-mode screens already use, backed by a preference included in settings
  backups.
- The microphone setting overrides that choice to motorcycle while the microphone is off, and the
  override is required rather than a convenience: Android Auto aborts connection setup with
  "No audio/mic" when a head unit announces no microphone service under any other vehicle type, so
  withholding the service and claiming a motorcycle only work together. A banner on the screen says
  so, because the picker would otherwise show a value that never reaches the wire.
- Withholding the service replaces declining requests. Gearhead 17.5.663204 ships two car services
  and both emit No audio/mic, which is why this has been read two different ways. Ljon;->run() tests
  Liwz;->c, written from the audio-source submessage of our own ServiceDiscoveryResponse and so null
  exactly when we omit the service, with a vehicle type of motorcycle as the only escape and a
  separate No audio playback service gate for the sinks. Lqso;->c() fires the same string when all
  three audio sink slots are null and reads neither the microphone nor the vehicle type. Nothing
  static says which one runs, so the claim goes out either way: it is required under one and inert
  under the other.
- The separate phone-microphone decision in Lwxq;->a() is a conjunction whose first term is a strict
  CarInfo->r == 3, so on a car the microphone list is never even queried. A head unit that advertises
  a microphone and then refuses every request leaves the assistant waiting on a stream that never
  arrives, and a round measured exactly that: the vehicle type reached the phone and was stored as
  motorcycle, and the phone still built the car recorder, asked for the microphone, took no bytes and
  stopped.
- Per-type identity: each announced type now carries its own vehicle id. The phone keeps two
  separate lookups and only one of them carries the vehicle type. The reconnect lookup logged as
  getCarInfoInternal for BT device is SELECT * FROM allowedcars ORDER BY connectiontime DESC with a
  Java-side first match on the Bluetooth address, no WHERE and no LIMIT, and it never reads the
  announced id; it feeds wireless setup. The type comes from Ljoh;->run(), keyed on manufacturer,
  model, modelyear and a hash of the vehicle id, and the stamp of stored type over declared type
  happens only when that lookup hits. A different id misses it, so the claim survives.
- The hash is base64(SHA-256(vehicle_id + android_id + our TLS certificate subject)), so the id is
  the only one of the three inputs we control. Without the split a head unit that had ever connected
  as a car would keep arriving as a car, and turning the microphone off would stop it connecting.
  Both earlier rounds hid this by clearing the phone's record between arms.
- A car keeps the id the user set, so nothing changes for a head unit that never claims another type.
  The cost is one consent prompt per type the user tries and one companion-app entry each.
- Known limit, stated in the settings copy and in the log line: Android 10 and older never write the
  column, so the value survives the first session only. There is no way to detect the phone's version
  from here, and the consequence is only certain on the newer car service, so both say may rather
  than will.
- Copy: the two microphone strings were wrong in both halves. They told the user Android Auto is
  still told a microphone exists "because it refuses to connect otherwise" and that the voice
  assistant "will not answer". Hardware round 2 disproved both, since the service is withheld and the
  assistant answered a spoken navigation query through the phone's own microphone, and through a
  helmet intercom paired to the phone. The new copy says what happens instead and carries the
  Android 11 requirement the stored vehicle type depends on. Nothing is said about calls; that was
  not tested.
- Also corrects four comments that described the wrong mechanism. The claim that omitting the service
  is safe because the required-service check reads only audio sinks came from the newer audio stack,
  which never looks at the microphone. Round 1 moved 327680 bytes through a working car microphone
  recorder, which that stack cannot do, so the older one is live and it does check.
- Recorded on the way and written down nowhere else: the system sink is accepted only if it offers a
  16 kHz mono configuration, and with the audio sink off it is the only sink left. Anything else in
  that config empties the endpoint list and does end the session, which is what the comment about
  keeping the connection alive was recording without knowing it.

- The nine strings this work added or rewrote now ship in all twenty language directories rather
  than English only, in step with the rest of the settings screens.

Hardware round 3 measured this on a UNISOC MT50 with a Motorola edge 30 neo, Android Auto
17.5.663204, without ever forgetting the car on the phone. First compile of the branch was clean at
906 tests and 0 failures. Turning the microphone off inserted a second record as a motorcycle, the
session formed with no No audio/mic, and the recorder moved to the phone with zero CarMicRecorder.
Turning it back on announced the base id, hit the car row and came back as a car throughout: full app
rail, a car puck on the map and four CarMicRecorder constructions. The riding configuration ran with
the audio sink off as well, took the assistant over a helmet intercom, and survived a disconnect and
reconnect.

WiFi Direct: a channel request nobody answers must not wedge the group

#907: Native AA never connected on a Qualcomm sm6150 unit on API 28. The
phone's Bluetooth socket was accepted and the handshake then sat on
SSID=<null>, IP=<null> until the phone redialled, over and over.

Below Android 10 the only way to ask for a band is the hidden
setWifiP2pChannels, and on that driver applying it reloads the P2P
interface: the pending ActionListener is dropped and neither onSuccess nor
onFailure ever arrives. standardCreateGroup() is reachable only from that
callback, so createGroup was never called at all - 4127 attempts in the
reporter's log, no success, no failure, and no p2p-wlan0 interface.

The reload also raises WIFI_P2P_STATE DISABLED then ENABLED within
milliseconds. The receiver read that as the user toggling WiFi Direct,
cleared isGroupCreatingOrCreated, and started another bring-up, which
reloaded the interface again: ~45 iterations a second on the main thread
for as long as the mode was on, wiping credentialsEpoch each time. That is
why no group ever formed and why the log lost 81% of its lines to chatty.

- WifiP2pChannelCompat bounds the wait at 2s. Its contract already said
  onResult must run on every path; a platform that never calls back is now
  one of them, and group creation falls through to the driver's own choice.
- P2pStateChangePolicy tells our own interface reload from a real toggle
  off one timestamp, so there is no latch to leak if a bring-up never
  reports an outcome.
- legacyChannelAttempt is no longer reset in startNativeAaQuietHost().
  The handshake calls triggerWifiDirectRefresh() every ten seconds while it
  waits, and each one landed back there, so rung 1 was the only rung the
  ladder ever tried.

The pre-Q ladder arrived in 3.3.0-beta1; v.3.2.6 and v.3.3.0-alpha go
straight to createGroup and do not carry this.

Native AA hotspot: record that no access point is up, don't just log it

#907's second log: the hotspot route waited on credentials that never came,
because no access point existed at all. The resolve loop said so - "No
usable access point after 30s. Turn this device's hotspot on before
connecting" - exactly once per run, into a log the unit was dropping faster
than the user could export it. Every trace of the one line that named the
problem was gone by the time the capture was attached, and nothing anywhere
else carried it.

The commonest way this route fails also had no durable surface.
HOTSPOT_CONFIG_UNREADABLE covers an access point that is up but will not be
named; there being no access point raised nothing, so the main-screen
banner stayed silent about it.

- ConnectionIssue.HOTSPOT_NOT_RUNNING, raised where the budget is reported
  and retired where credentials publish. Switching the hotspot on disproves
  it, so it needs no remedyApplied entry.
- The log line repeats on a 60s cooldown instead of once per run, so a
  capture taken minutes into the attempt still carries it.

triedAutoEnable stays once per run. Re-arming it on refresh is what put two
start sweeps on a slow access point at once, and that is a worse failure
than a second attempt is a fix.

USB: identify a phone by its descriptors, and let the user veto a device

Three things, one component.

The diagnostic. Every trigger now logs the raw device list with each device's
descriptors, endpoints and the verdict, so a report of "it sees nothing" can be
told apart from "it sees the device and refuses it". An empty bus says so in the
user's terms rather than printing nothing at all. The verdict a path prints is the
reason it refused rather than the descriptor check alone, which answers "accepted"
for a device the user has vetoed and left the same phone logged two opposite ways
in the same second.

The predicate. UsbDeviceIdentityPolicy replaces an inline check that accepted any
vendor-class interface, which is also what a USB ethernet controller presents: a
dock NIC was "accepted: AOAP" and auto-connected to. It is now rejected on the CDC
siblings in its composite enumeration and on the device class in its vendor-only
one, and it alternates between the two within a single replug. The network veto
keys on the CDC control subclass, ECM/EEM/NCM/MBIM, rather than on the CDC classes
themselves: a phone in file transfer can ship a CDC ACM pair whose data interface
is byte-identical to an adapter's, and only the control subclass separates a
serial port from a NIC. A billboard device, the alt-mode announcer inside every
USB-C dock, is named as such rather than falling through. The policy is pure, and
both descriptor forms of the adapter and every USB mode of two handsets are
fixtures.

The blacklist. It used to be consulted in one of seven paths that act on a device,
and skipped entirely when the user had not unlocked, so a blacklisted device was
still connected to, and the device list rendered a row "Blacklisted" in red and
started it anyway. One gate now, UsbDeviceCompat.isConnectable, used by the USB
button, the service scan, the attach listener, UsbAttachedActivity and the list's
own start button, with the list mirrored to device-protected storage the way the
auto-start settings already are. The key is manufacturer plus product rather than
VID:PID, because a phone's numbers change with its USB mode and its strings do
not; a device with no string descriptors falls back to the numbers, which is all
it had.

Measured on a phone host with a second phone, a dock, a flash disk and a Bluetooth
dongle: the adapter rejected in both enumerations with no auto-connect, phones
accepted in every mode including a full projection session over the accessory
link, and no system dialog for the Bluetooth dongle. One entry keyed on the name
covers the six VID:PIDs that handset presents across its USB modes, the accessory
one included, which the numeric key missed outright; a list written by an older
build still matches on the numbers; and taking a device back off the list returns
it to a full session.

Direct Boot: the app crashed before the user's first unlock

Every locked-boot entry point OHU has was dead. Plugging a phone at the lock
screen started UsbAttachedActivity, and Application.onCreate took the process
down before the activity's own onCreate ran:

  java.lang.IllegalStateException: SharedPreferences in credential encrypted
  storage are not available until after user is unlocked
      at utils.Settings.getPrefs(Settings.kt:36)
      at utils.Settings.getDebugForceMemoryProfile(Settings.kt:402)
      at AppComponent$videoDecoder$1.invoke(AppComponent.kt:20)
      at decoder.video.VideoDecoder.<init>(VideoDecoder.kt:323)
      at AppComponent.<init>(AppComponent.kt:19)
      at App.onCreate(App.kt:46)

The object graph is not buildable before the first unlock: AppComponent builds a
VideoDecoder whose field initialisers read the memory-profile override and the
fps limit, both of them credential-encrypted. App.onCreate touched that graph
twice above its own isUserUnlocked() guard, once for the root executor and once
for the three notification channels. So the device-protected mirror, the
directBootAware receivers and the auto-start-on-boot path were all dead weight:
the code that reads them is correct and was never reached. Measured on a phone
host, three crashes in one boot, one from a boot receiver and two from the plug
enumerations.

Nothing in onCreate touches the graph now. The channels take their manager from
the system service, and everything needing credential storage moved into
initUnlockedOnce(). A locked start registers for ACTION_USER_UNLOCKED and runs it
there instead, because the process outlives the lock screen and would otherwise
spend the rest of its life on defaults: no log level, no theme, and the
auto-start mirrors never written.

The four callers behind it are guarded the same way, each having reached either
the graph or a service that would build it. UsbAttachedActivity still refuses a
blacklisted device and still performs the accessory-mode switch while locked,
which is the whole reason it is directBootAware, but leaves the session for after
the unlock. The WiFi and Bluetooth auto-starts defer, and BootCompleteReceiver
already re-runs the WiFi one on ACTION_USER_UNLOCKED; a Bluetooth event that
arrives at the lock screen is not replayed, so that phone has to reconnect.

USB: stop Android offering us as the handler for every device on the bus

usb_device_filter.xml was <usb-device />, so the OS proposed Open Headunit for
anything attached. Measured on hardware in the diagnostics round: a plain USB
flash drive and a Bluetooth audio dongle each raised the system dialog, and one
hub session produced 7 confirm dialogs, 10 permission dialogs and 3 resolver
dialogs. The user-curated blacklist cannot help, because it runs inside the app
after the prompt it was added to suppress.

The entries are now the descriptor triples UsbDeviceIdentityPolicy accepts. The
two have to stay in step: broader here and the OS launches us for a device we
then reject, narrower and a device we would accept never auto-starts. Kept in
its own commit so it can be bisected away from the predicate change.

The objection to narrowing, raised on the tracker, is that an unlisted phone
then needs an app update. That is true of a VID/PID allowlist and not of this.
Android's DeviceFilter checks the device descriptor and then falls through to
every interface descriptor, identically from android-6.0.1_r1 to main, so an
entry with no vendor-id is a descriptor test rather than a vendor allowlist.

The case for it is the dialog, not protecting the peripheral. Nothing in either
tracker or in AOSP describes the accessory probe damaging a non-phone.

Two costs, both accepted deliberately:

- A USB ethernet controller carries the accessory triple on its control
  interface and will still raise the dialog. The manifest can express neither
  the interface name nor the CDC siblings, so this is as far as it reaches; the
  policy is what stops us connecting to one.
- A device that no longer matches loses the "always open" checkbox, because
  UsbDialogHelper.canBeDefault() parses this same file.

The vendor-class entry is the one that must not be dropped as too loose. A
phone in charging-only or file-transfer mode presents FF/FF/00 and nothing
else, so removing it would break the commonest way a phone is plugged in. Every
USB mode of a motorola edge 30 neo was swept on hardware to establish that.

The accessory PID set stays at 2D00 and 2D01, matching the policy. Widening it
to the AOSP set widens both together.

Native AA: say so when a unit will not host a WiFi Direct group

A head unit that refuses group creation outright had nothing anywhere to
say so. The terminal branch logged one line and cleared a latch, the main
screen stayed blank, and the phone sat on a loading screen while the head
unit retried into a log nobody reads from the driver's seat.

Measured on the reporter's Qualcomm sm6150 unit on API 28, comparing
v3.3.0-beta2 with v3.3.0-beta3:

- The bring-up loop that beta3 fixed is gone: 4127 createGroup attempts in
  92 s became 27 in 143 s. Because it is gone the platform finally answers,
  and beta3 is the first capture that contains any verdict at all. It is
  BUSY, on all 27 attempts, and createGroup never once succeeds.
- No group means no SSID, passphrase or address, so all ten handshakes read
  SSID=<null>, IP=<null> and not one byte of the wireless setup exchange is
  ever written. That is what the phone is waiting for.
- The unit's wlan0 is an associated station on another network for the whole
  capture. That is the commonest shape of this refusal and has never been
  measured as its cause, so the new line describes it and does not prescribe,
  as StationCoexistencePolicy already does for the coexistence case.

ConnectionIssue.WIFI_DIRECT_GROUP_REFUSED is raised where the ladder gives up
and cleared where a group forms, which is the only thing that disproves it.
No remedyApplied entry, for the same reason HOTSPOT_NOT_RUNNING has none: no
setting reaches a radio's refusal, so hiding the banner on a typed value
would hide a condition still exactly as true as it was. The report carries a
60 s cooldown because the ladder gives up several times a minute and each
report re-stamps the record, which is what brings the banner back after a
dismissal; without it the banner could not be dismissed at all.

setWifiP2pChannels now reports whether the platform answered at all, not just
whether it applied. A refusal arrives immediately and asking again is free; a
platform that never calls back costs the 2 s timeout on every bring-up and
cannot give a different reply. On this unit that was 25 timeouts, roughly a
third of the capture. The rest of the session now goes straight to creating
the group on the driver's own channel. stop() still clears the restriction
unconditionally: a request that never answered may still have been applied.

The session banner printed helperConnectionStrategy for every mode. Native AA
reads nativeApStrategy and consults the helper's selector nowhere, so a Native
capture opened with a value nothing in that mode uses, and a header could not
tell a WiFi Direct failure from a hotspot one. It now prints the selector the
reported mode actually reads. HotspotManager's missing-permission warning also
said "cannot enable" on the disable path, which is where it fired here.

Native AA: answer the wireless-setup dial over TCP

The phone dials the head unit and expects it to be the TLS client, so a session can start without Bluetooth carrying the exchange.

WiFi Direct: pin the 5 GHz channel, and put a hotspot back on exit

The platform's own pick rolled onto a channel the phone would not follow, and a user's own access point was left switched off.

WiFi Direct: derive the BSSID from the interface's own address

The phone rejects credentials carrying a masked BSSID, and this route reads a real one without privileged permissions.

Native AA: complete the hands-free link, and show the setup QR

The phone starts wireless setup only once the profile actually connects; the QR provisions the same record directly.

WiFi Direct: say where the BSSID came from, and stop claiming none can read it

The preflight reported no source on units that had one, which sent users after a fault they did not have.

Self Mode: watch for the call cover instead of requiring one up front

Demanding it before the session started shut out units that raise the cover late.

WiFi Direct: stand the station down for the bring-up, and count its scans

A joined station can starve the group of channels, and its own scans show up in the log as link gaps.

WiFi Direct: keep the group's name and passphrase, and measure its address

A new network on every create makes every reconnect a first-time join; whether the address repeats is a per-unit fact.

Native AA: offer the TCP endpoint on WiFi Direct once the address has repeated

A moving BSSID leaves the phone looping on a network it cannot find, with no fallback.

Native AA: keep the group across a session that ends on its own

Recreating it invalidates the profile the phone saved and pays for a full first-time join again.

Native AA: claim the group create early, and drop credentials on every teardown

A second create chain formed underneath the first, and three teardown paths removed a group without telling anyone.

Native AA: send the credentials that are live when the handover is written

The exchange wrote a snapshot taken a second earlier, which can name a group that is already gone.

Native AA: leave a group that is still coming up alone

A paired device arriving, or a P2P state change during the stand-down, started a second bring-up over the first.

WiFi Direct: name a P2P stack that another app is cycling

Every create is refused while that continues, and the log said nothing about why.

Bluetooth auto-start: make it general, not WiFi-only

Self Mode and the non-Native wireless modes never armed when a paired device arrived, and a group that was already up was torn down to re-arm.

Bluetooth auto-disconnect: end the session when a chosen device leaves

A parked unit stayed projecting with nobody in it; the watched list is separate from the wake list, and nothing fires inside a session's first minute.

Bluetooth auto-start: leave Self Mode alone in Native mode

A Native unit forced a Self Mode launch that cannot win, and the poke's own
socket.connect() raises the ACL that triggers it.

Self Mode: a launch that fails is not a session that ended

Running out of launchers reported a user exit, which latched userExitedAA and
left isActive set to poison the next session.

Audio sinks: ask the session whether Self Mode is the transport

A failed Self Mode launch left its flag set, so a wireless session announced
system sounds only.

Bluetooth: separate auto-start from the wake poke target

One list was both, and a completed handshake wrote itself back into it, so
clearing auto-start undid itself on the next poke cycle.

WPP over TCP: bind port 5299 the way 5288 is bound

The control channel is held open all session, so the port is in TIME_WAIT at
the next bring-up and the plain constructor threw EADDRINUSE.

Native AA: apply a transport change to the running stack

Saving the transport wrote the setting and re-armed nothing, so a unit set to
the hotspot kept hosting a P2P group and the setup QR refused as WiFi Direct.

Native AA: let this unit's Bluetooth address be supplied

The setup QR read the adapter directly, which Android masks, and the stored
address had no row left to set it in. It now takes the stored value first, the
settings row is back and says where to find the address, and a failed read says
which source answered what.

Connection: re-arm the disconnect scope and name a starved link

A service destroy left CommManager's scope cancelled for the whole process,
silencing every later disconnect. A starved-session streak now raises a banner.

Wireless: ask for less on a 2.4 GHz-only radio

With no 5 GHz band the video profile is capped to 720p30, switchable off, and
hotspot bring-up waits for the radio instead of sleeping at it.

Translations: add the seven strings missing from every locale

The later commits on this branch added them to values/ only, so all 20
locale files now carry them.

feat(native-aa): open the FYT module channel without root where possible

same: run the bridge's copy loop with sh as this app, and fall back to

  persistent or unreadable go to the root guard, which checks the
  process itself.
- Before falling back, wait for the no-root shell to exit by itself so
  its trap stops its reader and restores the tty mode. If it has to be
  killed, open nothing more until the carrier restarts.
- A closed channel drops lines its reader is still draining.
